Still waiting for tech like the Vision Pro, but in normal everyday glasses and sunglasses? The industry leader in AR glasses shipments has something to say.

The best Apple accessories share a distinct DNA: immaculate industrial design, lightweight ergonomics, tactile physical precision, and friction-free performance that feels native from minute one. Launched globally this fall, the RayNeo GT Max and RayNeo iO pair premium materials and bleeding-edge optics with the one thing Mac and iPhone owners actually want from a display accessory — plug it in, and it works.

RayNeo isn’t a small player making a big claim here. The company took the No. 1 spot in global AR smart glasses shipments across the first half of 2026, with 24.8% market share according to IDC and 23.9% according to Counterpoint Research.

Its Black Friday and Cyber Monday sale is live now through November 30, with the flagship GT Max at $335 (down from $429), the lighter GT at $249 (down from $329), and the camera-free iO smart glasses at $389 (down from $499). Everything is available on RayNeo.com and Amazon US.

Watching a movie on your iPhone is convenient, but craning your neck for a comfortable view is hardly cinematic. Having a premium AR display in sunglasses form, without packing a bulky mixed-reality headset or computing puck, opens up entirely new possibilities.

The RayNeo GT Max and RayNeo GT connect to your device over a single USB-C cable. Instead of clunky goggles, the GT Series puts a massive virtual display — 59 degrees of field of view on GT Max, to be exact — into a sleek, understated sunglasses design that blends into coffee shops and airport lounges at just 68 to 78 grams. That single USB-C connection carries uncompressed video and powers the glasses directly: no secondary battery packs to carry, no charging anxiety, and zero wireless lag.

One thing to check before you buy: the glasses need a device that outputs video over USB-C (DisplayPort Alt Mode). That covers the iPhone 15, 16 and 17 series, Macs from 2015 onward with USB-C, iPad from the 10th generation on, and USB-C handhelds like the Steam Deck. The iPhone 16e, 17e and iPhone Air have USB-C ports but don’t output video over them, so they aren’t supported. Consoles and older Lightning devices need RayNeo’s HDMI adapter.

Both GT Max and GT use dual 1080p Micro-OLED panels, delivering a Full HD image to each eye with ultra-smooth 120Hz refresh rates in 2D mode. GT Max adds 38 pixels per degree, 98% DCI-P3 cinematic color coverage, and TÜV Rheinland triple eye-comfort certification. Each model offers three selectable virtual screen sizes, depending on how immersed you want to be:

GT Max’s wider field of view provides a more expansive picture, while GT offers a featherweight design. For travel, the appeal is simple: an immaculate 307-inch personal theater that slips right into your daily bag alongside your Apple gear.

The GT Series also functions as an instant, private external display for a USB-C Mac. That makes the glasses invaluable far beyond streaming media, especially when you need an expansive, shoulder-surfer-proof dual-monitor workspace on a flight, train, or co-working desk.

Both GT and GT Max include three native 3DoF hardware display modes, meaning you can position your virtual screen around your head:

Because the tracking runs on dedicated silicon inside the glasses, none of it taxes the Mac or iPhone you’re plugged into. The glasses draw minimal power directly from the connected device and include a four-speaker spatial acoustic array co-tuned by Bang & Olufsen, with a directional Whisper Mode that cuts sound leakage on a plane or in an office.

GT Max also comes in three sizes based on inter-pupillary distance (IPD) — small for under 64mm, medium for 64–67mm, large for over 67mm — ensuring a tailored, comfortable fit.

If an everyday display frame came out of Cupertino today, it would look like RayNeo iO. Rather than heavy visors, iO pairs with your iPhone through the RayNeo app to project glanceable, contextual intelligence into genuine everyday eyewear.

iO uses a high-efficiency binocular MicroLED optical engine to float high-contrast green text into your sightline, presenting a virtual image equivalent to a 33-inch screen viewed from two meters away. With peak eye-level brightness rated at 1,300 nits, reading notes and prompts stays crystal clear even under direct midday sun without occluding your real-world surroundings. The waveguide is 97% transparent and the optical engine is hidden inside the frame, so from the outside these read as ordinary glasses — most people never clock them as smart eyewear at all.

For presentations and pitches, the built-in teleprompter scrolls your notes in sync with your natural speaking cadence, so you keep your eyes locked on your audience instead of looking down at your phone. During face-to-face meetings or international travel, the glasses deliver live subtitles and two-way translation right on the lenses, with support for 55 languages and 109 accents at roughly one second of latency.

Beyond live translation and teleprompting, RayNeo iO acts as a constantly evolving heads-up companion. RayNeo pushes frequent over-the-air (OTA) software updates, continually expanding what the glasses can do throughout your day.

Just now coming to iO is heads-up turn-by-turn navigation, which projects glanceable directional arrows, street names, and real-time transit alerts directly into your line of sight. Whether you’re walking through a new city or cycling down busy streets, you can navigate without holding your iPhone in front of you or looking down at your wrist. Alongside navigation, regular software updates continue to introduce new lifestyle tools, customizable notification filters, and contextual dashboard widgets that keep the hardware feeling fresh.

There’s more coming in December, too: RayNeo is opening the iO SDK to the public, so third-party apps — and community-built ones from people with no development background — start landing on the platform shortly after the holidays.

A four-microphone array with a bone-conduction sensor captures clear audio for automated meeting minutes and AI summaries that extract key action items. RayNeo V1 and Google Gemini 3.1 Flash Lite are built in and free out of the box — no subscription required for everyday voice response, contextual reasoning, and ambient assistance. On the temple, an intuitive Smart Crown lets you scroll notifications and highlight key moments with familiar, physical micro-precision.

The titanium frames weigh just 33 grams and are rated IP54 for dust and water resistance, with a battery good for up to two days of typical use, 6.2 hours of continuous live translation, and a 25-minute charge to 80%.

#3147. Three Reasons Not to Use ‘Buy Now, Pay Later’ During Black Friday

Gone are the days of needing to wait until after Thanksgiving to shop some seriously substantial Black Friday sales. As you're adding item after item to your cart during the sale, you might be tempted by offers for an "affordable monthly payment system." Also known as "buy now, pay later" (BNPL), the pitch is a tempting one: Buy what you need now, and pay later, "on your own timeline." But as convenient as it sounds, you should think twice before using buy now, pay later options, whether during Black Friday, Cyber Monday, or at any other time.

While BNPL plans can allow you to pay for purchases in installments without interest, they come with a cost that can easily outweigh any big discounts. Let's take a look at the hidden costs of BNPL, and why you're better off paying upfront for all your Black Friday purchases.

To be clear, Amazon doesn't have its own buy now, pay later program, and the company is not uniquely misleading on this front. The process is straightforward: you choose your items, select Affirm (a third-party lender) at checkout, complete a quick application, and receive an instant decision on your loan terms. Individual transactions initiated through Affirm are limited to $25,000, with a daily maximum of $100,000 across multiple purchases—but of course, your Black Friday splurge will be nowhere near that big, right? (Right?!)

The main draw of these programs is the ability to "pay at your own pace." If you are required to pay a down payment, that is due at the time of the transaction. From there, your first monthly payment is usually due one month after your purchase is processed. Each following payment will be due one month later, on the same day of the month.

You can choose your own timeline, usually spanning 3, 6, 12, or 24 months, depending on the purchase amount and your creditworthiness. Unlike traditional credit cards, Affirm shows you the exact payment amount and total cost upfront, and claims no hidden fees or compound interest.

You need a separate Affirm account in addition to your Amazon Prime membership. The application process requires basic information, including your name, mobile phone number, date of birth, and the last four digits of your Social Security number. Affirm performs a soft credit check initially, which doesn't impact your credit score, though they may conduct a hard inquiry for some loans.

BNPL plans are helpful if you really need to finance something big, but whenever possible, it’s best to avoid taking on debt for everyday expenses.

The ease of this sort of financing can make expensive purchases feel more affordable than they actually are. When you can buy a $1,000 tablet for "just $67 per month," it's easy to lose sight of the total cost, as well as your overall financial picture. In turn, this makes it all too easy to overspend on items you might not have purchased otherwise. You're better off taking a breath, stepping away from your shopping cart, and setting alerts to be notified when a product hits a price you can stomach, at a time you can afford it.

Despite what you may have heard in the past, BNPL providers may report to credit bureaus, meaning your BNPL purchases can in fact affect your credit score. For instance, all Affirm payments (including on-time, late, and missed payments) are now reported to the credit bureau Experian. So if you miss payments or default on the installment plan, it will cause damage to your credit score—making it even harder to get approved for mortgages, auto loans, credit cards, and other financing down the road.

Still, not all BNPL providers report to credit bureaus or use the same type of credit check, so it’s important to understand the specific terms and practices of any service you’re considering.

When you use a credit card, you get valuable purchase protections like extended warranty coverage, price protection, and the ability to dispute fraudulent charges. BNPL plans generally don't come with these safeguards. This means you're on the hook if something goes wrong with your BNPL purchase and the retailer doesn't make things right. The smarter move is to only buy what you can afford during a sale, no matter how tempting those deals may seem.

Although installment plans are helpful if you really need to finance something major, it’s best to avoid taking on debt for everyday expenses. Better to wait for a good price for something you truly need and can afford to pay for right now.

If there's a big-ticket item on sale for Black Friday but it's still out of your budget, consider these two questions before you turn to BNPL through Affirm:

Is this really an essential purchase? BNPL should really only be used on completely necessary purchases that you can’t afford right now, but can afford in six weeks. On that note...

Will I be able to pay this off within six weeks? When a bigger payment gets broken down into smaller installments, you might find yourself overspending in the long run, because it "feels" like you can afford it. Stay on top of how much you’re actually spending—especially if you're considering multiple BNPL purchases—and how it will impact your overall budget going forward.

For more information about deals and discounts, keep an eye on all of Lifehacker's Black Friday coverage.

In short, yes, Black Friday still offers discounts that can be rare throughout the rest of the year. If there’s something you want to buy, or you’re shopping for gifts, it’s a good time to look for discounts on what you need, especially tech sales, home improvement supplies, and fitness tech. Of course, if you need to save money, the best way to save is not to buy anything.

Follow our Black Friday coverage for the latest and best deals our team finds. Another good tip is to only buy what you need. It sounds simple, but making a list of the things you want before jumping into a sale with millions of products helps you focus and make smarter decisions.

The best thing you can do is compare the prices with other retailers that have Black Friday sales. If that seems like too much work, you can just follow our Black Friday coverage (we're already doing all the searching and vetting for you). Some other tips are making sure you're not being sold an older or cheaper version and always reading reviews.

#3146. Will Siri AI threaten Apple’s environmental target, given Google and Meta admissions?

I think Apple can reasonably claim to be the leading tech giant when it comes to its environmental credentials. It has led the way with its use of renewable energy, made significant strides with carbon-neutral production, and removed plastic from all its packaging.

All of this could potentially be put at risk by the company’s ambitions for Siri AI, however, as Meta joins Google in admitting it is now unlikely to meet its own 2030 net zero promise, thanks to the huge power demands of the data centers powering its AI services …

Apple’s environmental record isn’t entirely perfect. For example, when it claimed that the Apple Watch Series 9 and Ultra 2 were carbon neutral back in 2023, that claim was described as “bogus,” with the EU banning Apple from repeating it. The company has also been criticized for pushing a relentless annual iPhone cycle, encouraging frequent upgrades.

Overall, however, Apple has first-rate credentials when it comes to the environment. It was way back in 2018 when the company hit its goal of running its own operations off 100% renewable energy. This includes all Apple facilities, from Apple Park through data centers to its worldwide retail store network.

I said at the time that using more environmentally friendly packaging should be the company’s next priority, and it has indeed made great progress with this over the years, succeeding in removing all plastic packaging earlier this year.

After its own operations, Apple set about trying to tackle the power usage of its manufacturing partners. Back in 2020, the company set a goal of having its entire supply chain be carbon neutral by 2030. Just four years later, Apple said it was 95% of the way there.

The company also helps fund and support a wide range of environmental initiatives around the world. Just a few examples include conservation in China’s national parks, environmental protection and carbon removal in Australia and New Zealand, and helping to fund the build-out of renewable energy capacity in India.

Potentially, however, the vast energy demands of the data centers powering AI services could put its 2030 goal at risk. Other tech giants have already admitted that it may lead them to fail to hit their own renewable energy promises.

Back in 2024, for example, Google CEO Sundar Pichai said that the AI boom was “challenging” to the company’s 2030 carbon-free goal. CNET reports that Meta is now also admitting that it may fail to hit the same target.

Meta’s data center and sustainability chiefs wrote that the company is “re-evaluating our timelines, sequencing, and interim milestones — including the 2030 timeframe for our net zero emissions goal and our near-term intensity targets.” In an emailed statement to CNET, a Meta spokesperson added, “We remain committed to net zero, but are re-evaluating the 2030 timeline.”

Notably, a lot of Siri’s most advanced AI capabilities are currently powered by Google’s Gemini models.

At the same 2024 event where Google expressed doubts, Apple reiterated its commitment to its 2030 target. Then-CEO Tim Cook repeated this assurance later the same year, although admitted it would be challenging.

More challenges, yes. But are we coming off the goal? No, definitely not. With more data centers, you use more renewable energy, and we’ve built that muscle now […] I feel very good about 2030.

In the company’s most recent environmental progress report, it said that it was was still using 100% renewable energy despite using over 2.5 billion kWh of electricity to power its data centers.

We’re proud that 100 percent of that electricity came from renewable sources including solar, wind, and low-impact hydropower. To cover our needs, we build our own renewable power projects and work with utilities to purchase clean energy from locally obtained resources. We’re staying at 100 percent even as Apple’s data center capacity continues to grow.

The same report said the company had achieved zero water use for cooling at its latest data centers.

At our three newest data centers, we use high-efficiency air-cooled chillers instead of water-cooled systems, resulting in zero water use for cooling.

However, the greatest challenge for Apple lies ahead. The reason that Google and Meta are now backtracking on their promises is that both companies now have massive AI capabilities. As yet, Apple does not.

What happens as Apple expands Siri AI capabilities as usage increases, and as the company moves into agentic AI features? Is it realistic for the company to maintain its 100% track record with vastly greater data center energy usage?

Greenpeace expressed its own doubts earlier this year.

“AI will be the defining test of Apple’s climate commitments,” spokesperson Avex Li says. “To preserve Tim Cook’s environmental legacy, the company will need to show that AI growth can be accommodated within its existing climate commitments through absolute emissions reductions, additional renewable energy investment, and longer-lasting products.”

Apple did not respond directly but merely pointed to its past statements and most recent environmental progress report.

I don’t doubt the company’s desire to maintain its track record, but if Apple does join the likes of Google and Meta in becoming a major AI player, sticking to its 2030 timing is going to become increasingly difficult.

Do you think Apple will succeed? Please share your thoughts in the comments.

#3144. How Often You Need to Order From Amazon to Make Prime Worth It

Black Friday isn't until Nov. 27, but Amazon's early Black Friday sales have been ramping up for several days. For frequent Amazon shoppers, Prime can quickly pay for itself—mostly thanks to the free shipping perk. But how does the math shake out if you aren't regularly ordering from Amazon? Is it worth signing up if you only shop during major sales?

Millions of Amazon Prime users currently pay $14.99 per month or $139 per year for their memberships—though other plans cost less if you qualify. For example, the Amazon Prime Student program allows young adults between the ages of 18 and 24 to get all of the Prime perks for half the cost—$7.49 per month or $69 annually.

If you’re on the fence about signing up for (or renewing) your Prime membership, here’s how to judge whether or not the benefits outweigh the $139 cost.

Here are the main perks of Amazon Prime that make it worth the cost for so many users.

Free two-day shipping on millions of items: This is the main draw of Prime. If you shop frequently on Amazon and want quick free delivery, the shipping perks alone may make Prime worthwhile. Prime members also get free same-day delivery on over 3 million items in eligible areas. The ultra-fast (and morally suspect) shipping usually costs $9.99 per order for non-members, though you can choose lower-cost or free shipping options if you're willing to place larger orders and wait longer to receive them.

Access to Prime Video: Prime includes unlimited streaming of movies, TV shows, and Amazon Originals. If you ask me, the content library isn’t as robust as Netflix or Hulu, but this is still an added value.

Other Prime benefits: You also get Amazon Music for streaming songs, Prime Reading for ebooks, magazines, and audiobooks; Prime gaming, free photo storage, and occasional exclusive discounts/deals.

Amazon Prime Rewards Visa card: Cardholders get 5% back on Amazon/Whole Foods purchases. Prime members who use this card extensively can earn rewards that offset the annual fee.

Number of users: Prime benefits can be shared with other members of your household. The more users, the more value per person.

Let's say you don't care about Prime Video, Amazon Music, or free e-books, and just want to know if you'll save money you would otherwise be spending on shipping.

For non-Prime members, Amazon requires a minimum order of $35 to qualify for free shipping on eligible items. The average shipping costs for non-members aren't publicly listed, and can vary by item and shipping speed, typically ranging from $5 to $10.

For our purposes, I messed around on my non-shared, non-Prime Amazon account to find an average shipping cost of around $6 per order (assuming the order total fell below the $35 threshold, of course). Of course, shipping costs will vary depending on the item and how quickly you want it, but let’s compare the cost to the appeal of Prime’s two-day shipping option. So, we have the cost of individual online orders (around six bucks) compared to the free delivery that comes with an $139 annual fee. This means the costs you’d save on shipping alone make Prime worth the cost as long as you place more than two dozen orders in a year.

In other words: The $139 annual fee pays for itself as long as you order from Amazon Prime at least twice a month.

Of course, this conclusion is strictly in terms of shipping costs. How it stacks up ethically is between you and the person in the mirror.

And then there's this important caveat: You can still get free shipping from Amazon without a Prime membership, provided your order has $35 or more of eligible items. However, this won't grant you Prime shipping speed—your order will typically take five to eight days to be delivered. But you can place fewer, larger orders and wait a little longer, and still never pay for shipping.

Also worth considering is how much of that membership cost you'll be able to recoup via exclusive Prime Day offers. During the sale, some items will be heavily discounted only for Prime members—but whether the Prime Day price is really a "deal" will vary greatly based on the item you're buying. Some of those "big discounts" aren't any greater than what the item typically sells for. The Prime Day price can even be higher than other sale prices throughout the year. That's why it's important to make sure what you're ordering is something you planned to buy anyway—and that the sale price is actually a true bargain—before you order.

The cost of a Prime membership is a solid value for anyone using Amazon 23 times per year or more—especially if you're also watching shows on Prime Video or purchasing something that is deeply discounted for Prime Day. But if you only shop on Amazon a few times a year and don't take advantage of Prime Day offers or the other benefits, then that $139 annual fee isn't necessarily paying for itself.

Of course, if you are interested in Prime Day bargains, you can always sign up right before the start of the sale and then cancel your membership after Prime Day is over—but Amazon doesn't always make it easy on you.

Yes, Amazon has Black Friday sales, and we vet our deals to make sure they’re the best ones. You can also refer to guides like our live blog that have already done all of the vetting for you. And if you have an Amazon Prime membership, make the most of it.

Nowadays, both large retailers and small businesses compete for Black Friday shoppers, so you can expect practically every store to run sales through Monday, November 30, 2026. The “best” sales depend on your needs, but in general, the biggest discounts tend to come from larger retailers who can afford lower prices: think places like Amazon, Walmart, Target, Best Buy, and Home Depot. You can find all the best sales from major retailers on our Black Friday coverage.

Yes. Walmart, Best Buy, Target, and Home Depot will all have in-store deals, some of which you might not find online, so if you're able to take a trip to your local retailer, keep your eyes open for different deals.

#3142. I Tried Building My Own Interactive World in Google Genie, but Real-Time AI Engines Aren't There Yet

David Nield is a technology journalist from Manchester in the U.K. who has been writing about gadgets and apps for more than 20 years.

He has a bachelor's degree in English Literature from Durham University, where he also spent a term as editor of the award-winning student newspaper Palatinate. His journalism career started in print media, where he contributed to and edited several technology magazines and bookazines sold in the U.K. and internationally. More recently, he has worked as a freelancer for some of the biggest technology publications on the web, covering everything from on-the-ground reporting about product launches, to detailed explainers and how-to guides on apps, gadgets, and platforms. His expertise covers broad areas of consumer tech, including smartphones, laptops, wearables, and AI.

Beyond the Gemini assistant, Gemini Notebook, and various other AI offerings, Google also develops Genie, a world-building engine intended to help you create immersive visual experiences and games using only text prompts. Think of them like AI videos you can interact with and move through.

With the recently launched Genie 4 update, this tool is purportedly even more powerful. It now allows you to request live edits (like "make it snow") and incorporate sound and dialog into your prompts. Google is also promising more realistic physics and natural movements in its renderings.

These promises point to the future of AI in all kinds of ways—from robotics to world sims—but the tool requires a lot of computing power, and access is limited for the time being. You can dive in now if you're on one of the Google AI Ultra plans ($99.99 or $199.99 a month), or join the waitlist if you're a Google AI Pro user ($19.99 a month). But if you've got access, is it worth the effort (and money)? I put it to the test.

It's no exaggeration to say you can build an entire virtual world in Google Genie. It's going to be a more basic, less developed, and more chaotic world than the one in, say, GTA 6, but you can do it. Think of it like generating an AI video from a prompt, but you can then walk through the video and go as deep as you like, taking turns along the way.

Everything is rendered in real time, at a resolution of 720p and at 24 frames per second. That's not to say the engine is storing a massive 3D map in memory, however—after a minute or so, it's going to start to forget the places you've already seen. And while the basic layout will stay fixed, you might notice disappearing trees or changing colors.

Google's official line is "visual details and object permanence can still shift or drift over time" in Genie 4, so it's a known limitation. The tool is presented as-is, with the intention to develop it further over time as models improve, and it's aimed at filmmakers, historians, designers, scientists, robotics engineers, and game developers. Or indeed, anyone who just wants to get lost in a world that isn't real.

Some of the demos you'll find as you step through the Genie 4 portal give you a great idea of the possibilities. There's a "Dino Field Guide" that, you guessed it, lets you wander safari-style through a prehistoric habitat. All the flora and fauna are neatly rendered, and you even get dinosaur quiz questions along the way—a nod to Genie's potential as an educational tool.

There's a "Villa Giallo" mini-game, which involves searching a haunted 1970s Italian villa and clicking on objects as you go; these objects act as clues to help you progress to the next room. I was also intrigued by a "White House: Code Red" experience that takes you into the West Wing during a "high-stakes national crisis." I couldn't quite figure out what the crisis was, but I definitely felt the highness of the stakes.

Someone's even built a "GTA 7" engine that drops you into a bright and vibrant cityscape. The slow speed and warped physics of the experience suggest Rockstar Games has nothing to worry about just yet—check out the disappearing cars and backwards-driving cops in the video above—but it's impressively detailed all the same, considering it all comes from a few text prompts.

Having checked out a few demos, I felt ready to put Genie 4 to the test myself. Eager not to infringe on any IP, I decided to generate a world where I wouldn't mind getting lost for a few minutes—somewhere I could get away from the stress of my day and enjoy some warmer weather.

I started with the prompt "Create a fully immersive, photorealistic 3D environment showing a pub in an English village in the middle of a hot and sunny day. The pub is surrounded by country lanes, old buildings, and woods, and a handful of villagers are walking around and drinking outside the pub. Use a first-person view and use a quiet background of birdsong and wind rustling in the trees."

It took a couple of minutes for my peaceful, idyllic world to be ready, and then I was immediately able to navigate through it using my keyboard and mouse. Once you're in your world, you are suggested certain prompts you can make use of, like strolling into the pub or getting the villagers to make a toast, and these worked well—evidence that your virtual world really is interactive (to a point).

Unsurprisingly, the usual AI video tells are in abundance: Everyone looks generic, the physics often go sideways, the text on signs is gibberish, and details don't remain fixed. Do a full 360-degree spin around, and you might find that not only have all the customers in the pub changed their appearance, but you're also at an entirely different pub.

The best feature is the ability to make real-time edits: I summoned both a storm and a cricket pitch with a few text prompts, though Genie decided to put a hut in the middle of the cricket pitch for some reason. I think I was most impressed by the moment when a cricketer walked past me and commented on the rain, providing hints of how this kind of tech could expand or augment games and virtual experiences in the future.

That said, even at v4 of Genie, this tech is still very much in the experimental stage, and while I can see the potential, it also shows just how difficult a task world-building is for an AI engine. Without 3D maps and proper physics engines as a foundation, you'll encounter a great deal of hastily rendered slop as you explore your environment. Even if you're a prompting pro, for the time being this is something to mess around with, rather than use in a practical way.

#3141. iOS 27 basically turns your iPhone and AirPods into an Apple Watch at the gym

GymKit has been one of Apple Watch’s smartest fitness features since it launched in 2017. Tap your watch to compatible gym equipment, and Apple Watch shares your heart rate while the machine sends back metrics like distance, incline, pace, and calories.

With iOS 27, Apple is expanding that idea beyond Apple Watch. I tested the new GymKit on iPhone and AirPods Pro 3 ($149, reg. $249) experience with a GymKit-compatible treadmill. It basically gives you the Apple Watch GymKit workout tracking experience, just without the watch. This could be useful in a lot of scenarios.

The setup is simple. I tapped my iPhone to the treadmill, picked Indoor Walk (Indoor Run is also offered), and started the workout from the treadmill. With GymKit, workout data is stored privately on iPhone and removed from the equipment.

Once the workout started, the treadmill received heart-rate data from AirPods Pro 3. Meanwhile, the Fitness app on iPhone received the treadmill’s distance, pace, incline, and calorie data. Treadmills know details that an iPhone and AirPods can’t know on their own, especially incline and precise belt distance.

As a side note: Apple Watch has more accurate treadmill workout tracking as part of watchOS 27. GymKit remains the gold standard for accurate data, though.

GymKit also avoids two awkward gym habits. You don’t need to hold the treadmill’s metal heart-rate contacts while jogging. You also do not need to wear a Bluetooth heart-rate strap.

AirPods Pro 3 become the heart-rate source (and likely your podcast or music audio source as well). iPhone becomes the workout computer, which you can monitor during your workout. And the treadmill fills in the machine data while providing the surface for walking or running.

Apple has been moving more fitness features onto iPhone for years. iOS first made the Fitness app useful without Apple Watch as Apple Fitness+ leaned into iPhone as an entry point. AirPods Pro 3 pushed that further as the first AirPods with heart-rate tracking, after Apple tested the idea with Powerbeats Pro 2.

iOS 27 brings those pieces together. GymKit on iPhone shouldn’t replace Apple Watch for people who wear one every day. Instead, it’s a great backup when your Apple Watch is dead, charging, or left at home.

It also gives iPhone and AirPods users a taste of the Apple Watch experience, which could attract future Apple Watch customers.

In testing with iOS 27 beta 1, my Exercise ring didn’t update as I worked out without wearing Apple Watch. But after I put my watch back on, the Exercise ring caught up, and the workout appeared in Fitness with the right data.

My sample 16-minute treadmill walk showed 0.66 miles, 65 active calories, 97 total calories, 32 feet of elevation gain, and a 115 BPM average heart rate, just like if I’d worn an Apple Watch.

I had been getting the impression that gym equipment manufacturers had been abandoning GymKit support - if they ever had done so initially. I even got the impression that the majority of equipment in Apple's own onsite Gym at the Apple Park may not have supported it - at least originally.

Does Apple have a webpage listing compatible brands and models? Like they do/did for HomeKit.

What is other people perception? Any rowing machines that support it?

…checks - surprisingly it looks like Peloton do support it on their bikes.

If I tried to use GymKit on iPhone without AirPods, the iPhone disconnected when the workout started because it had no heart-rate source. If I tried to start GymKit from iPhone while wearing Apple Watch, iOS pointed me back to the Workout app on Apple Watch instead, though you can continue without using the watch.

GymKit on iPhone is one of those iOS 27 features that sounds small until it solves a real problem. If Apple Watch is your default workout tracker, it probably stays that way.

But if your watch dies or you forget it at home, iPhone plus AirPods Pro 3 can now log a treadmill workout with real heart-rate data and real treadmill metrics.

#3139. Berkshire Hit a Record High While AI Power Stocks Sold Off. Here’s What That Says About Where Energy Money Is Going.

Berkshire Hathaway rose as stocks like Bloom Energy and Caterpillar dropped, suggesting safety is increasingly important.

By Reuben Gregg Brewer – Nov 24, 2026 at 6:42PM EST

10 stocks we like better than Berkshire Hathaway ›

Over the past three months, Berkshire Hathaway (BRKA +0.73%)(BRKB +0.85%) is up roughly 15% as of this writing. By comparison, Bloom Energy (BE -6.98%) and Caterpillar (CAT -1.17%), both headline-grabbing artificial intelligence (AI) energy plays, are down 29% and 38%, respectively. Investors aren't giving up on the companies that provide energy for AI, but they may be shifting toward more conservative investments. Here's what you need to know.

Artificial intelligence is really just a fancy computer program. Without electricity, it can't exist. But AI uses a tremendous amount of power, resulting in consumer backlash against the data centers that host it. This is why investors have been so attracted to Bloom Energy and Caterpillar.

Bloom Energy makes hydrogen fuel cells. These factory-produced items can be placed wherever they are needed to provide off-grid power. Caterpillar, while best known for its heavy earth-moving equipment, also makes generators that provide off-grid power. However, given the backlash against AI, investor enthusiasm for AI stocks has diminished, and these stocks have fallen alongside the broader AI trade despite still-high expectations for power demand.

Meanwhile, Berkshire Hathaway's shares have been on the rise. That is at least partly a flight-to-safety trade. Berkshire Hathaway is a giant conglomerate with businesses ranging from insurance to homebuilding, and much in between. It also has more than $370 billion in cash sitting on its balance sheet to cushion it against a market downturn. That cash also provides it with the ability to buy if a bear market opens up attractive investment opportunities.

That's a good start, but there's another small wrinkle here. Over the last three months, Southern Company (SO +1.07%), a large regulated U.S. utility, is up nearly 5%, and Kinder Morgan (KMI +1.67%), a large North American pipeline operator, is down just 2%. These businesses will both be integral to powering AI. They aren't as exciting as Bloom Energy or Cat, but that's the point right now. Investors are looking for a safe haven as AI enthusiasm hits a road bump and are shifting toward boring, reliable businesses.

Notably, Southern offers a reliable 3.2% dividend yield, while Kinder Morgan's yield is 3.9%. Berkshire Hathaway doesn't pay a dividend; however, two of its largest divisions are its utility and energy segments. Add that to the rest of the company's owned business portfolio and its large collection of publicly traded stocks, and you have diversification along with continued exposure to the growing demand for electricity. This is not a small matter, given that electricity demand increased by 10% between 2005 and 2025 and is projected to grow by 60% between 2025 and 2045.

Basically, Berkshire Hathaway could offer the best of both worlds. You own a diversified and financially strong company that is prepared to take advantage of a bear market. And you continue to have exposure to AI's growing appetite for power. All in one investment. Investors may not be dumping AI power companies; they may just be getting more selective and conservative.

The caveat here is that Berkshire Hathaway is now trading near all-time highs. However, the company has been buying back its own stock over the last two quarters, which it has historically done only when it believes the stock is trading below its intrinsic value. While it probably isn't fair to suggest Berkshire Hathaway is a deep-value opportunity, if you are looking for a safer way to play long-term energy demand from AI, the company itself thinks its stock is attractive. It's probably worth a deep dive, even if you only end up putting it on your wish list.

#3138. AI Is Giving Optical Computing Another Shot

The push to cut AI inference’s energy use could pay off in unexpected ways

Data centers already use light in networking. Startup Optalysis aims to use specially engineered waveguides to add computational capacity to the networking path, doing math while data is in transit.

The idea of computing with light has been around for over 70 years, but until recently it’s remained largely in the realm of research. Over the past few years, though, optical computing has emerged as a fast-growing industry: Market valuation of companies in this sector now totals US $2.22 billion, up from $0.4 billion in 2022. One projection suggests that the market will continue to grow exponentially in the coming years.

The reason for this sudden surge will surprise no one: AI. In particular, AI inference—the process of using AI models to respond to user queries—has driven much of the construction of huge, power-hungry data centers, and relatively energy-efficient optical systems are seen as a potential way forward.

“Most of the interest in [photonics] is driven by the fact that AI inference has literally become limited by power, and in a rather striking manner,” says Peter McMahon, associate professor of applied and engineering physics at Cornell University, in Ithaca, N.Y., who has researched optical computing for over a decade.

Optics, at least on paper, carries the promise of doing the same math as today’s GPUs at a drastically lower level of power. Switching from electronics to optics would be a pretty radical solution. Nevertheless, like mushrooms after a rainstorm, optical-computing startups are popping up in the United States, China, Germany, and Israel. And while competing against such GPU makers as Nvidia is an ambitious goal, the investment in optical computing has spurred development of complementary approaches, such as designing alternative AI algorithms, taking on scientific computing, and enhancing in-network computing.

Optalysys, based in England, is inserting optical-computing elements into the networking path, where data centers already use light. The company’s basic on-chip optical element, shown in the inset, is a Fourier transform calculator.Optalysys

“I think it would be good for the technology if many of these companies made a good run at it,” says Logan Wright, assistant professor of applied physics at Yale University, in New Haven, Conn., and a former postdoc in McMahon’s lab. “I think that the technology that will be developed through this would be really, really useful, and enable photonic systems that maybe don’t get on this wave of AI but would be capable of doing really quite special things.”

Inference makes up the bulk of AI energy use. The industry is already spending billions of dollars designing advanced GPUs and other chips to run inference as efficiently as possible. At the heart of the inference computation is one operation, done countless times a second: matrix-vector multiplication.

Back in 1978, optical-computing pioneer Joseph W. Goodman and his coworkers proposed a method for doing matrix-vector multiplication with light. The setup was relatively simple. Let’s say a vector of length N needs to be multiplied by a matrix of size N by N. N light-emitting diodes, all in a row, encode the elements of the vector into the intensity of light—the brighter the light from an individual diode, the greater the value that diode encodes. Then, a cylindrical lens spreads out the light vertically, essentially copying the vector N times. The light then passes through an attenuator of N by N pixels. At each pixel, the light is attenuated according to the corresponding value at that location in the matrix. Passing the light through the attenuator performs the multiplication. Finally, a cylindrical lens oriented perpendicular to the first lens re-collects the light from each row, summing it up. The final vector is measured by a row of detectors.

VECTOR-MATRIX MULTIPLICATION The most computationally expensive part of common AI today is vector-matrix (or matrix-matrix) multiplication. For a vector of length N (here, N = 3), it takes N2 (here, 9) multiplication steps and three accumulation steps—multiple additions at once. The argument for why optics might be advantageous over electronics goes something like this: Multiplying a matrix of size N by N by a vector of length N takes N2 multiplication steps. In electronics, each multiplication takes some energy, so the total energy used scales as N2. In optics, however, the multiplication step is passive: As long as the matrix stays the same, passing light through the attenuator costs almost no energy. The only cost is encoding the vector into light and reading out the answer, but the vector is of length N, not N2. So the energy used will scale as N, not N2, as bigger vectors and matrices are multiplied.Since Goodman’s 1978 proposal, the quality of the available optical elements has improved dramatically. Indeed, in 2022, a team of researchers at Cornell led by McMahon demonstrated an optical neural network that consumed less than one photon of energy—approximately 2.5 x 10-19 joules—per multiplication operation. In a standard computer, a single multiply operation can take between 10-14 and 10-12 joules, which suggests that optics could possibly reduce energy use by a factor of 100,000.But McMahon cautions against such extrapolation. First, the cost of encoding data into optics was not included in the calculation. Even if the scaling is favorable with light, in practice it’s not just the scaling that matters, it’s also the coefficients. Let’s say the energy cost of doing one multiplication with electronics is 1 picojoule, and the cost to encode one vector element with optics is 1,000 picojoules. The electronic approach still wins if the length N of the vector is fewer than 1,000 elements.McMahon says this example is not far off from reality: “One of the key questions is, How big do you have to make the system before you start winning? Lots of people have done this calculation for various kinds of neural networks. The very rough answer is somewhere between N equals 1,000 and N equals 10,000.”It’s also important to keep in mind a computing principle known as Amdahl’s law.“Amdahl’s law shouldn’t even be called a law. It’s a simple piece of common sense,” McMahon says. “If you have something that’s going to accelerate a computation, and it can accelerate 90 percent of the code, but there’s 10 percent of the code that it can’t accelerate, then the maximum possible speedup you can get is 10x.”With AI inferencing, the point is to save energy, not time. But Amdahl’s observation still applies. What fraction of today’s AI inferencing code can be better handled with optics is a complicated question that varies by approach. But it’s not 100 percent. Matrix-vector multiplication, or matrix-matrix multiplication, is only part of the inference workload—there are other, nonlinear operations that need to be performed on the data.Taking all of these caveats into account, optical-computing companies today are aiming for a 10- to 80-fold improvement in energy efficiency over today’s GPUs. The question is whether they can deliver on that promise at scale before traditional electronics catches up to those gains.Bridging the gap in free spaceThe startup Lumai, based in Oxford, England, has taken perhaps the most direct inspiration from Goodman and his team. Lumai’s head of product, Phillip Burr, declares that a free-space approach, where the light travels through air rather than on-chip waveguides, is what will enable the company’s tech to beat GPUs.Instead of the fixed attenuator used in Goodman’s proposal, Lumai is using a modern programmable device called a spatial light modulator—a pixelated membrane akin to a fancy liquid-crystal display that can modulate both the intensity and phase of light. The rest of the design is more sophisticated in practice but similar in principle to Goodman’s design: A vector is encoded into light, copied N times via a lens, passed through the spatial light modulator, collected with another lens, and the result is converted back to digital electronics. The electronics then handle the nonlinear functions. “A full vector-matrix multiply completes in a single optical cycle,” Burr says.To accurately compare the energy expenditures of the optical and GPU approaches, you must first specify which part of the workload you’re considering. Modern inference is often split into two phases: prefill, where the input query is processed and propagated through the model, and decode, where the output is generated one word (or token) at a time. Prefill is the more computationally intensive of the two. It basically involves doing vector-matrix multiplications for the same matrix over and over. Decode also involves vector-matrix multiplies, but not as intensively—the time-consuming part of decode is reading the necessary matrices in and out of memory. Vector-matrix multiplication with free-space optics Chris PhilpotThe Goodman optical computer is the simplest version of a photonic vector-matrix multiplier. Here, the vector elements are encoded into the intensity of light from three light sources, such as LEDs. Then, a cylindrical lens spreads the light vertically. The matrix elements are encoded into the opacity of an attenuator, such that when light passes through each pixel it is multiplied (attenuated) by that matrix value. Finally, another cylindrical lens collects the light horizontally, performing the accumulation step, and a photodetector measures the output vector. Lumai, and other companies in the space, are focusing on the compute-intensive prefill phase of inference. Lumai claims that its Iris Nova optical server, made available for evaluation in April 2026, is a proof of concept, and its next-generation Iris Aura server will do prefill using roughly one-tenth of the energy a GPU would use.The startup Neurophos, based in Austin, Texas, is putting a different spin on the Goodman computer design. To pack more punch into a small device, the company is leveraging its expertise in metamaterials—complex structures that can manipulate light at scales smaller than a single wavelength. The structures it has designed are bigger than a wavelength but still quite small—just several micrometers per side.“The equivalent of the optical transistor that you can get from standard silicon photonics today is like 2 millimeters long,” says Patrick Bowen, CEO of Neurophos. “You just can’t fit enough [of] them on-chip to get a compute density that remotely competes with the latest and greatest [that] TSMC [Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co.] does.”Based in Austin, Texas, Neurophos is using tiny metamaterials packed onto a chip to manipulate incoming light for efficient vector-matrix multiplication.NeurophosBowen’s team designed metamaterial-based modulators that can be programmed to manipulate the phase and intensity of light at the micrometer scale, resulting in an array of 1,000 by 1,000 modulators in a square chip with 5-mm sides. According to Bowen, Neurophos’s modulators switch over 10,000 times as fast as a standard liquid-crystal spatial light modulators do.Bowen also claims a performance advantage over Nvidia’s Blackwell GPU: “We’re targeting 50 times Blackwell B200’s speed and 35 times its energy efficiency, and have a road map to reach 250 times the speed and roughly 90 times the energy efficiency in subsequent generations.”The approach is CMOS-compatible, Bowen says, which should allow Neurophos to manufacture its chips on the semiconductor industry’s existing high-volume production lines. Larger models, longer context windows, and agentic workloads are all pushing prefill in that direction.”Bridging the gap on-chipFree-space optics carries the promise of almost energy-free multiplication, as in Goodman’s design. But another big advance in optics since Goodman’s work in the 1970s is integrated photonics, which allows you to guide and manipulate light on-chip.“The name of the game is to do as large a vector size as possible to maximize the benefit of using optics, and for that reason the free-space approaches are promising,” says Yale’s Logan Wright. “But it’s still fundamentally harder” to use the free-space approach, “because there’s just so much less infrastructure than in silicon photonics.”Other companies—like Shanghai-based Lightelligence and Q.ANT, based in Stuttgart, Germany—are trading the 3D advantage of free-space optics for the manufacturability of photonics integrated directly onto a silicon chip.“There is a good reason that free-space optics are usually limited to 1,000 units a year,” says Q.ANT’s CEO and founder, Michael Förtsch. “The reason for this is lens inspection, assembly strategy, and so on. Semiconductor-manufacturable integrated photonic circuits are at this point way more promising to reach volume production.” Vector-matrix multiplication with integrated photonics Chris PhilpotOne way to do vector-matrix multiplication with light on-chip involves encoding vector elements into the amplitudes of pulses of light, traveling sequentially through a waveguide. The multiplication is performed by Mach-Zehnder interferometers: A waveguide splits in two, and the phase of light traveling through one of the paths is shifted by a controlled voltage. When the two paths reunite, the resulting light intensity depends on that phase shift, performing a multiplication. Encoding the matrix elements into the phase shifts turns this into vector-matrix multiplication. A photodetector then collects the light from all three pulses, performing the accumulation step.

The most computationally expensive part of common AI today is vector-matrix (or matrix-matrix) multiplication. For a vector of length N (here, N = 3), it takes N2 (here, 9) multiplication steps and three accumulation steps—multiple additions at once.

The argument for why optics might be advantageous over electronics goes something like this: Multiplying a matrix of size N by N by a vector of length N takes N2 multiplication steps. In electronics, each multiplication takes some energy, so the total energy used scales as N2. In optics, however, the multiplication step is passive: As long as the matrix stays the same, passing light through the attenuator costs almost no energy. The only cost is encoding the vector into light and reading out the answer, but the vector is of length N, not N2. So the energy used will scale as N, not N2, as bigger vectors and matrices are multiplied.

Since Goodman’s 1978 proposal, the quality of the available optical elements has improved dramatically. Indeed, in 2022, a team of researchers at Cornell led by McMahon demonstrated an optical neural network that consumed less than one photon of energy—approximately 2.5 x 10-19 joules—per multiplication operation. In a standard computer, a single multiply operation can take between 10-14 and 10-12 joules, which suggests that optics could possibly reduce energy use by a factor of 100,000.

But McMahon cautions against such extrapolation. First, the cost of encoding data into optics was not included in the calculation. Even if the scaling is favorable with light, in practice it’s not just the scaling that matters, it’s also the coefficients. Let’s say the energy cost of doing one multiplication with electronics is 1 picojoule, and the cost to encode one vector element with optics is 1,000 picojoules. The electronic approach still wins if the length N of the vector is fewer than 1,000 elements.

McMahon says this example is not far off from reality: “One of the key questions is, How big do you have to make the system before you start winning? Lots of people have done this calculation for various kinds of neural networks. The very rough answer is somewhere between N equals 1,000 and N equals 10,000.”

It’s also important to keep in mind a computing principle known as Amdahl’s law.

“Amdahl’s law shouldn’t even be called a law. It’s a simple piece of common sense,” McMahon says. “If you have something that’s going to accelerate a computation, and it can accelerate 90 percent of the code, but there’s 10 percent of the code that it can’t accelerate, then the maximum possible speedup you can get is 10x.”

With AI inferencing, the point is to save energy, not time. But Amdahl’s observation still applies. What fraction of today’s AI inferencing code can be better handled with optics is a complicated question that varies by approach. But it’s not 100 percent. Matrix-vector multiplication, or matrix-matrix multiplication, is only part of the inference workload—there are other, nonlinear operations that need to be performed on the data.

Taking all of these caveats into account, optical-computing companies today are aiming for a 10- to 80-fold improvement in energy efficiency over today’s GPUs. The question is whether they can deliver on that promise at scale before traditional electronics catches up to those gains.

The startup Lumai, based in Oxford, England, has taken perhaps the most direct inspiration from Goodman and his team. Lumai’s head of product, Phillip Burr, declares that a free-space approach, where the light travels through air rather than on-chip waveguides, is what will enable the company’s tech to beat GPUs.

Instead of the fixed attenuator used in Goodman’s proposal, Lumai is using a modern programmable device called a spatial light modulator—a pixelated membrane akin to a fancy liquid-crystal display that can modulate both the intensity and phase of light. The rest of the design is more sophisticated in practice but similar in principle to Goodman’s design: A vector is encoded into light, copied N times via a lens, passed through the spatial light modulator, collected with another lens, and the result is converted back to digital electronics. The electronics then handle the nonlinear functions. “A full vector-matrix multiply completes in a single optical cycle,” Burr says.

To accurately compare the energy expenditures of the optical and GPU approaches, you must first specify which part of the workload you’re considering. Modern inference is often split into two phases: prefill, where the input query is processed and propagated through the model, and decode, where the output is generated one word (or token) at a time. Prefill is the more computationally intensive of the two. It basically involves doing vector-matrix multiplications for the same matrix over and over. Decode also involves vector-matrix multiplies, but not as intensively—the time-consuming part of decode is reading the necessary matrices in and out of memory.

The Goodman optical computer is the simplest version of a photonic vector-matrix multiplier. Here, the vector elements are encoded into the intensity of light from three light sources, such as LEDs. Then, a cylindrical lens spreads the light vertically. The matrix elements are encoded into the opacity of an attenuator, such that when light passes through each pixel it is multiplied (attenuated) by that matrix value. Finally, another cylindrical lens collects the light horizontally, performing the accumulation step, and a photodetector measures the output vector.

Lumai, and other companies in the space, are focusing on the compute-intensive prefill phase of inference. Lumai claims that its Iris Nova optical server, made available for evaluation in April 2026, is a proof of concept, and its next-generation Iris Aura server will do prefill using roughly one-tenth of the energy a GPU would use.

The startup Neurophos, based in Austin, Texas, is putting a different spin on the Goodman computer design. To pack more punch into a small device, the company is leveraging its expertise in metamaterials—complex structures that can manipulate light at scales smaller than a single wavelength. The structures it has designed are bigger than a wavelength but still quite small—just several micrometers per side.

“The equivalent of the optical transistor that you can get from standard silicon photonics today is like 2 millimeters long,” says Patrick Bowen, CEO of Neurophos. “You just can’t fit enough [of] them on-chip to get a compute density that remotely competes with the latest and greatest [that] TSMC [Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co.] does.”

Based in Austin, Texas, Neurophos is using tiny metamaterials packed onto a chip to manipulate incoming light for efficient vector-matrix multiplication.

Bowen’s team designed metamaterial-based modulators that can be programmed to manipulate the phase and intensity of light at the micrometer scale, resulting in an array of 1,000 by 1,000 modulators in a square chip with 5-mm sides. According to Bowen, Neurophos’s modulators switch over 10,000 times as fast as a standard liquid-crystal spatial light modulators do.

Bowen also claims a performance advantage over Nvidia’s Blackwell GPU: “We’re targeting 50 times Blackwell B200’s speed and 35 times its energy efficiency, and have a road map to reach 250 times the speed and roughly 90 times the energy efficiency in subsequent generations.”

The approach is CMOS-compatible, Bowen says, which should allow Neurophos to manufacture its chips on the semiconductor industry’s existing high-volume production lines. The company is currently choosing a site for a production facility ahead of its rack deliveries to customers in 2028.

Both Lumai and Neurophos are betting they’ll get their products to market before traditional CMOS can catch up to their energy savings. “Silicon will keep improving, but digital efficiency gains now come slowly and at rising cost,” Burr says. “Optics offers a different scaling relationship, in which efficiency improves as matrices grow. Larger models, longer context windows, and agentic workloads are all pushing prefill in that direction.”

Free-space optics carries the promise of almost energy-free multiplication, as in Goodman’s design. But another big advance in optics since Goodman’s work in the 1970s is integrated photonics, which allows you to guide and manipulate light on-chip.

“The name of the game is to do as large a vector size as possible to maximize the benefit of using optics, and for that reason the free-space approaches are promising,” says Yale’s Logan Wright. “But it’s still fundamentally harder” to use the free-space approach, “because there’s just so much less infrastructure than in silicon photonics.”

Other companies—like Shanghai-based Lightelligence and Q.ANT, based in Stuttgart, Germany—are trading the 3D advantage of free-space optics for the manufacturability of photonics integrated directly onto a silicon chip.

“There is a good reason that free-space optics are usually limited to 1,000 units a year,” says Q.ANT’s CEO and founder, Michael Förtsch. “The reason for this is lens inspection, assembly strategy, and so on. Semiconductor-manufacturable integrated photonic circuits are at this point way more promising to reach volume production.”

One way to do vector-matrix multiplication with light on-chip involves encoding vector elements into the amplitudes of pulses of light, traveling sequentially through a waveguide. The multiplication is performed by Mach-Zehnder interferometers: A waveguide splits in two, and the phase of light traveling through one of the paths is shifted by a controlled voltage. When the two paths reunite, the resulting light intensity depends on that phase shift, performing a multiplication. Encoding the matrix elements into the phase shifts turns this into vector-matrix multiplication. A photodetector then collects the light from all three pulses, performing the accumulation step.

In Q.ANT’s approach, the input data is encoded into the phase and amplitude of light pulses via on-chip modulators. A vector in this scheme is represented as a sequence of such pulses, each representing one vector element. The light is guided around the chip with waveguides. The basic computational element is an interferometer: A waveguide splits into two paths, and the light beam traveling down one path is subjected to a phase shift, controlled by a set voltage. When the two paths recombine, the resulting interference performs a computation. Then, photodetectors and analog-to-digital converters turn the result back into digital data. The serialized vector-matrix multiplication approach is slower than Goodman’s computer, where the whole calculation happens at once. However, the slower speed can be mitigated by using multiple wavelengths at once, effectively encoding multiple vectors into light simultaneously.

Q.ANT’s Native Processing Server is already being used in research institutions like the Leibniz Supercomputing Centre in Munich and the Jülich Supercomputing Centre in Jülich, both in Germany. Earlier this year, the company announced a commercial sale to the cloud provider Ionos. Similarly, Lightelligence’s PACE2 processor is capable of multiplying 128-by-128-element matrices. In a paper released in 2025, the company described vector-matrix multiplication at a 1-gigahertz frequency and 3-nanosecond latency, claiming two orders of magnitude lower latency than with traditional GPUs.

The energy advantage is yet to be conclusively demonstrated, however, and Q.ANT’s Förtsch admits there is still a ways to go. The main issue is the energy cost of analog-to-digital conversion and back. As long as a fast, low-energy converter does not exist, Förtsch says, “we don’t see realistic chances that…a general vector-matrix multiplication machine in optics makes sense.”

Not everyone in the field is focused on matrix-vector multiplication, despite it being all the rage in the AI inference world. In fact, while the optical vector-matrix multiply idea goes back to the 1970s, other computations with optics have been investigated as far back as the 1950s. For example, a Fourier transform—a common operation that decomposes a complex wave or signal into its constituent frequencies—can be done in optics with a single lens.

“A digital chip has to approximate [Fourier transforms] in many small steps, using hundreds to thousands of transistors and more compute cycles,” says Q.ANT’s Förtsch. “Models that use such nonlinear functions can reach the same or better accuracy with fewer parameters and fewer operations.”

Even though Q.ANT’s optical processor has been used for traditional vector-matrix multiplication, the company believes its greatest advantages lie in alternative AI architectures that leverage more complex functions. “Tasks such as image classification and segmentation rely heavily on operations like Fourier series, transformations, and other nonlinear functions, which photonics handles natively. We see similar potential in generative AI, especially image and video generation,” Förtsch says.

The Israel-based startup LightSolver is also targeting algorithms that are a more natural fit for its device. “If you look at propagating electromagnetic waves, essentially, they are running differential equations in their nature,” says Ruti Ben-Shlomi, CEO and cofounder of LightSolver. She says differential equations can be solved much faster and with higher energy efficiency on the company’s laser processing unit (LPU) than on a traditional computer.

LightSolver’s LPU is an interesting twist on the Goodman optical-computer design. It has input light, a programmable membrane in the form of a spatial light modulator, and output light, but the whole thing is placed in a cavity, where light bounces back and forth many times before reaching a steady state. In addition, the team places a gain medium inside the cavity. This gain medium functions much like those found inside a laser, causing the bouncing light to build up in intensity.

LightSolver, a startup based in Israel, is using free-space optics to quickly solve differential equations by harnessing the natural properties of light. LightSolver

LightSolver’s team is currently working on AI applications for its LPU as well, using the company’s own algorithm to do image generation from text. “We’re not doing vector-matrix multiplication very fast. We are doing something different. We need to assume that the way you train the model, and you then do inference, is completely different. But if you do it differently, you’ll be able to do image generation with dramatic energy-consumption decrease and speedup,” Ben-Shlomi says. LightSolver has a working prototype of its LPU, and the team is working on a larger, rack-mountable box.

Yet another way to leverage light’s particular strengths is being pursued by Optalysys, a startup based in Leeds, England. Nick New, founder and chief product officer, has a background in free-space optics, and so he understood that taking a Fourier transform is very easy to do with light.

The key idea behind Optalysys’s technology is taking that Fourier capability of optics in free space and making it work on-chip. “Rather than using a lens these days, we have our own component, which is a passive component in the plane of the silicon that does that same job,” New says. And by cleverly designing that component with multiple outputs, the team figured out how to perform different operations as well. “Because of how the Fourier transform response is generated, you can actually pull out different mathematical operations from it,” New says. “We can produce very large, high-precision digital functions at superhigh efficiencies, using our analog photonics approach.”

“We’re effectively adding processing to where there is none right now.” —Nick New, Optalysis

Instead of redesigning an accelerator from scratch, Optalysys is targeting a piece of the AI workload that’s often already in the optical domain: networking. In the data center, racks of computers are connected to each other with fiber optics, and the optical connections are increasingly getting closer and closer to the GPUs and CPUs themselves.

Some computations already happen while the data is en route. These computations, which include combining results from multiple GPUs, are executed inside network switch cards. But the cards naturally use power to do that math. With passive optical components, these computations could be done essentially for free.

New says that in addition to communication between GPUs, Optalysys’s technology could be used to facilitate a GPU’s communication with memory, doing things like compression and format conversion on the fly. Going back to AI inference, this approach could improve the decode part of the workload. Unlike prefill, decode is memory bound: The most costly part is shuffling model data in and out of memory. “We’re more focused on the memory-bound applications, which fits very well with this principle of adding processing into the communication path,” New says. “We’re effectively adding processing to where there is none right now.”

How likely are optical computers to replace GPUs in the data center? Yale’s Wright is not too optimistic. “The direction of algorithm development is not going to be a direction that is automatically favorable for optics,” he says. “In fact, it’s most likely to go in the opposite direction, because [AI model developers] want it to work better on GPUs.”

However, even if our AI queries aren’t going to be computed in light in the next few years, that investment in the technology won’t be in vain. Says Wright, “The reason that I and many other people in the field are at least somewhat optimistic is that there’s real investment from companies like Nvidia and TSMC in developing co-packaged silicon photonics—not for computing, but for circuit switching and interconnects, and that just kind of opens the door to do a little bit more in the future.”

Whether that technology ends up crunching vector-matrix multiplication, doing bespoke simulations, or performing in-network computations, the computing ecosystem seems ripe for a variety of approaches. “We see the data center of the future as heterogeneous: CPUs, GPUs and photonic NPUs [native processing units] each take on the tasks they are best suited for,” says Q.ANT’s Förtsch. “Running each task on the most efficient hardware can significantly reduce energy use and operating costs.”

This article appears in the December 2026 print issue as “The Return of the Optical Computer.”

Dina Genkina is an associate editor at IEEE Spectrum focused on computing and hardware. She holds a PhD in atomic physics and lives in Brooklyn.

i saw some published test results of a 1950's airborne radar system using an optical computer to do a Fourier transform of the 2D radar return data for military target detection. Basically you have a cathode ray TV tube, and a lens in front of it, and at the focal point of the lens is a Fourier Transform of what showed up on the TV tube. it is Fundamental Fourier optics. Xerox used this in some of their photocopiers too. Really fast processing! Femtoseconds. Maybe its time had come to bring it back again!

I recall HP looking at this in the late 90s. Also, it is not just energy consumption possibility but the reduction of byproduct heat by using photons.

Will be interesting to watch and see if the energy costs of the analog-digital transformations drop enough to spread optical into more parts of the computing hardware. Meantime, I'd be interested in what our readers think of the idea of diversifying methods for different parts of computing.

There's a lot of money, talent and education invested in silicone. A technology has to be a lot better at the start and have a clear path to continuous improvement before real money is put into it. Inertia is a very powerful force.

who SAYS "digital computing" is the best way? it is just all we had to deal with in large scale. Digital computers have a LOT of baggage--such as having to digitize an entirely analog world into 1's and 0's. Analog computers were popular in the 1940's thru the '60's. Our brains are not digital computers, maybe there is a biological computer coming soon?

#3137. Tidal Is the First Streaming Platform to Ban AI Music

You have a few options when it comes to choosing a music streaming service. If you own an iPhone and a Mac, you might be tempted by Apple Music; if you have more friends on Spotify, you may feel that's the best platform for you. But if your goal is avoiding AI music as much as humanly possible, there appears to be a new uncontested winner: Tidal.

On Tuesday, Tidal announced plans to ban AI music from its platform entirely. Starting Dec. 9, the company will begin taking steps to remove music it believes is entirely made with AI. Tidal says it thinks the move “will resonate with both artists and listeners alike.”

This isn't the first stand Tidal has taken against AI-generated music. Back in July, the company announced that it would start labeling songs completely made with AI, as well as remove tracks it found to be "fraudulent and deceptive." Other platforms have similar policies, or are rolling out similar features. Apple Music, for example, is working on AI labels for its app, too, and Spotify has pushed back on AI to some degree. However, this most recent move makes Tidal the first music streaming service to outright ban AI-generated music from its catalog.

Robert Anderson, Tidal's Music Lead, posted on X about the change. According to Anderson, Tidal identified 43% of the tracks it received in the last 90 days were AI-generated. Per the company's plan, Tidal will remove 29 million songs by the beginning of 2027, roughly 80,000 to 85,000 removals per day. Some 96% of Tidal's AI-generated songs have zero plays whatsoever.

I wouldn't be surprised to see other music streaming services follow suit, particularly Apple Music. Despite rolling out AI-powered features over the past couple of years, including Apple Music's AI-generated playlists, Apple has taken some stands against AI-generated material in general. The latest Apple TV intro was shot in-camera with practical effects, in an era where the company could have easily generated something with AI. If other companies plan to follow Tidal's lead here, my money's on Apple being first in line.

However, as it stands, Tidal is the only streaming service that supports this initiative. Soon enough, it'll be the sole music app you can use with near-zero ambiguity that the music you're listening to was at least mostly created by humans. (What a sentence.) Avoiding AI-generated music can be tricky, frustrating, and, frankly, exhausting. If that's important to you, Tidal might just be your new pick.

iOS 27.3 is coming soon, and it’s a big update for new iPhone features, including additions that span six built-in Apple apps. Here’s what’s new.

Apple Music adds a pair of upgrades in iOS 27.3. Selfie Sing is an all-new feature that lets you record short videos of yourself singing along to your favorite songs, aided by onscreen lyrics. It’s perfect for sharing on TikTok or other social platforms.

If you’re not the type to share karaoke videos online, another nice iOS 27.3 change is that the lyrics view for songs has gotten an iPhone Duo-inspired upgrade in landscape mode. Now, artwork for the song you’re listening to blends beautifully into the stream of lyrics.

Safari is getting several exciting new features in iOS 27.3, including:

Gym Strength lets you build a strength program that fits your schedule and the equipment you have on hand. It’s fully customizable and provides Apple’s best offering yet for traditional strength training.

Whether you’re brand new to strength training or just benefit from some additional structure, Gym Strength is a great reason to try out Fitness+.

Read more: Apple announces Fitness+ Gym Strength program with personalized workout plans

Apple’s Freeform app gets a handful of improvements in iOS 27.3, including new text styling options and preset background colors to choose from. You can also generate custom shapes using Apple Intelligence.

Which new iOS 27.3 features are you most excited about? Let us know in the comments.
