New pumps sold increased more than 30% year-over-year, helped by the continued rollout of the MiniMed Flex, including expanded coverage for people on Medicare and the launch of Flex with the Instinct sensor. Flex is attracting patients who are new to pump therapy, winning patients from competitors and strengthening our position in automated insulin delivery. The majority of U.S. Flex new pumps sold continues to come from patients who are new to pump therapy or who switched from a competitor, showing that Flex is expanding our reach beyond existing MiniMed customers.

With Flex, patients can now choose a smaller, more discreet durable pump that they control from an app paired with our SmartGuard adaptive algorithm with 2 modern sensors, Simplera and Instinct. This combination is resonating with patients and providers. During Q2, we held several regional Flex training programs across the United States and the number of new MiniMed prescribers increased 36% sequentially. These results reinforce our confidence in the strength and long-term opportunity of our U.S. business. Turning to international. We delivered another strong quarter. Growth was broad-based. In Western Europe, new pumps sold grew more than 20% year-over-year, reinforcing the strength of demand and our confidence in durable growth across the region.

We continue to benefit from new products, our investments to increase sensor supply and growing adoption of automated insulin delivery in markets where adoption remains relatively low. Several of our largest European markets performed especially well with double-digit growth in the U.K., France and Spain. And Germany delivered its highest revenue growth in 2 years. In the U.K., Instinct gave patients sensor choice and supported strong pump demand. In France, growing use of Simplera drove strong CGM growth and supported pump sales. In Spain, we delivered more than 20% revenue growth despite increased competitive activity. And in Germany, strong prescription demand and solid sales execution drove the improvement.

These results give us confidence in our international business as we begin the next phase of the Flex rollout. Last week, we launched MiniMed Flex with Simplera in Western Europe, with Flex now available in 9 European countries following a successful early customer experience phase across 5 markets. The initial interest from patients and physicians has been strong. Flex with Instinct received CE Mark last month and remains on track to launch in our fiscal fourth quarter. Together, these launches give people more choice in pumps and sensors and give us more ways to meet the needs and preferences of people living with diabetes.

We believe we are well positioned to launch Flex into a strong and growing Western European business with strong pump demand, more sensor options and established commercial and market access infrastructure. Our ability to commercialize at scale is an important advantage. Simplera is now available in over 50 countries and Instinct in 14, supported by our reimbursement capabilities, clinical relationships and customer support infrastructure across the region. Together, these capabilities and our expanding product portfolio give us confidence in a long runway for durable international growth. Now let me turn to our innovation pipeline. Last quarter, I told you we were not launching individual products. We were building the next generation of MiniMed, one company, every option, one ecosystem.

Three months later, several of those programs have taken another important leap forward. More importantly, we continue to deliver on the roadmap we laid out when we separated from Medtronic with products moving from development to pivotal trials, from trials to submission to approval and from approval to commercialization. Let me start with MiniMed Fit. Earlier this month, we received FDA clearance for Fit several months ahead of expectations and just a couple of months after our submission in late August. As a result, we now expect to accelerate our early customer experience phase in Q4 this fiscal year and shift left the full U.S. commercial launch to spring of 2027. MiniMed Fit is a major strategic milestone for MiniMed.

It brings our differentiated therapy platform to a new segment for MiniMed and the fastest-growing segment of insulin delivery. We began preparing for commercialization ahead of clearance, building our manufacturing capability, market access and commercial infrastructure in parallel with the regulatory process. That work continues as we prepare for launch. We expect to have enough capacity to support approximately 20,000 patients in the first year of launch. And we designed our manufacturing network to scale significantly as the launch expands. Fit is simply not another patch pump. It's the first of its kind, designed from the ground up with what patch users need.

Patients have told us they want 3 things from a tubeless pump: longer wear, more insulin capacity and better automation. Fit is everything a tubeless system should be. Fit pairs up to 7 days of wear with a 300-unit insulin reservoir, so patients can change patches less often without giving up insulin capacity. It's app-controlled and designed to be waterproof. It keeps a persistent Bluetooth connection, so patients don't have to re-pair every new patch with their phone, and it can be worn in multiple places on the body. Fit also works with Simplera and Instinct and runs our SmartGuard algorithm. Until now, they've had to trade off one against another. With Fit, they don't.

That means fewer changes and less to think about with strong glucose control in a system that's easy to live with. We believe customers will feel the difference. And Fit is not the endpoint. It's designed to take wireless software updates, giving users a seamless path to Vivera, our fully closed-loop algorithm when it becomes available. As we discussed last quarter, Vivera is designed to eliminate carb counting or meal announcements while still delivering strong outcomes above the ADA guidelines of 70% time in range. We have fully enrolled our pivotal trial and are in the final stages of data collection.

Based on our current timelines, we expect to submit Vivera to the FDA and report pivotal trial data in the first half of calendar year 2027, and we remain on track for a U.S. launch in the second half of calendar '27. Across the industry, most new competitor algorithms are built for one patient population and one style of use. That leaves patients and clinicians making trade-offs: simplicity or performance, hands-free or hands-on, type 1 or type 2, adult or pediatric, durable pump or patch pump. Our goal with Vivera was not to solve one of these trade-offs, it was to eliminate them. Diabetes is not one-size-fits-all. Needs differ between type 1 and type 2 and between adults and children.

And even within these groups, they vary widely and change over time. Nowhere is this clearer than at mealtime. Carb counting is the last manual task in automated insulin delivery. And for 25 years, it has quietly decided who can use a pump. Other systems treat it as a switch, either you announce every meal or you give up control. Vivera treats it as a dial. Patients who want peak performance can choose to enter their meals. Patients who don't want to count carbs at all can skip it, and Vivera still delivers strong glucose control. Patients choose how to be involved at every meal, and that choice can change from one day to the next.

Vivera is also designed for type 1 and type 2, children and adults at launch. We expect to offer it on Flex and Fit as a seamless over-the-air update, so patients can choose a durable pump or patch pump without giving up algorithm performance. This flexibility in one algorithm took more than a decade of R&D, clinical research and simulation tools to build. The better the app automation, the broader the addressable population that will adopt AID therapy. Think of Vivera like a full self-driving car. The car drives, but you can take the wheel anytime you want, and that's exactly why people trust it enough to let it drive. Vivera works the same way.

It handles insulin every 5 minutes, day and night. When you want even tighter control at a meal, you can enter carbs and take the wheel. When you don't, Vivera keeps driving. Other fully closed-loop systems work like a switch. Once it's on, you're a passenger. You only get what that algorithm can do on its own. And when something goes wrong, there's very little you can do about it. With Vivera, you never have to choose between letting go and getting the outcomes you deserve. Our sensor pipeline is moving too. Through our partnership with Abbott, we are integrating a dual glucose-ketone sensor into the MiniMed ecosystem.

We expect to be the first to bring glucose and ketone monitoring together in one app with the sensor expected to launch with our new pumps next summer. Step back and the story isn't any single milestone. It's the momentum across the portfolio. A year ago, these programs were in development. Today, they are in pivotal trials, winning approvals and reaching patients. We're building the most complete platform for people who take insulin: Smart MDI, durable pump, patch pump and a choice of sensors, all connected by one algorithm and one digital ecosystem. And increasingly, we are no longer just building that platform. We are putting it in the hands of patients.

That innovation sits on a business that's getting stronger, demand is building, our underlying profitability is improving, and we just delivered our first quarter of positive free cash flow as an independent company. Flex, Fit, Go, Vivera and our sensor pipeline will expand the number of patients we serve from here. This is the strategy we laid out: deliver in our core business, expand the markets we serve, advance our pipeline and turn that growth into higher earnings and cash generation. Q2 was another meaningful step forward on every one of those priorities. With that, I'll turn it to Chad to walk through our Q2 financials and guidance.

Chad J. Spooner: Thanks, Que. Q2 revenue was $822 million, up 9.4% on a reported basis and 9.7% organically, slightly ahead of organic growth expectations. As we said last quarter, we expected Q2 organic growth in both the U.S. and international to be similar to the underlying growth rates we delivered in Q1. That's what we delivered, with U.S. organic revenue growth of 8.3% and international organic revenue growth of 10.4%. Foreign currency lowered reported revenue by approximately $3 million in the quarter. Organic growth was strong across our portfolio, led by 15% growth in pumps and 10.8% growth in CGM. Pump growth was driven by our recent launches, including MiniMed Flex in the U.S.

Globally, CGM growth was supported by greater sensor supply and continued adoption of Simplera and Instinct. Consumables grew 4.6% in the quarter and together with CGM, represent 81% of revenue, continue to provide a large and durable recurring revenue base. Q2 adjusted EBITDA was $140 million, up 19.7%, more than twice our reported revenue growth. Adjusted EBITDA margin was 17.0%, an increase of 150 basis points year-over-year. We continue to deliver operating leverage across the business while investing in new product launches and our innovation pipeline. Walking through Q2 P&L, adjusted gross profit was $486 million, resulting in adjusted gross margin of 59.0%.

As we've discussed, we expected gross margin to decline this year, primarily reflecting the increased mix of Simplera, which currently carries a lower margin than our legacy and Instinct sensors. Despite that expected mix impact, gross margin continues to track meaningfully better than our assumptions, driven by continued improvement in Simplera yields. Adjusted SG&A was $285 million or 34.7% of revenue, growing 9.3% as we support our expanding commercial portfolio. We continue to invest behind our product launches while driving productivity across the organization. Adjusted R&D was $104 million, essentially flat year-over-year and represented 12.7% of revenue.

R&D continued to provide operating leverage, reflecting productivity across regulatory, clinical, engineering and operations R&D and the progression of several major programs from development toward approval and commercialization. At the same time, we continue to invest in the next generation of MiniMed. Altogether, Q2 provides another clear proof point in the MiniMed business model. We can drive operating leverage and improve profitability while continuing to invest in the innovation and commercialization that supports our current and future growth. Turning to our key business metrics. Q2 new pumps sold or NPS, were 38,000, up 18% year-over-year and 11% from last quarter.

That is a significant increase from the 8% year-over-year growth last quarter, reflecting the strong pump demand Que discussed across both the U.S. and Western Europe. Q2 CGM attachment rate increased to 70%, up 100 basis points from Q1 and 500 basis points year-over-year. This continued progress demonstrates the strength of our integrated AID ecosystem with nearly every new MiniMed pump user pairing our pump with our CGM to get the benefits of SmartGuard automation. Together, these business metrics demonstrate the strength of our underlying demand and a growing recurring revenue opportunity. Let me now turn to our balance sheet and cash generation. We continue to maintain a strong balance sheet and significant liquidity.

We ended Q2 with $256 million of cash, up $49 million from the prior quarter, no debt and a fully undrawn $500 million revolving credit facility. Our capital allocation priority remains investing in the business, and this liquidity gives us substantial flexibility to complete our separation, scale manufacturing capacity and fund our key growth opportunities. Q2 marked an important milestone in our cash generation. We generated $55 million of positive free cash flow, our first positive quarter as an independent company. This includes $31 million of separation and stand-up costs. Excluding those items, free cash flow was $86 million and operating cash flow was $146 million, demonstrating the underlying cash generation profile of the business today.

As we have discussed, free cash flow may vary from quarter to quarter over the next year and may not be positive every quarter while we continue to incur these one-time separation-related costs. Importantly, excluding these temporary separation-related items, we expect the underlying business to remain free cash flow positive. We expect separation and stand-up costs to largely end by the close of calendar 2027. As these costs roll off and revenue and profitability grow, we expect the business to generate significant positive free cash flow. Next, let's cover our outlook for the remainder of fiscal 2027. We are maintaining our fiscal 2027 organic revenue growth outlook of approximately 10.5%.

This outlook continues to include the 1 to 1.5 percentage points benefit from the extra week in Q1. Over the rest of the year, we continue to expect our recent product launches to add more to revenue and revenue growth. For the second half of fiscal 2027, we expect U.S. and international organic growth to remain broadly consistent with Q2 levels. Strong demand, faster growth in new pumps sold and continued product launch momentum and strength across our markets give us confidence in our full year outlook. Turning to Fit. We're very encouraged by FDA clearance and our accelerated launch timeline. As we've discussed before, pharmacy access and formulary coverage take time to build.

Starting next spring, we expect Fit to be an important driver of new pumps sold and installed base growth. Its contribution to revenue and profit will be smaller initially and build over the first 18 to 24 months as we gain formulary access and scale manufacturing capacity. Over time, a growing base of Fit users creates long-term recurring revenue from ongoing patch pump and CGM use, which we expect to drive meaningful profit growth and our outlook continues to reflect this ramp. Turning to profitability. Our strong Q2 performance reinforces our confidence in the underlying earnings outlook for the business.

And now with the earlier-than-expected FDA clearance of Fit, we expect to pull forward manufacturing, sales and marketing investments that were previously planned for future periods to accelerate the launch in the spring. Our Q2 outperformance gives us the capacity to fund these incremental fiscal 2027 investments while reaffirming our adjusted EBITDA margin guidance. Absent the accelerated Fit investments, the underlying strength of the business would have supported increasing our operating outlook. Put simply, the strength of the underlying business is absorbing the additional investments required to bring Fit to patients sooner. We are, therefore, reaffirming our fiscal 2027 adjusted EBITDA margin guidance of approximately 11.3%.

As a reminder, we updated our guidance in the 8-K filed last week following FDA clearance of Fit solely to reflect the accelerated $162 million Blackstone charge that we expect to recognize in Q3. That update did not reflect any change in our underlying operating performance or expectations for the business. So excluding the Blackstone charge for Fit, our adjusted EBITDA is still approximately 16% as we previously guided. For the balance of the year, we continue to expect building revenue and revenue growth contributions from our recent product launches. On the gross margin, the second half gross margin will reflect the manufacturing investments we're pulling forward to support the accelerated Fit launch.

While we will also have accelerated OpEx investments to support Fit launch, we continue to expect underlying operating leverage across the business. As we indicated last quarter, excluding the Blackstone Fit charge, we expect a larger portion of the full year EBITDA improvement to occur in the second half. Before I turn it back to Que, let me provide a brief update on our separation progress. We began with approximately 160 TSAs with Medtronic and through Q2, our dedicated teams have exited more than 30 TSAs. We continue to work closely with Medtronic and are making meaningful progress across the remaining TSA portfolio and the operational readiness activities required to support each exit.

We remain confident in our established timelines with most TSAs exiting expected during the calendar of 2027. As we complete this work, we're building more focused, efficient and fit-for-purpose capabilities for MiniMed as an independent company. Que, back to you.

Que Thanh Dallara: Thanks, Chad. As we look ahead, we believe the opportunity in front of MiniMed has never been greater. We operate in one of the largest markets in MedTech with significant opportunity to expand the use of advanced diabetes technology around the world. Automated insulin delivery has meaningfully improved outcomes and quality of life, yet today remains significantly underpenetrated. To accelerate adoption, these technologies need to be simpler and less burdensome for people living with diabetes and the healthcare professionals who support them.

That is why we believe the future of our industry will be defined not by who serves today's pump users, but by who can bring advanced therapy to the millions of people who are not benefiting from it today. Our innovation is making diabetes management more intuitive and fully automated. But doing so at scale takes more than one product or device. It takes an ecosystem that offers choice and meets people wherever they are in their diabetes journey. That is exactly what we are building at MiniMed. Our broad and growing portfolio lets us serve people across durable pumps, patch pumps and smart MDI, sensors, algorithms and the digital tools that connect them.

And with Flex, Go, Simplera and Instinct expanding commercially, Fit now FDA cleared and Vivera and our sensor portfolio advancing, that ecosystem is increasingly becoming a reality. Innovation does not create this opportunity. Innovation unlocks it, and we are rapidly bringing that innovation to patients. We are entering this phase with strong momentum, rising profitability, our first quarter of positive stand-alone free cash flow and the broadest portfolio in our history. Execution remains our focus and the progress we have made over the past few months demonstrates our ability to move innovation from development to approval and commercialization.

We believe we are uniquely positioned to lead the next phase of advanced diabetes technology adoption, delivering better outcomes, less burden and greater choice for people living with diabetes, all while creating long-term value for shareholders. Before I close, I want to thank our employees around the world. Their focus, urgency and commitment to improving the lives of people with diabetes are what makes achievements like this possible. With that, let's go to Q&A. Operator?

Operator: [Operator Instructions] Our first question comes from the line of Travis Steed with Bank of America Securities.

Travis Steed: Congrats on the good quarter and progress as a stand-alone company. I guess I'll ask on the Fit approval. Just understand exactly what all needs to happen. Could the spring launch maybe be accelerated if things go really well? And then another kind of question around that is like why would there not be maybe some pauses ahead of that launch in the base business that you saw with the launch before Flex?

Que Thanh Dallara: Thanks, Travis. We're really excited to get approval. I think if you look at just the timelines of this brand-new platform with a 7-day label, it's been incredible to get approved so quickly, even surprising ourselves, but I think a great reflection of the execution that you're seeing from MiniMed. What we said previously was that we would have capacity in the first year of launch to support 20,000 patients. And what we're actually doing is pulling that forward where that installed capacity will be available at the summer. So that's a pull forward. And then by the spring, when we plan to launch, we'll have over 60% installed capacity available.

And what we're doing between now and then is with the manufacturing lines that we have in place is starting to make product. We're moving up the experience curve and driving down the cost curve. What we want to do is to make sure that we support the early customer phase of several hundred patients in our fiscal Q4. That's also a pull forward. And then ultimately, what we're trying to do is not simply race to get these -- the new product on the arms of a handful of patients, but actually to support a nationwide launch. We plan to be very aggressive in winning share, more than our fair share of MDI.

And we want to give people who are currently on patch pumps a reason to switch. And that's at least 400,000 to 500,000 patients available there. So that's what we're gearing towards. We have pulled it forward significantly. That's not an easy feat to accomplish with manufacturing and making sure that the supply chain is ready. But we're doing that. And then in addition to that, we're in very advanced discussions with the PBMs to get Fit on the formulary.

Travis Steed: Great. And maybe help us understand some of the margin upside this quarter and how sustainable that is moving forward. Some people are worried about the margin ramp through the course of the year, and you've derisked some of that after this quarter, but just kind of making sure if you have confidence in kind of the margin ramp over the course of the year and some of the upside this quarter sustaining.

Chad J. Spooner: Travis, thanks for the question. In regards to the margin, we had said last quarter that we anticipated this happening this quarter, right? And so we were confident that we would get the growth in the margin from where we ended last quarter. So one of the things that happened is that we had pulled forward costs from this quarter into first quarter, right, which is sort of the dynamic of the first quarter results as we spoke about. So you see some of that benefit here.

But in addition to that, what you're seeing really is our gross margin is consistently ahead of where we expected as Simplera continues quarter after quarter to do better than we initially anticipated and yields continue to get better. The story around our warranty also continues to get better as you look at products like Flex rolling out that are going to be better from a warranty perspective. So those gross margin things are above where we expected them to be. You can see that we continue to drive operating leverage as well. So that's going to continue throughout the second half of the year.

And in reality, it will be even stronger because we are going to see that elevated revenue growth like you always do in the second half of our year. So that's going to continue to propel our operating leverage. So I think that all the elements are there for that continued growth in the second half of the year. One way to think about it is we had some of that gross margin benefit this quarter. It will kind of be some of that stuff that we're pulling now forward to support Fit is going to moderate some of that gross margin, right? So the 59% you see this quarter and you say is that a continuous run rate.

We need to do some things in the cost of goods to accelerate forward Fit. So you'll see some of that. And then we'll continue to get the operating leverage. So we're very confident that we can get what we've guided to. The way we kind of look at it is it's really almost like an implicit raise because the performance this quarter would have supported an increase in our operating outlook, but we've got costs that we're bringing forward just like you did with Flex. But you can imagine this is a little bit more complicated because the amount of production, et cetera, that we're doing here is very different than we did for Flex.

So we can support all of that with the operational performance we've done this quarter, what we're seeing.

Operator: Our next question comes from the line of Lawrence Biegelsen with Wells Fargo.

Larry (Lawrence) Biegelsen: [indiscernible]

Chad J. Spooner: Larry, you're a bit muffled actually. It's not a very good connection.

Larry (Lawrence) Biegelsen: I apologize. Let me see what I can...

Larry (Lawrence) Biegelsen: Okay. So on Fit. Que, how are you thinking about payer coverage when you launch? When will you have unconstrained capacity to meet demand beyond the roughly 20,000 patients at launch? And how are you thinking about the split of durable versus patch pumps for new starts going forward?

Que Thanh Dallara: Thanks, Larry. In terms of getting onto the formulary, where -- as I mentioned, I'm very confident that we will get onto formulary position with the big 3 PBMs. We actually started that well before clearance actually. There's such high demand and interest in the Fit pump, so we had a pre-information exchange under NDA with a lot of the PBMs. So we're fairly -- we're far along with the big 3. And then in addition to that, we're also talking to the downstream health plans to make sure that whatever barriers that might be in place in the various health plan designs, we can start removing with direct contracting with those plans. So that's on the market access side.

In addition to that, we also have plans to address affordability because we want to make sure that, especially in the early innings as we're building formulary coverage that, that's not a barrier to adoption. We don't want it to be a friction point as prescribers are interested in this product. And so there will be co-pay assistance programs and things of that nature that we'll have in place as well so that it's an extremely smooth nationwide launch.

And then when it comes to manufacturing, I think the good news is by bringing forward our installed capacity being in place in the summertime, we will be starting to work on the expansion of that manufacturing capacity for the second year in the second half of calendar year '27. So essentially, we've pulled everything to the left with the early clearance. And what that means is just like you saw in Simplera, the production ramps in orders of magnitude. It's not a 20% increase, but it's an order of magnitude increase in terms of the production capacity we'll have in the second year and beyond.

And in terms of your last question on the durable versus patch, I think we'll see. We see Fit really addressing the fastest-growing segment of really people coming from MDI, they're interested in AID, but they like the patch form factor. That's probably the largest cohort. And we think that Fit is really extremely differentiated, the only tubeless option that's going to give people who are currently on Omnipod a reason to switch. The longer wear, the larger insulin capacity and the better algorithm, I think that's going to swing a lot of people over.

And so I think there's a possibility that the mix of patch from a market standpoint grows even faster than the durable pump market, but we believe that there are still people who want the disconnect and the functionality and the flexibility that MiniMed Flex offers. So you can see that in our new pumps sold metric continues to accelerate and is extremely strong. So we feel good about both platforms.

Operator: Our next question comes from the line of Patrick Andrew Wood with UBS.

Patrick Andrew Wood: Through the whole presentation, there was a strong theme around building a platform. And so I guess by next summer, you'll have kind of assembled all the infinity stones and have the whole bag for pretty much all of the customer base. So I guess from your perspective then, when you have everything under one roof, does that enable you to go to tenders in a different way? Does that enable you to go to formularies in a different way in a more holistic way? Does it enable you and the docs to approach the patient differently by having all the solutions under one roof? It was just a very clear theme from the prepared remarks.

I'm just trying to think how that shifts growth going forward.

Que Thanh Dallara: I think those are great examples, Patrick, of the possibilities that are available. I think the first thing that I'm personally very excited about that I think is the ultimate killer app in our space that will expand the pie is this patch pump with Vivera. It really combines what people are looking for from a form factor standpoint, so freedom from the tubing, but with freedom from not carb counting any longer. So together, those 2, I think, are extremely exciting that will come in '27. But beyond that, you'll see that if you're on, for example, Flex today and you got your Flex through DME, you can get your patch pump through pharmacy.

And the good news is when you download our app, there will be a single app. So whether you choose to be on the Flex one day and move to patch the next, you don't have to download another application, whether that's on Android or Apple, or simplifying the experience and making it easy for people to switch therapies depending on where they are in their journey. And then I think if you look long term, I think that -- there are a lot of challenges to be solved still in diabetes to make things even simpler, more intuitive and more fully automated.

And so you can imagine different form factors and possibilities because we are the only company that has commercialized sensor technology, different dosing devices, a software suite that integrates the user app, the caregiver app and CareLink, the provider platform, we're able to innovate a lot faster in the future and deliver new form factors and newer experiences that I think others will take longer or struggle to deliver.

Operator: Our next question comes from the line of Matthew O'Brien with Piper Sandler.

Matthew O'Brien: I'll ask them both upfront here. But just Que -- sorry to stick with Fit more -- again. But just curious, you guys have a big installed base in the U.S. and globally. How are you going to go about launching Fit? Are you going to really focus on MDI patients with it? Are you going to focus on some of your existing installed base? And if you do the former on the MDI side, are you -- do you risk irritating your large installed base? And how do you keep them happy as you go through that?

And then the second part of the question is just Fit, it's a 300-unit product, longer wear, but it is bigger than other tubeless or patch pumps that are out there. Is that something you get feedback on from clinicians or patients that, hey, that's kind of big and that might be somewhat of a gating factor as you do roll that out?

Que Thanh Dallara: Thanks, Matt. On the way that we're launching it out, we see Flex and Fit really living side by side as 2 very important choices for people. A lot of people like the ability to disconnect from your pump. They like the ability to wear all over their body. And so we see a role for Flex continuing. And then when it comes to Fit, we think that Fit ultimately will bring really incremental patients to MiniMed. Most of that will come from MDI, people who are new to pump therapy. There's a clear trend that they're attracted to the patch form factor. And so that's where we think it comes from.

But we also believe that Fit offers something that the other entrants don't in terms of giving people who are currently on Omnipod a reason to switch. And the 3 biggest reasons that we hear from the research that we've done is Omnipod users want longer wear. They want a larger reservoir because especially if you're a type 2 or you're an adult type 1, you need more insulin capacity, so less changes, and then an algorithm that gives you better outcomes with less work. So we deliver all of that with Fit. So we think about the -- our ability to attract those segments are pretty high.

Will there be patients in our installed base that want a patch pump? I'm sure there is. We just don't think that's the majority of who will be attracted to Fit because I think if you look at our installed base, they had plenty of years and many options to go to a patch pump, they haven't chosen to do that. But certainly, for those that do, we'll have it available to them. I think for your second question around the size, I'm sure there are people who will look at the size of things.

I mean it's -- I think in consumer electronics, if you look at a watch, that's why you've got a small watch and a bigger watch. People sometimes pick the bigger watch. It's not always the case that you want something small if the functionality that you're going after, the larger capacity reservoir, the longer wear gives you features that you care about. So I'm sure that's true. However, it's a very -- it's a relatively easy objection to overcome, just wear the device. We can sample the product. You can wear it. I think when you put it on, you see that the load and the height of it is extremely easy to wear.

That's why we've done the wear studies. And so we don't -- I'm sure there will be some people that may want something smaller, but the reality is when you think about the total value proposition that it represents, it's head and shoulders in terms of what's available in the market. So we think we can overcome those objections with making the product available as a starter kit and as samples to use.

Operator: Our next question comes from the line of Richard Newitter with Truist Securities.

Richard Newitter: Congrats on the quarter. Continuing the questions on Fit here. As we think of the gross margin impact even beyond kind of the initial launch, but including the initial period of launch, can you just give us a little bit more on how to think of the gross margin impact as this scales and you grow into the capacity? And then I have a follow-up.

Chad J. Spooner: Thanks, Rich. What we've always said about Fit is that the first year is really all about building a user base, expanding the formulary and health plan access and scaling manufacturing. So as such, in that first year, we're going to be using co-pay assistance, as you said, and other patient access programs while we build the coverage. So we've said that there will be limited impact in terms of revenue and margin for the beginning of the launch, and that's just being realistic as to what the financials look like.

And then as it scales and builds over the first 18 to 24 months, we're going to get more capacity scale, so we're going to get more margin enhancement from that. And as we get more formulary coverage, the co-pay assistance and things like that will also fall off. So we'll see increasing margins from both of those regions. So that's kind of how we see it from a scaling standpoint, going from a minimal impact to a much greater and very profitable impact over the long term.

Richard Newitter: That's helpful. And then maybe just for Que. One of the questions we get just on competitive bidding and the rental model that's coming. Can you just remind us of how you are thinking about that and kind of where you have confidence on potential long-term pricing implications across your businesses?

Que Thanh Dallara: Yes. Look, we expect that the administration will continue to press forward with competitive bidding. And I think -- in general, I think you agree that competitive bidding is not a good thing for the industry as a whole. It's -- the Medicare business for us is single-digit number of our overall business. So this is something that we expect to withstand. And so when we look at our overall portfolio, we've got MiniMed Fit going through pharmacy, our CGMs available through pharmacy. And as the pumps -- that mix goes -- increases through pharmacy, we expect that there will be price opportunities with that channel in the U.S.

We continue to advocate for choice and access with the administration with CMS as they go through the details in rolling this out. I think the rental model is still -- there are details to be figured out. Given that the devices in this space are single-use devices, renting them out is -- there are certain barriers that we have to overcome. So I think there's still details to be figured out. So we're managing this. And the fact that we have the strength of this portfolio with all these new products opening up the pharmacy channel, I think that helps us -- it provides a number of levers to offset challenges that competitive bidding may provide.

Operator: Our next question comes from the line of Chris Pasquale with Barclays.

Christopher (Chris) Pasquale: I wanted to ask about Vivera. You talked a lot about choice as a key design consideration. Users can pick and choose how they interact with the algorithm, which certainly adds a lot of flexibility. But does that mean that the training required to get new users comfortable with the system will be more involved than it will be for algorithms that just don't give them as many options since they've got to be comfortable with all the different ways they can use it? And how do you think about what that means for the ability of non-endocrinologists to prescribe it?

Que Thanh Dallara: Thanks, Chris. We actually designed it to be very easy to onboard onto therapy. All you need is your total daily dose. So if you're on an MDI, you know what your total daily dose is, that's all you need to enter therapy. There are no settings to be done by the physician. You don't need to do any programming. It's as close to self-start as you can get. So the training is extremely simple. So that's Vivera, and it's designed to really eliminate carb counting, but not sacrifice outcomes. So we want people to be above 70% time in range without needing to carb count whatsoever.

Now a lot of the feedback we hear from patients though is when you have something like a forced full closed loop that we hear from some of our competitors, people are nervous about that because they don't know how it's going to perform. It may not get you to 70% time in range. And if you get into a sticky situation, there's not much you can do because there's no -- there aren't any levers to pull. You're in a forced full closed system. In our system, if you want tighter control, you can input and say something like, "I'm eating," or you can put in a carb count.

And the system will also take that input and give you better control. And so we've really designed it to accommodate the full spectrum: people who don't want to do anything and people who do. And one algorithm can handle all of that. And I think that actually builds trust because just like in our commentary, the car analogy, a lot of people are nervous about going to a self-driving car because it's quite a foreign concept.

But once you're in one and you see how it works and if you can take control at any time, you're more likely to trust that system than trust your health to a forced algorithm that can only get to a certain maximum, doesn't get you out of trouble should you get into those sort of tricky corners.

Christopher (Chris) Pasquale: That's helpful. And then the announcement on the dual glucose-ketone sensor was an interesting update. Curious how you think about who across your user base that is going to appeal to.

Que Thanh Dallara: Look, I think it's still early days with how to use the ketone information. I think we're very excited to be the first. We believe the first app that's going to incorporate ketone and glucose on the same screen. I think the other implementation you're going to see in the market will have 2 apps. You've got your CGM app that may have -- that will have the ketone on it and then you've got the pump app, and we're going to integrate that all into one. So I think it still is something that needs to be studied.

But I think for people who want the bells and whistles and additional information, they would be attracted to the ketone sensor. We hear a lot of interest from pediatric accounts that it's sort of belts and suspenders for parents. And so, but it's still early days in terms of that user experience. There's more to be studied. But by having all that information onto the one app, I think we're simplifying the experience for providers and for patients. And I think that facilitates what else can you do with ketones and where can that be helpful into the future. But certainly, on peds accounts, for example, I think it will be a very strong value proposition with our system.

Operator: Our next question comes from the line of Joanne Wuensch with Citi.

Joanne Wuensch: It seems like the Vivera algorithm will be available after the launch of Fit. Can you sort of walk through how you think about sort of post hoc adding that into the systems? And then my second question is, is there a way to measure the percentage of revenue that's going through the pharmacy today? And is there a goal for what that might look like in the future?

Que Thanh Dallara: Thanks, Joanne. On Vivera, it will be a simple over-the-air update. As you know, when you get a Flex pump, it's really less than 10 minutes to upgrade the firmware and get the latest software update, and it will be the same with MiniMed Fit as well as MiniMed Flex. So very simple over-the-air update. So as soon as Vivera is cleared, and we're preparing for launch, we can push that to all our customers and all the devices. So it's pretty seamless. In terms of the pharmacy channel, today, our pharmacy mix is relatively low in the single-digit category. We haven't given you a number. I think, obviously, we've got big ambitions to increase that.

We're pretty excited with Fit exclusively going through pharmacy in the U.S. And so I think as that ramps, we'll be able to share more in the future.

Operator: Our next question comes from the line of Daniel Markowitz with Evercore ISI.

Daniel Markowitz: Congrats on a strong update. First, I wanted to ask, really strong gross margin execution in the second quarter. Could you talk about the drivers of that gross margin strength versus the initial expects, which I think is enabling the pull forward of the investments in Fit? And then any other thoughts you can share on the evolution of gross margins over the coming quarters and years?

Chad J. Spooner: Thanks, Daniel. Yes, gross margin execution, it's really around -- the main factor is Simplera, right? We've talked about this year having the depressed margin from prior years because Simplera currently has a lower margin than our legacy and Instinct CGMs. But we have done a phenomenal job from increasing our yields even more than we expected when we launched this year off. So that's a huge driver. We're seeing benefits in our warranty. So as our products get more and more reliable, our warranty costs are getting even better than we anticipated. We're seeing manufacturing variance favorability across the board and even favorable PPV. So really, it's really strong execution across everything manufacturing from a gross margin standpoint.

So that's great news, right, from where we anticipated being. And then as we think of the evolution, we talk about all the new product launches. So as we launch new products, as we said, as they scale manufacturing-wise, they'll get more and more profitable. So Simplera is an example of something that you need to build significant scale to get to profitability, we're getting better. Flex is one where we're seeing very good conversion quickly to getting to near profitability or better than 780G given the simplicity of the bill of materials.

As we think of the patch pump, it's going to obviously have a lower gross margin as we spoke about earlier, given the things that we're doing to get on formulary and as the scale needs to build up. So we're going to see some ebbs and flows, but it's -- that's why we always talk about our bottom line EBITDA is going to be driven consistently year in and year out by operating leverage, which we have very good control over. But you can be sure that in the years to come, our gross margin will continue to also get better as Fit and these products that we keep launching get to scale as well.

I think that we're proving our track record of strong manufacturing and building out some of these new products and getting to better profitability faster.

Daniel Markowitz: That's helpful. And then my follow-up, can you talk a little bit more about the organic outlook for the second half? It looks like it implies some step-down versus the second quarter despite the growing contribution from new product launches. Are there some moving pieces we should think about in terms of potential delayed starts around competitive launches? Or is it just layering in conservatism continuing to build this track record of execution?

Chad J. Spooner: So what I'll say is your math is correct, and we are not saying that there's any slowdown. But what we've always said is that we give guidance on numbers that we're confident that we can hit. And we think that given all the timing of things happening, we've given a number that we're very confident that we can hit 10.5%.

Ryan Weispfenning: Thank you, Daniel. I see, Shannon, that we're coming close to the end of our time here. So we'll take the last question, please.

Operator: Our last question comes from the line of Marie Thibault with U.S. Bancorp. BTIG.

Marie Thibault: I wanted to just double-click on the strong U.S. new pump sales performance here this quarter. I'm assuming some of that was driven by Instinct being added to Flex. So just some commentary on that, the sustainability of that. And based on prior commentary, I'm assuming or is it fair to assume that we don't expect any sort of pause or slowdown as people await the Fit launch?

Que Thanh Dallara: Thanks, Marie. No, we're really happy with the over 30% growth in new pumps sold and really reflects the very strong demand that we're seeing and an acceleration actually in the second quarter for the newest products that we have. It's clearly share gain. I don't think the durable pump market is growing above 30% and we're adding to our installed base. So it definitely contributed in a meaningful way to the second quarter. And in terms of the -- just the sort of launch dynamics that you asked about. Look, I'm sure there are some people in our installed base that could be waiting for Fit.

We still believe that the majority of people who are attracted to Fit will come from MDI and competitive switches. So I think it will end up offsetting that. We've already incorporated purchase comments into the guide of what we're confident we can hit that, that will not be a material impact on us in the second half.

Ryan Weispfenning: Okay. Thank you, Marie. And I know there are a couple of analysts that we weren't able to get to today. So we're happy to follow up with you after the call. I'd also like to thank everyone for joining us today and your continued interest in MiniMed. We believe today's results reflect the progress we're making across our business, the innovation pipeline and financial profile, and we're excited about the opportunities ahead. I want to say for those of you joining from the United States, I want to wish you and your families a happy Thanksgiving. Thank you again for your time and interest in MiniMed, and we look forward to speaking with you again next quarter.

Operator: This concludes today's conference. Thank you for participating. You may now disconnect.

#3120. GTA 6 is a generational masterpiece — and one of the few games I’ve given a perfect score in 16 years

Keep exploring and earning more as a member.

Unlock and manage exclusive Tom’s Guide member rewards.

Join the Tom's Guide Club for quick access. Enter your email below and we'll send confirmation, and sign you up to our newsletter.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

GTA 6 is easily the most impressive entry in the (in)famous series and a technical showcase that raises the bar for open-world games. Its expansive map and myriad activities offer countless hours of crime-fueled mayhem, while the intriguing characters keep you invested in the narrative. This game was worth the wait and will arguably go down as the finest title of this console generation.

Why you can trust Tom's Guide Our writers and editors spend hours analyzing and reviewing products, services, and apps to help find what's best for you. Find out more about how we test, analyze, and rate.

Platforms: PS5 (reviewed), Xbox Series X/SPrice: $79 / £69 / AU$129Release date: November 19, 2026Genre: Open-world action-adventure

GTA 6 is the most impressive video game I’ve ever played. I’m not surprised, given Rockstar Games’ history of releasing technically proficient (and insanely profitable) titles, but the storied developers have truly outdone most other games with what they’ve accomplished here. The long wait and anticipation are more than justified.

Larger than any locale in the franchise’s history, the fictional state of Leonida is a character unto itself, evoking real-life Florida with its myriad eccentric characters and diverse locations. You explore this vast landscape alongside the game’s two protagonists, a Bonnie-and-Clyde-like couple who help keep the emotional center in place amid the chaos of the main story and side quests. Together, the narrative and open-world elements deliver an experience that keeps you hooked for hours.

I’ve been a huge fan of the GTA series since GTA 3 arrived in 2001 and completely changed the gaming landscape. I had some trepidation about GTA 6, given how long we’ve waited for it and how much gaming (and the world) has changed since GTA 5was released in 2013. Thankfully, GTA 6 far exceeds my expectations and will more than likely be my favorite game of the generation. Here’s why...

GTA 6 straddles the line between the more grounded tone of GTA 4 and the over-the-top insanity of GTA 5. It’s fair to say this game feels like Red Dead Redemption 2 set in the 21st century, in both tone and theme. Given that RDR 2 is in my top 10 favorite games of all time, this is a major bonus.

That Red Dead inspiration is most evident in the game’s first chapter, where we slowly learn about the two protagonists, Jason Duval and Lucia Caminos, a criminal couple trying to build a new life. The slower-burn intro will turn off anyone who's played the arcade-y GTA Online for the past 13 years—and it’s a valid criticism, even if I personally didn’t mind it. After chapter 1, it’s full-on GTA-style mayhem.

Jason and Lucia have more grounded personalities than some of the wilder protagonists in older GTA titles, but the game generally does a good job of showing what motivates them and making you feel invested in their journey. Jason and Lucia balance each other, with the former more stoic and calculated and the latter more impulsive and instinctive. The characters are at their best together and feel incomplete apart. The leads’ relatively toned-down attitudes also contrast nicely with the absolutely bonkers characters they meet along the way.

In true GTA fashion, this is a rags-to-riches criminal tale that builds with each subsequent mission. You feel the sense of progression as you move up in the world and take on bigger, more dangerous heists. Watching the protagonists evolve over the course of the story is also satisfying.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

In the Grand Theft Auto series, driving has often been a point of contention, and that hasn’t changed here. At least initially. During the first few hours, I found the driving mechanics overly sensitive and loose. It felt like I was driving on ice, especially in the beat-up jalopy Jason owns at the beginning.

Then I realized that, at least on PS5, the triggers are pressure-sensitive, and I shouldn’t just hold R2 all the way down. In fact, you can feel a bit of resistance when you depress the button halfway. When I figured this out, I was golden. Though some vehicles naturally control better and differently than others, I now have a good handle (no pun intended) on the pretty intricate driving mechanics.

Pay & Spray shops are not only great for a quick paint job to lose the cops, but also for tuning your car’s performance for better handling. This can be expensive, so it’s best to wait until you have enough money and a car worth investing in, since you don’t want to upgrade a piece of crap. I like tuning cars because it reminds me of Rockstar’s Midnight Club racing series. And yes, you can totally add neon lights and nitrous!

Stealing cars is more involved than ever. While you can easily steal most cheaper or older cars, higher-end vehicles will have alarms, key fobs, and trackers. And even when you successfully jack a car, you need to hotwire it. The game doles out specific tools needed to steal various cars at specific points, so you'll need to be patient to grab the really high-end rides. Even if jacking cars requires more than a button press, the extra steps make stealing them feel more immersive.

As criminals, Jason and Lucia always end up getting into gunfights—either with fellow lawbreakers or law enforcement. Though the shooting and cover mechanics aren’t as precise and responsive as a dedicated third-person shooter like Gears of War: E-Day, they’re the most refined of any previous GTA game.

Auto lock for weapons was essential in GTA 5 and RDR 2 because the free-aiming mechanics were so dodgy and imprecise. That’s not the case here, as I can easily land headshots with auto lock disabled. This game has its own version of Red Dead’s “Dead Eye,” called Focus Mode, which slows the world down so you can target specific body parts. This is crucial if you want to shoot arms or legs to disable rather than kill, especially since it ties into the game’s morality system. Jason and Lucia both have a Focus meter that drains while you’re in Focus Mode.

The cover mechanics are good but not great. I say that because while your character sticks to walls or the sides of cars you’re hiding behind, it’s too easy to snap out of cover when you try to move. Still, the mechanic works well enough most of the time, and you definitely want to stay in cover during intense shootouts with gang members or the police.

You have access to all manner of handguns, shotguns, assault rifles, and more, which you can purchase from Ammu-Nation, pilfer from dispatched enemies, or find in the open world. Like cars, you can modify weapons. Of course, buying upgrades that improve handling, extend magazine capacity, add scopes, and more can get expensive, but it’s well worth it given the number of insane shootouts you’ll encounter during the story or out in Leonidas.

Sticking up pawn shops and robbing banks has always been fun in GTA, but it’s even more enjoyable now with two protagonists. I never get tired of watching how shop owners and customers react when Jason and Lucia bust in with guns drawn. While one makes sure no one tries anything funny, the other threatens the clerk into emptying the register. Sometimes someone tries to be a hero and stop you, so you have to stay on your guard.

That scenario is for small shops, but if you want to break into a bank, you’ll need to prepare. Scoping out a place, either from the inside or outside, to locate exits and where the goods are kept is crucial to pulling off a successful heist. And don’t forget to have a getaway vehicle nearby, as the cops will arrive quickly if alarms are triggered (though you can always try to disable them).

Along the way, you’ll also discover or be told where gangs hang out or where other criminal activity occurs. These locations often have jewelry, drugs, or other contraband that you can then sell to a fence for a big haul. As with bank robberies, you’ll want to scope out a location to identify entry points and other opportunities to exploit.

The wanted system is more intricate than before. Committing crimes in a specific area raises your wanted level by up to six stars, with each star bringing more heat from law enforcement. You can drive to another county to lose the heat, but the cops will remember your vehicle, face, hairstyle, clothing, and that there were two of you. To really lose the cops, you’ll need to change your clothes, repaint your car, or temporarily split up.

For example, I got a 4-star wanted rating after a robbery went wrong. I drove my car deep into the woods and got out, using the trees for cover to avoid being spotted by helicopters. After finding a truck depot, I broke into a truck using a slim jim carjacking tool and stayed in the truck without turning it on. The cops swarmed the area but didn’t find me because I was lying low. After a few minutes, they left, and I drove off to change clothes and switch vehicles. None of this was scripted.

Since this is a crime game, I’m glad Rockstar updated the wanted system to feel more realistic and give you the freedom to evade the fuzz in ways not available in previous titles.

Now, I won’t go into exhaustive detail about all the side activities available. Suffice it to say that if you need a break from your criminal pursuits, there is plenty to do. That said, I want to discuss some of my favorites.

Like in previous games, you can do side missions for some of the zany characters you meet. I enjoy these because they are small stories unto themselves, and also let you experience more of Leonidas’ environment and cultures. No spoilers here, but some of these side missions are completely bonkers, and sometimes quite literally out of this world.

This may sound weird, given how I neglect to do this in real life, but I’m obsessed with taking Jason and Lucia to the gym. And it’s not just because I want them to look buff and hot. For instance, lifting weights boosts your strength, making you a bit harder to kill and letting you punch enemies out more easily. Boosting your cardio lets you run and swim longer, while raising your Focus can extend your Focus Mode. You can also boost these stats by brawling, running, or eating, but I find hitting the gym more efficient and fun.

You’ll also find several events that lead to missions not marked on the map. For example, you might return to your car only to find a random woman in the backseat asking for help retrieving her dog from a biker gang, or an influencer might decide to snap photos of herself with your fancy ride. This is why it pays to explore methodically, as surprises are literally around every corner.

Among other things, you can participate in street or boat races, get drunk and blow all your money at strip clubs, do some mud wrestling, or unwind by watching TV (the in-game TV shows are hilarious) or doomscrolling on your phone with your partner in bed after a long day of chaos. There is no shortage of interesting activities to partake in here.

I say this without a hint of hyperbole, but GTA 6 is the most graphically impressive and detailed game I’ve ever seen. Rockstar’s proprietary RAGE Engine is in full effect, delivering awe-inspiring visuals that bring Leonida to life. Videos online can’t compare to the experience of playing GTA 6 firsthand.

The map is immense. Even at full speed on the highway, it can take five or more minutes to reach a destination. And you won’t even mind, since everything you pass is so wonderfully rendered, from distant bridges to forests beneath thick, darkening clouds. I especially love driving through Vice City at night, as the metropolis’ gleaming buildings and neon-drenched streets are a sight to behold.

Since Leonida is essentially a miniature version of Florida, it has similar biomes. These include muggy swamps, dense woods, and the terrifying marvel of the Caribbean Sea. As in RDR 2, the world is filled with all manner of animals, from small rats to enormous sperm whales. You can easily spend hours exploring each locale, as long as you’re wary of hungry alligators or sharks.

Humans are as intricately detailed as the animals and environments. During my playthrough, I didn’t see a single NPC who resembled another. I’m also impressed that certain character types appear only in specific neighborhoods, which adds to the realism. You can spend all day people-gazing, as the fine folks of Leonidas always have something interesting to say. But as with exploring the wilds, keep a weapon handy for when someone inevitably tries to mug you.

I played on a PS5 Pro, which, like all consoles that GTA 6 is available on, is capped at 30 frames per second. During my time, I never once saw the frame rate dip, even during intense shootouts or fast-moving chase sequences. Naturally, your experience may differ, even if you’re also playing on a PS5 Pro, but I never encountered performance issues. And though I wish we could have gotten at least 40 fps on the PS5 Pro, the locked 30 fps runs as smoothly as possible.

Beyond the gorgeous visuals, the GTA 6 experience isn’t complete without its incredible soundtrack. With over 22 radio stations featuring dozens of songs, there’s no shortage of awesome tracks to play while you commit crimes.

As before, you get a nice mix of stations featuring contemporary and classic tunes. There are also a handful of talk radio stations, which have always been a favorite of mine. Every station has an eclectic DJ or two to keep things lively. The radio stations also round out the world of GTA 6, offering entertaining insights on celebrities, famous establishments, current news, and more.

The original tunes are just as nice as the expansive licensed soundtrack. You mostly hear this music during cinematic scenes, but it also pops up when you’re fleeing the cops. There’s also a particular track from rap duo Bau-Luxe that will have you laughing out loud because of its obscene lyrics that I won’t even hint at here!

This has been one of my longer game reviews, and even it only scratches the surface of the GTA 6 experience. Suffice it to say, you can (and some will) sink countless hours into this world and still not see everything Rockstar managed to cram into it. Like an expensive drink you can buy in Vice City, this is a title you’ll want to savor, not rush.

GTA 6 is everything we could have hoped for and more. Despite a few minor quibbles, nothing here detracts significantly. I’ve never given a game I’ve reviewed at Tom’s Guide a full five stars, but if any game deserves that honor, it’s certainly GTA 6. It’s a once-in-a-generation title that shows what’s possible when you give a talented team the budget and time to craft something exceptional. GTA 6 really is that damn good!

Tony is a computing writer at Tom’s Guide covering laptops, tablets, Windows, and iOS. During his off-hours, Tony enjoys reading comic books, playing video games, reading speculative fiction novels, and spending too much time on X/Twitter. His non-nerdy pursuits involve attending Hard Rock/Heavy Metal concerts and going to NYC bars with friends and colleagues. His work has appeared in publications such as Laptop Mag, PC Mag, and various independent gaming sites.

#3119. Community-Focused Academic Brings AI Tools to Colorado Farmers

This senior member’s chatbot helps them start agritourism businesses

Willie Jones covers transportation for IEEE Spectrum and the history of technology for The Institute.

Alice Dong has created an AI chatbot website that helps Colorado farmers plan and operate agribusinesses that draw visitors to their properties.

Many farmers and ranchers in eastern Colorado are curious about artificial intelligence, but they don’t have a local tech-savvy person to show them how to use it. Xue “Alice” Dong has made that her job.

Dong, an IEEE senior member, is an extension regional specialist with the Colorado State University Extension, CSU’s outreach arm. She works in Logan County and serves a 10-county farming area in Colorado’s northeast corner. Her job is to turn university research into practical help for the people who live there.

Xue “Alice” Dong Employer Colorado State University Extension in Logan CountyTitle Extension regional specialistMember grade Senior memberAlma maters Inner Mongolia Normal University, in Hohhot; Beijing Normal University; State University of New York College of Environmental Science and Forestry, in Syracuse; Colorado State University Global

Colorado State University Extension in Logan County

Inner Mongolia Normal University, in Hohhot; Beijing Normal University; State University of New York College of Environmental Science and Forestry, in Syracuse; Colorado State University Global

She built the AI-Powered Agritourism Chatbot (AgriTourismAI.com), which helps farmers and ranchers launch and run “agritourism” businesses. Agritourism is when farmers open their property to visitors for fun, education, or shopping events. Familiar examples include pick-your-own fruit orchards, lessons on how to grow vegetables, and sales of handmade products.

Dong also teaches workshops where she shows farmers and ranchers how they can use AI tools to help grow and manage their business.

She says she sees herself as a link between the university and the countryside.

“We [extension specialists] act as a bridge,” she says. “We bridge our campus to the rural communities we serve.”

Many farmers and ranchers are older, and they typically have no technical training. Often their children and grandchildren have left the farm to work in a city or otherwise aren’t around to teach them about new tools. Without help, the benefits of AI could pass the farmers by. Dong’s workshops give them a way in.

Dong was named a finalist in the 2026 GenAI for Good Challenge for her AgriPivot AI Agent. The challenge was organized by IEEE Humanitarian Technologies and theU.N.’s International Telecommunication Union, and her project was selected from 318 teams across 79 countries. She also won the 2026 Award for Innovation from the National Extension Technology Community (NETC), and both the 2025 national and Western regional Educational Technology Awards from the National Association of Community Development Extension Professionals (NACDEP).

She has secured seven competitive grants totaling more than US $250,000 as principal investigator or co-principal investigator, including funding supported by the Department of Agriculture’s National Institute of Food and Agriculture.

Dong was born in Beijing. Both her parents are doctors.

As a child, she liked drawing new and inventive things. Sketching, she says, lets her picture solutions to problems in her head and put them on paper as practical designs.

That habit grew into a way of relating to her surroundings.

“I’ve always had a passion to create something tangible that can solve problems in the real world,” she says.

She doesn’t credit a single mentor for the direction her life has taken. Instead, she says all her teachers helped lay the groundwork for her career.

She attended the Inner Mongolia Normal University, in Hohhot, an institution that trains teachers. She earned two bachelor’s degrees there in 2013—one in geographical science and one in education.

She then earned a master’s degree in curriculum and instruction from Beijing Normal University in 2016.

That year, she moved to the United States to continue her graduate studies at the State University of New York College of Environmental Science and Forestry, in Syracuse. She earned a master’s degree in environmental biology in 2020.

After earning her second master’s degree, she joined Paul Smith’s College, in Paul Smiths, N.Y., as an education and outreach coordinator.

She managed several national watershed projects to protect rivers, lakes, and aquifers. Watersheds are areas of land from which water drains into bodies of water.

She also undertook invasive-species-prevention projects, wrote grants to secure project funding, and designed two educational websites and several outreach publications. One website, Maintain the Chain, helps lake residents, boaters, and visitors from around the world keep invasive species out of the Fulton Chain of Lakes in New York’s Adirondack Park.

In 2022, she joined Stewards of the Coast and Redwoods as program manager. The nonprofit, based in Guerneville, Calif., works with California State Parks to protect, restore, and educate the public about the parks along Sonoma County’s coast and the Russian River area. The region is known for its redwood forests, wineries, and resort towns.

She left in 2023 to join the CSU Extension as a regional specialist, a title she still holds.

Her employer is part of the Cooperative Extension System, a nationwide network run by land-grant universities, schools founded with federal grants to teach farming and other practical subjects. Extension faculty and staff share what researchers at their universities learn with the citizens of those states.

The cooperative system operates on three levels. It is overseen federally by the Department of Agriculture’s National Institute of Food and Agriculture, managed statewide through land-grant universities, and delivered locally by county offices and Extension agents across more than 3,000 counties.

The work goes well beyond farming, Dong says, also covering community and economic development, health initiatives, and the 4-H program, which teaches children hands-on skills in agriculture, science, leadership, and citizenship.

Extension faculty members’ performance is judged on their research, teaching, and service to the community, Dong says—similar to the way professors in academia are evaluated. The difference, she says, is the audience: Professors teach students; most extension specialists teach adults, including farmers, ranchers, and community leaders. The setting is different, too. Dong doesn’t commute from the campus to the countryside; she lives and works in it. Her office is in Sterling, a small rural town. But her projects serve the whole state, and many of the people she helps live one to four hours’ drive away. So, most of her work with farmers and ranchers happens by email, phone, and virtual meetings. County fairs, farmers markets, and agricultural events give her chances to meet large groups of them in person.

She can’t just hand Colorado residents research findings and expect them to figure out the information they need, she says.

“We need to translate that research into something more practical, and easier to use, that farmers and ranchers can understand immediately,” she says.

Dong also focuses not on only on whether people use AI, but also on how they use it. In 2026, she and Paul Hill from Utah State University Extension published “From Access to Governance: Generative AI Literacy for Extension Professionals and Small Businesses, and a Governance-Aware Design Framework” in the journal AI. The paper offers a framework for helping Extension professionals and small businesses adopt generative AI responsibly.

In 2025, Dong earned a third master’s degree, in artificial intelligence and machine learning, from CSU Global.

She immediately put those skills to work on agritourism, she says. She built the chatbot in Python, a popular programming language. It answers typed questions, and its user interface looks much like ChatGPT’s, but it works differently. Under the hood, it uses retrieval-augmented generation, a technique that has the AI look up information in a set of trusted documents before it answers. Dong curated that collection from Extension publications, so the chatbot’s answers rest on authoritative sources and are less likely to be made up. She presented the project at NeurIPS 2025 (Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems). The code is openly available on GitHub, so other Extension offices can adapt it.

The bot runs in a web browser rather than as a phone app. Many farmers she works with don’t own a smartphone, Dong says, but nearly all have a computer, tablet, or other gadget that can connect to a website. The bot works on any of them, with no app to download.

Extension specialists “act as a bridge. We bridge our campus to the rural communities we serve.”

Farmers often ask the bot how to attract visitors and how to write a business plan. A farmer thinking about opening a corn maze, for example, can ask how to price admission, what kind of insurance to carry, and which permits to get. The bot also gives advice on managing risk.

One of her test sites was Prairie Ridge Buffalo Ranch, in eastern Colorado. Dong documented how the ranch put AI to work in a peer-reviewed case study, “Revolutionizing Agritourism with AI and Machine Learning: A Case Study of Prairie Ridge Buffalo Ranch in Colorado,” published in 2025 in CABI Tourism Cases.

Surveys and interviews she conducted with other users showed that people find it’s easy to use the bot, learn from it, and act on its advice, she says. She is preparing the full results for publication.

Her work extends beyond agritourism. In 2026, she contributed an AI assistant to Project Pythia, an open-science program funded by the U.S. National Science Foundation and led by the National Center for Atmospheric Research (NCAR). The AI assistant turns raw airport weather report data into plain-language guidance for farmers and other non-technical users, and it tells users when data is missing rather than guessing.

She also teaches workshops on AI tools such as ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini. She has taught her workshop 20 times to more than 200 entrepreneurs and business owners, who came from 32 Colorado counties. In follow-up surveys, 90 percent of participants reported trying at least one new AI task in their business. Some of the workshops take place at a community center run by the Logan County Economic Development Corp., in Sterling. She has also co-hosted the workshops with the Rural Community Assistance Corp., Colorado Startup Week, and Boulder Startup Week. And she occasionally presents them as webinars, so people don’t have to travel.

Her outreach has taught her that many farmers are eager to try new tools, she says. She shows them how simple her chatbot is to use.

She also offers advice to high school students drawn to the field. Extension specialists each have a specialty, such as livestock, natural resources, food systems, or 4-H. Students should pick one based on their passion, she says.

Land-grant universities offer related programs at the bachelor’s and master’s levels. For graduate students, she adds, Extension offers a third career path beyond academia and industry: “You apply advanced skills directly to the communities that need them.”

Dong joined IEEE in 2025 and soon was elevated to senior member. Her professional home is the IEEE Society on Social Implications of Technology. She also serves as vice treasurer of the IEEE Denver Section’s Young Professionals group.

IEEE supports all three parts of her job, she says. For research, she presented “Entrepreneur AI Agent: Empowering Small Businesses and Bridging the Digital Divide through Context-Aware Generative AI” at the 2026 IEEE Global Humanitarian Technology Conference (GHTC). For teaching, she has offered to bring her AI workshop to Denver Section members and local entrepreneurs. For service, she reviews papers for IEEE conferences.

IEEE conferences matter most to her, she says: “Through them, I can present my research and network with other researchers in the field.”

She attended the IEEE World Forum on Public Safety Technology in Boulder, Colo., in September 2026. The event, she says, opened her eyes to many new projects underway across IEEE.

Still, she says, her work always points back to the farms and ranches of eastern Colorado. Its people are curious, she says, but they can’t make the leap to new technology alone.

“They really need this kind of a bridge,” she says.

Willie Jones is an associate editor at IEEE Spectrum. In addition to editing and planning daily coverage, he manages several of Spectrum's newsletters and contributes regularly to the monthly Big Picture section that appears in the print edition.
