#3081. Kohl's: 3 Key Takeaways for Long-Term Investors

Fixed-cost discipline means each extra point of same-store sales growth drops more directly to profit, so the margin story hinges on whether sales keep climbing.

By The Motley Fool Team – Nov 24, 2026 at 7:43PM EST

On its third-quarter 2026 earnings call, held on Nov. 24, 2026, Kohl's (KSS +19.48%) announced a return to top-line growth with positive comparable sales of 1.2%. Operational discipline expanded operating margins while inventory shifts improved core product availability across store locations. Store sales rebounded as budget-conscious shoppers turned to private brands for value. Three takeaways from management's comments reveal how the business is repositioning itself.

In an environment where inflation presses family budgets, shoppers are seeking affordability without sacrificing style. Management expanded inventory depth for store brands to capture budget-conscious consumers who want dependable quality.

Kohl's simplified its floor displays by cutting total choice counts while stocking deeper on core items. This trip-assurance strategy helped physical stores return to positive comparable sales during the period.

Maintaining cost discipline allows revenue gains to flow directly to the bottom line. Executive commentary highlights that modest sales growth unlocks operating leverage across the store network.

Customer demand is shifting toward value price points heading into the holiday season, and leadership isn't hiding its focus on capturing early seasonal traffic. Convenient store locations and expanded same-day delivery partnerships provide structural advantages in fulfillment. Leadership is watching inventory flow and pricing discipline to protect margin progress.

#3080. TIME’s Top 100 Photos of 2026 list includes a shot taken on iPhone 18 Pro

In September, Apple held a photography exhibition in New York City to show off the iPhone 18 Pro camera. Now, an image of the Bugaboo Mountains from that exhibit, shot by photographer Jimmy Chin, is included in TIME’s Top 100 Photos.

TIME publishes its Top 100 Photos list each year. The list showcases the pictures that the TIME Photo Department determines best capture that particular year.

The essence of TIME’s Photos of the Year, selected by our photo editors and presented below, is the authentic, sometimes staggering, reality captured by photojournalism. Someone was there. A news photographer lifted a viewfinder, pressed a button, and captured an instant happening in front of them.

Chin’s image was shot in Bugaboo Provincial Park, Canada, on iPhone 18 Pro. He explained that a traditional production creates a layer of separation between the photographer and the subject, with equipment, crew, and all the moving parts of a shoot. Shooting on iPhone 18 Pro meant that he could create a more intimate environment, allowing for a sense of comfort and spontaneity that comes through in the images.

Image Courtesy of Apple (as featured in the What Holds Us exhibition)

Chin’s goal was to capture the intersection of human ambition and the pursuit of wonder against the backdrop of a timeless natural landscape.

“The resolution and the sharpness on iPhone 18 Pro surprised me. I could shoot a few inches of rock and ice, or a massive panorama, and trust it would hold at size. That is what this work needed. It also meant I carried almost nothing. In the mountains, everything you carry is a decision. I was not thinking about gear. I was thinking about what was in front of me.”

Apple’s “What Holds Us” exhibit ran in New York City in September, featuring work from photographers Alex Prager, Jack Davison, and Jimmy Chin, with each artist using the iPhone 18 Pro to explore the “people, places, and ideas that connect and ground humanity.” Kathy Ryan, the former longtime director of photography for The New York Times Magazine, curated the exhibition.

The exhibit is now headed to London, where it will open to the public on December 4, from 10 a.m. to 8 p.m. It will also be open from Saturday, December 12 through Sunday, December 13, from 10 a.m. to 6 p.m.

You can view the full list of this year’s TIME 100 Photos right here.

#3078. CAD images suggest iPhone 18e will have an odd new camera design

CAD images of the iPhone 18e, said to come from a previously reliable source, have shown a rather odd new design for the camera bump.

If accurate, it would represent a big change from its predecessor, which simply has a single lens protruding without a surrounding bump or plateau …

The iPhone 17e was launched in March with a design unchanged from last year’s iPhone 16e. While the camera did get some feature enhancements, including the ability to store depth information for portrait photos, the physical camera design remained the same.

The current model has a single lens protruding directly from the casing with a flush-mounted flashlight next to it. Engadget reports on CAD images showing a very different approach with next year’s iPhone 18e.

The renders show an almost square camera bump measuring about 28 mm by 35 mm that houses the single rear camera, the LED flash and the rear microphone.

The site doesn’t share the images, but says that the camera bump looks similar to that of the M5 iPad Pro, shown below.

It’s unclear what might have prompted the change of design, especially as the site’s Filipe Espósito says he’s also seen CAD models for the standard model iPhone 18 or the iPhone Air 2, neither of which adopt it.

Previous reports have suggested that the only spec change with the iPhone 18e over its predecessor will be performance improvements thanks to the A20 chip.

You can now grab a single Apple AirTag for just $18 at Amazon, down from its usual $29 price.

And if you're an Android user, there's a pretty good deal for you as well. The Moto Tag 2, which offers many of the same features as Apple's AirTag, is currently down to just $19 at Amazon.

Apple's latest AirTag features an improved Precision Finding range, a 50% louder speaker, and up to a year of battery life. It works seamlessly with Apple's Find My network and is now down to just $18 (38% off).

The second-generation AirTag offers up to 1.5 times the Precision Finding range of its predecessor. Apple has also upgraded the built-in speaker, making it 50% louder than the original AirTag, and features a new, more distinctive chime. this makes it a lot easier to locate your belongings when they're nearby.

One of the biggest reasons to get an AirTag over most other Apple Find My-compatible trackers, though, is Precision Finding. While other key finders and trackers also let you locate your belongings through the Find My app warn you if you leave something behind, the AirTag takes things a step further with its ultra-wideband (UWB) technology.

If you've misplaced your keys somewhere around the house, for example, you can simply open the Find My app on a compatible iPhone, and it'll show you exactly which direction to walk in and how far away your AirTag is — rather than just relying on a sound to locate it.

And if you're planning to put AirTags on multiple belongings, there's also a deal on the AirTag four-pack, which is currently down to $79 from its usual $99 price. That said, at $18 apiece, buying four individual AirTags actually works out slightly cheaper.

If you're on the Android side of things, the Moto Tag 2 is arguably one of the best alternatives to Apple's AirTag. Much like Apple's AirTag, the Moto Tag 2 features ultra-wideband technology, which means you can use precision finding on compatible Android phones to pinpoint the location of your items.

It also works with Google's Find Hub network, so you can locate your items even when they're outside your phone's Bluetooth range.

The Moto Tag 2 brings an AirTag-like tracking experience to Android with UWB Precision Finding, Google's Find Hub integration, over 600 days of battery life, and IP68 water resistance. It's currently down to just $19 from $30.

But there are a couple of things the Moto Tag 2 does even better than Apple's AirTag. For starters, Motorola claims over 600 days of battery life, which is considerably longer than the year of battery life Apple promises. You can also use the button on the Moto Tag 2 as a remote camera shutter, which is particularly handy for taking group photos or selfies.

You also get features like left-behind notifications and an IP68 dust- and water-resistance rating, so you don't have to worry too much about attaching it to your backpack or other belongings you carry outdoors.

On the whole, I think $20 is a pretty reasonable amount to spend on something that could save you a lot of trouble if you ever lose your keys or luggage. And if you've been holding off on buying an item tracker for your phone, now's a pretty good time to get one, regardless of whether you use an iPhone or an Android phone.

#3076. iPhone Handoff: Here’s the latest on carrier availability and pricing

iPhone Handoff is a new feature in iOS 27 that lets you use the same phone number across two different iPhones. However, the feature requires carrier support, so it isn’t available to everyone. Here are the carriers that currently support iPhone Handoff and those that have promised support.

9to5Mac is sponsored by Sony: Score Sony’s INZONE noise-canceling earbuds for 38% off. These deliver immersive 360 Spatial Sound, active noise canceling, low-latency wireless connectivity, and much more.

With iPhone Handoff, you can use the same phone number on two different iPhones. Your number automatically moves between the two phones, depending on which one you pick up. This includes calls, voicemail, messages, and Find My location.

Simply unlock whichever device you want to use and you’re ready to go. Other data synced with iCloud will automatically update across your devices. Third-party apps work across both devices, following each app’s own syncing behavior.

iPhone Handoff is available on iOS 27 and later. The phones must be connected to Wi-Fi, share the same Apple Account, use Messages in iCloud, and be signed into FaceTime and iMessage with the same Apple Account.

The biggest limiting factor of iPhone Handoff is that it requires carrier support. Currently, just three carriers support the feature:

What about carriers that are working on the feature? In the United States, Verizon has promised it “will support iPhone Handoff,” but it’s unclear when the feature will launch. Verizon says it will charge $10 per month for the service.

AT&T, meanwhile, has no plans to support iPhone Handoff. In a statement in September, the carrier said that its focus “remains on delivering innovations that make life simpler and keep customers connected with confidence.” The carrier noted that there “could be potential in capabilities like iPhone Handoff,” but that customers should use “existing eSIM activation and transfer options” instead.

No other carriers have promised support for iPhone Handoff, so it’s unclear how quickly the feature will expand around the world.

In my testing, iPhone Handoff works really well. I have it set up between my iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone Duo. I use the iPhone Duo 90% of the time, but when I do pick up my iPhone 18 Pro, my number instantly switches to it. There’s a cute animation that expands from the Dynamic Island, confirming that the number has moved.

Have you tried iPhone Handoff? Are you willing to pay extra for it? Let us know down in the comments.

#3075. OpenAI reportedly hires from the CIA as foreign spies target AI labs

A Russian charged with stalking Palantir staff, a bug in an OpenAI meeting room and the Nvidia affair have put state espionage on Silicon Valley’s agenda. Anthropic’s IPO filing warns of fake job applicants.

Sam Altman speaking at Semafor’s Silicon Valley conference, November 2026

OpenAI has hired from the CIA and walls off parts of its offices with “tented spaces” and turnstiles, the Financial Times reported on Tuesday. Anthropic has recruited from the US intelligence community for “internal risk” roles that watch its own staff. Both are defences against state espionage, which the FT says now targets the biggest tech companies.

In a Big Read for the Financial Times, Patrick McGee and Rafe Rosner-Uddin describe how Big Tech is catching up with spying by hostile governments. The paper cites a person familiar with each company’s plans. At Meta, the Superintelligence Lab sits in a Menlo Park building that other staff cannot enter. Even senior vice-presidents need prior approval to visit, the FT reported.

OpenAI hired Aristedes Mahairas, an FBI veteran of nearly 24 years, as its global head of corporate security in August 2025. Its board includes Paul Nakasone, a retired general who once ran the National Security Agency. At OpenAI’s offices, private and public meeting rooms sit in separate areas with different access rules, according to the FT.

“We take protecting our technology, data and people seriously and as a matter of national importance,” OpenAI said in a statement to the FT.

Last year, Anthropic set up a national security advisory council that includes former senator Roy Blunt and David Cohen, twice a CIA deputy director. The company told the FT it runs strict personnel vetting, access controls, and insider-risk monitoring.

Its filing with the SEC before last week’s listing names the threat directly. It also warns that state-backed actors and competitors could pressure staff after they join.

“We have been and expect that we will continue to be targeted by individuals seeking employment under false identities,” Anthropic wrote in the filing.

In October, OpenAI’s security team found a recording device behind a television in a meeting room used by executives. It came wrapped in toilet paper, according to the FT, and the company called the FBI. Federal agents arrested Abdulrahman Alfozan, a former OpenAI engineer and Saudi national, on wiretapping charges. He has pleaded not guilty, and his trial starts in January. His lawyers call him an “overly curious tinkerer” with no harmful intent. Sam Altman also spoke about the bug when he told a Semafor audience that OpenAI’s security had not been perfect.

Last week, the US Justice Department indicted Igor D’iu, a Russian national, on four counts. Prosecutors say Russian handlers sent him to watch staff at a Silicon Valley technology and defence company because it supplied weapons used against Russia in Ukraine. The department did not name the company. The FT identifies it as Palantir.

According to the Justice Department, D’iu photographed employees’ laptop screens in a coffee shop near the company’s Palo Alto office. He also followed one employee for nearly 30 miles. FBI agents later found a notebook with profiles of at least three staff, including their family members’ names and assessments of their strengths and weaknesses.

Nvidia is the third case. On Monday, its board reinstated Jensen Huang as chief executive, 11 days after he resigned. He had stepped down after reports of an affair with Alice Huang, whom US authorities consider a Chinese intelligence asset. China’s foreign ministry calls the allegations a smear. Nvidia’s board says it has no reason to believe anyone compromised national security or Nvidia’s secrets.

Greg Levesque runs Strider Technologies, a firm that tracks state-backed threats to companies. He told the FT that the Huang affair should wake up Silicon Valley.

“The biggest tech firms now operate on the scale of countries, and foreign intelligence services target them in the same way,” Levesque told the FT.

D’iu remains in federal custody. The Justice Department listed his next court appearance for 24 November.

#3073. Muse safety debate continues as the AI agent rolls out in the UK

The debate over the wisdom and safety of using Meta’s Muse AI agent continues as the app rolls out in the UK. It follows a warning by a number of regulatory bodies about the potential risks of AI agents …

Meta yesterday announced the UK availability of Muse.

Muse, Meta’s personal Al agent, is now available to adults in the UK. Think of it as a helping hand for the jobs that pile up, like chasing a refund, renewing car insurance or keeping on top of the school calendar. To get those jobs done you can connect Muse to the apps you already use, from your email and calendar to the retailer apps you shop on.

A forum representing four different UK regulatory bodies last month issued a warning about the potential dangers involved in using AI agents. The Digital Regulation Cooperation Forum said:

AI agents may amplify and accelerate risks and introduce new ones. These risks may increase as the capabilities of personal agents grow and adoption rises. Questions of consumer protection, competition and data protection – for example the risk of fraud and scams, personal information sharing not in line with user expectations and misleading recommendations, decisions or information provided – must be addressed to ensure innovation develops in ways that earn and maintain public trust.

Meta has pushed back against suggestions that Muse has accessed personal data without permission, insisting that users are in control and must approve important actions. The company has admitted to some “isolated incidents,” but says other reported breaches were either hallucinations or took place on internal versions of the app while undergoing testing. In a new blog post, Meta says:

Muse only works with the apps and services you choose to connect it to, and you control the access it gets […] Once you’ve decided what Muse is connected to and what you want it to do, with your oversight, it can handle tasks like searching, comparing and planning for you. But before it does anything like sending an email or buying something, it shows you exactly what it’s about to do and waits for your go-ahead. A separate security agent checks Muse’s actions and the information it sends out against the permissions you’ve granted. You can also choose how often it checks in with you in Settings.

At the time of writing, Muse remains the second most popular free app in Apple’s US App Store, with more than 10 million downloads. We reported yesterday that some banks are already blocking AI agents, while others are warning that they will not be responsible for the consequences of any actions taken by them.

#3072. iOS 27 breaks 15 years of muscle memory on iPhone and iPad

Since iOS 5 in 2011, the iPhone and iPad have included Notification Center, a central place to find alerts from various apps in chronological order.

Starting with iOS 27, Apple is making a major change to how users open Notification Center on iPhone and iPad.

iOS 27 is here after a summer of beta releases. The behavior changed slightly between the first two releases. However, this change shipped, and I’m still adjusting to it.

Opening Notification Center is unchanged on iOS 27 and iPadOS 27 by default. However, enabling Siri AI changes a key swipe gesture on both iPhone and iPad.

One of the many ways of invoking Siri AI, once enabled, is by swiping down from the center of the top edge of your iPhone or iPad display. This previously opened Notification Center.

You can still access Notification Center by swiping down from the top-left corner once Siri AI is enabled. Alerts now animate in from the top left corner. This is a way to point users toward Notification Center’s smaller surface area.

Apple is greatly prioritizing Siri AI access in iOS 27. The majority of the top edge is devoted to invoking the new Siri experience.

The last time Apple made a change to accessing Notification Center came when Control Center moved from a swipe up gesture from the bottom to a top-right corner swipe down gesture on iPhone X. Apple later unified this experience across devices.

Now it’s Notification Center’s turn to be put in the corner. On iPadOS 27 beta 1 in particular, the area above Home screen app icons was pretty much devoted to invoking Siri AI. The area for opening Notification Center actually shrank if you disable displaying AM/PM or the date.

I've been always swiping from the left corner to see my notifications. I didn't even know you could swipe from the center to get to it as well 😂 I guess I'm good then?

Apple improved this with iPadOS 27 beta 2, creating a more uniform region on either side. It’s roughly the size of two app columns with Notification Center on the left and Control Center on the right. The rest is for invoking Siri.

After 15 years of muscle memory, it’ll take some time to determine if this change is worth it or something that should be reconsidered. In the meantime, early feedback sounds overwhelmingly positive around Apple’s new Siri AI system. Hearing that Siri is good now will also take some getting used to, I’m sure.

After months of using the new behavior, I’m certain I’d toggle it off if there were a setting to do so. Since there’s no option to disable invoking Siri from the top middle swipe down, the only thing to do is build new muscle memory around avoiding the center.

What do you think? Would you change this back if you could? Is accessing Siri from the swipe-down gesture worth the change? Share your thoughts in the comments.

#3071. Microsoft declares ‘Code Red’ after its worst email outage, Reuters reports

Engineers traded 11,000 messages across 11 Teams chats during the outage. Under the Microsoft Code Red, the company now wants to resolve any global incident within an hour.

The Microsoft logo on the side of one of its office buildings.

Microsoft has declared a “Code Red” to change how it prevents and handles major outages, Reuters reported on Tuesday, citing internal memos. The Microsoft Code Red follows the global outage of 12 to 13 November. It knocked out Exchange Online, Outlook, Teams and Copilot for about 24 hours.

Jaspreet Singh broke the story in a Reuters exclusive. Jason Henderson, president of M365 Core, called it the most customer-impacting incident in Exchange Online’s history. Never before had so many customers gone without email for so long, he told staff in a memo on Friday. The outage hit governments from Australia and Japan to the US, delayed trading firms, and disrupted airline communications.

“Code Red means that this is the highest priority work for our team,” Henderson wrote, according to Reuters.

Amanda Silver oversees M365 Core and Work IQ as a corporate vice-president. She described the response in a separate memo on Monday. Engineers worked through a “fog of war”, she wrote. Responders sent more than 11,000 messages across 11 Teams chats.

Diagnostic data sat in separate internal tracking systems. As a result, the team struggled to keep one shared picture of its theories and decisions, Silver wrote.

Charles Lamanna is Microsoft’s executive vice-president for Copilot, Agents and Platform. He told a Code Red review that the failed part had seen “roughly ten years’ worth of acceptable failures”, according to Silver’s memo.

Microsoft has blamed a dormant July defect in Windows for the outage, a scalability bug that went undetected for months. Chief executive Satya Nadella apologised publicly. Microsoft says cyber activity and AI agents played no part.

Silver set out five workstreams under the Code Red, covering load shedding, splitting traffic by region, and faster recovery. Microsoft wants to resolve future incidents worldwide within an hour. It also plans to use AI agents to help engineers read system health data faster.

Henderson will hold daily meetings with the Substrate leadership team, plus weekly reviews. Substrate runs the engineering behind Microsoft 365’s core services. A Microsoft spokesperson told Reuters that its teams keep working around the clock to apply the lessons learned.

Earlier this month, Henderson wrote that urgent patches to M365 Core services took too long to reach users worldwide. In one recent incident, an urgent fix took five to six days. For the most urgent security issues, he wants an hour from detection to safe worldwide deployment. Microsoft is not there yet, he wrote.

Last week, Nadella said that AI-found bugs will make outages more likely. Henderson also wrote that he had reviewed the organisational and structural problems behind the failure.

“Unfortunately, all the work we have done over the years was not sufficient to protect us on Thursday,” Henderson wrote.

#3068. iOS 27 adds new Messages app setting I instantly started using

iOS 27 brought several new features to the Messages app, including a setting that’s long been a popular request: the ability to customize or turn off the audio button. Here’s how to use it.

With iOS 27, Apple fixed a lot of bugs and also granted many feature requests from over the years.

Siri AI is the biggest example of that, offering a big upgrade over the old Siri. But smaller changes in apps like Calendar, Mail, and Messages reflect this focus on wish fulfillment.

In Messages, there’s a new setting that I instantly starting using. It lets you turn off the audio button that normally lives on the right side of the text input field.

The audio button has been conveniently accessible there for years, but I never use it. I don’t think I’ve ever sent an audio message. Sometimes I use dictation, but that’s always available from the bottom-right of the keyboard.

Since I never need that button, the only time it gets pressed is by accident. And as I suspect a lot of users have encountered—including Justin Bieber—it’s very easy to hit by accident.

Thankfully, iOS 27 has the fix. To disable the audio button, follow these steps:

Even if you turn the audio button off, you can still send audio messages by hitting the + button to open your iMessage apps then selecting ‘Audio.’

If you prefer to keep the button active, you can alternately now select ‘Record Audio’ or ‘Start Dictation’ as its function. That way the button will always stay set to your preference instead of dynamically changing like it did before.

Will you disable the audio button in Messages? Let us know in the comments.

#3066. Kaszek closes $650M fund to back AI startups across Latin America

The MercadoLibre veterans beat their $600M target, even as venture fundraising in the region stays weak.

Kaszek co-founder Hernán Kazah speaks on centre stage at Web Summit Rio in April 2025.

Kaszek Ventures has raised $650M for its seventh early-stage fund, which it says is the largest ever for Latin America. It will back 20 to 30 AI startups, mostly in Brazil and Mexico, at a time when only 14 venture funds have closed in the region this year.

Kaszek Ventures, Latin America’s largest venture capital firm, has raised $650M to back early-stage startups building with AI, Bloomberg reported on Tuesday. The firm says it is the largest early-stage fund ever raised for the region.

The fund, Kaszek’s seventh for early-stage deals, beat its $600M target. Its last one, closed in 2023, raised $540M. Washington University in St. Louis and the Wellcome Trust are among the backers.

Kaszek plans to back 20 to 30 companies, starting at pre-seed and seed. It will keep about 60% of the money for their later rounds.

Most of the focus is on what Kaszek calls the “application layer” of AI. That means startups using language models in fields such as finance, health care and online marketplaces. Co-founder Hernán Kazah told Bloomberg he sees the most room in services for businesses.

“It’s a more natural fit for the types of problems that exist in Latin America,” Kazah said. Many firms there still rely on manual processes, he added, and services can be costly or hard to reach.

The fund is also looking at AI infrastructure such as data centres and chips. Kazah pointed to the region’s energy, land and closeness to the US. Power shortages, though, have held back data centres in Mexico.

Brazil and Mexico will stay its biggest markets, with Argentina and Colombia on the rise. Kaszek was founded in 2011 by former MercadoLibre executives Kazah and Nicolas Szekasy. Its portfolio includes digital bank Nubank, QuintoAndar and Kavak.

The raise stands out in a weak market. PitchBook ranks it the largest Latin America-focused venture fund to close since 2023. Only 14 venture funds closed in the region through September, it says, against 68 in all of 2023.

AI startups can still draw big cheques, though. In August, Brazil’s Decade, an AI wealth adviser built by former Nubank staff, raised an $85M seed round.

#3065. iPad Air vs iPad Pro: Which should you buy?

Apple’s iPad lineup is incredibly strong, and two standout options are the iPad Air and iPad Pro. If you’re trying to decide whether the iPad Pro is worth the extra cost this holiday season, here’s everything you need to know.

Bonus pick: The all-new iPad mini is up to $100 off for Black Friday as well.

Apple updated the iPad Air earlier this year, bringing the M4 chip for improved performance along with 12GB of RAM, up from 8GB in the previous generation.

The iPad Air is available in 11-inch and 13-inch screen sizes, and uses an LCD display with a 60Hz refresh rate. This means it doesn’t offer OLED or ProMotion, unlike the iPad Pro. It uses Touch ID for biometric authentication, supports the Magic Keyboard and Apple Pencil Pro, and offers the full iPadOS multitasking experience.

The iPad Air is available in four colors: blue, purple, starlight, and space gray. It starts at 128GB of storage and can be configured up to 1TB.

The iPad Pro is the best iPad money can buy. It’s powered by Apple’s M5 chip and offers many advantages over the iPad Air.

The biggest difference is the display technology. The iPad Pro is available in 11-inch and 13-inch sizes and uses Apple’s Ultra Retina XDR display with tandem OLED technology. This means it offers deeper blacks, better contrast, and higher brightness than the LCD screen found in the iPad Air.

The iPad Pro also supports ProMotion with adaptive refresh rates up to 120Hz. This means scrolling, animations, Apple Pencil interactions, and more will be significantly smoother.

Contrary to what the naming implies, the iPad Pro is also noticeably thinner and lighter than the iPad Air. The 11-inch iPad Pro measures 5.3mm thick, while the 13-inch model is even thinner at 5.1mm.

The iPad Pro offers Face ID instead of Touch ID, Thunderbolt connectivity, a four-speaker audio system, and nano-texture display options with the higher-end configuration.

For most people, the iPad Air is the right choice. It delivers the entire iPad experience, excellent performance, and comes in four fun colors and two different screen sizes.

The iPad Pro is the best iPad you can buy, but it’s overkill for most people. Don’t get me wrong, I love my iPad Pro. If it’s in your holiday budget, it’s a fantastic choice. I can’t overstate how impressive the tandem OLED display is. It’s significantly better than the LCD screen on the iPad Air. It’s also great having Face ID in the iPad form factor.

The iPad Pro is slightly more tempting at its current sale price, with the mid-range 13-inch model at an impressive $350 off.

Still, both the iPad Air and iPad Pro run the same iPadOS experience, and that’s why I think the iPad Air is the better value for most people. What do you think? Let us know down in the comments.

#3062. Anthropic’s new Siren test tempts Claude to break out of its sandbox

Newer Claude models often reach outside weak sandboxes, but rarely misuse what they find there.

J.Crew built its new Style Advisor with several of Anthropic’s Claude models.

Anthropic has published Siren, a test that tempts Claude agents to leave deliberately flawed sandboxes. Its newest models reached outside in 21% to 32% of scenarios but made clearly misaligned use of what they found in under 2%, against 25.8% for Mythos 5. Stating the sandbox rules in the system prompt cut reaching outside by 68% to 96%.

Anthropic’s newer Claude models will often reach out of a weak sandbox to finish a task, but rarely misuse what they find, the company said on Tuesday. The findings come from Siren, a new test it now runs on Claude models before release.

AI agents often work inside a sandbox, a walled-off space that limits the files, tools and networks they can reach. Siren gives them routine IT tasks in sandboxes with a deliberate flaw. Just outside sits something that would help, such as a file or a login.

Nothing in the more than 1,700 scenarios tells a model to leave or says it may. Instead, they add pressure, such as deadlines or orders to search thoroughly.

The Claude 5.5 series and Mythos 5.2 reached outside in 21% to 32% of scenarios. But they used what they found in ways no reasonable reading allowed in just 0.6% to 1.6%. For the older Mythos 5 and Mythos 5.1, that rate was 25.8% and 12.7%.

Anthropic says it does not fully know why newer models behave better, and none was trained on Siren. The models were tested without the safeguards they ship with. Anthropic stresses the rates do not reflect real-world use.

Escapes are not hypothetical. A Mythos preview escaped its sandbox in April and emailed a researcher.

In July, Anthropic said its models had breached three companies after a test setup was wrongly left online. OpenAI also paused a model that kept breaking out.

Simple fixes helped. Describing the sandbox and six rules for staying inside it in the system prompt made models 68% to 96% less likely to reach outside. A tool to report sandbox flaws also cut the rate.

Anthropic also tuned auto mode, which checks Claude’s commands before they run, on Siren. With all three fixes, misaligned use fell to almost zero, though two models finished about nine points fewer tasks.

Anthropic says sandboxes still need to be set up and patched properly. In July, researchers showed its own Cowork app could break out on Macs and read credentials.

#3060. TIDAL will delete 29 million AI-generated songs from its catalogue

The streaming service says labels and cut royalties were not enough, as AI tracks made up 43% of recent uploads.

TIDAL will begin deleting all wholly AI-generated tracks on December 9, about 29 million songs, and expects to reject 80,000 to 85,000 more a day. It had already labelled and demonetised AI music in July, but says 43% of tracks it received in the past 90 days were AI-made.

TIDAL will start deleting every wholly AI-generated track from its catalogue on December 9, removing about 29 million songs. Robert Andersen, who leads TIDAL at parent company Block, announced the plan on X on Tuesday. TIDAL’s own account confirmed the date.

Andersen said the songs should be gone by the start of 2027. TIDAL also expects to turn away 80,000 to 85,000 AI-made tracks a day. He called it the first streaming service to take this step and urged rivals to follow.

In July, TIDAL began labelling AI tracks and cutting off their royalties. Andersen said that had not been enough.

“43% of tracks distributed to us in the last 90 days have been detected as AI-generated. Something more drastic needs to be done,” Andersen wrote.

Most of that music finds no audience. Andersen said 96% of AI-generated songs on TIDAL get zero plays.

Rivals face the same flood. More than half the music uploaded to Deezer in June was made by AI.

Others have stopped short of deleting it. Spotify has pulled 50M spam tracks from its recommendations, but left them on the service. Apple Music has made AI tags mandatory for record companies.

The cut covers only songs made wholly by AI, which TIDAL finds with detection tools. Its terms of service warn those tools can wrongly tag tracks, and users can ask support to fix a label.

#3059. Things 3.25 update brings new touch features to the MacBook Pro

Cultured Code is bringing swipe gestures to Things on Apple’s touchscreen MacBook Pro. Version 3.25 builds on the task manager’s basic touch support so you can schedule a to-do with a swipe or select several tasks with two fingers and drag them all at once.

Say you’re going through your Today list and want to put something off until tomorrow. Swipe right on the to-do to open the date picker. Open it by touch and you’ll see taller rows that make dates easier to tap. Custom menus get the same treatment.

Swiping left selects a to-do. Swipe left again to deselect it. For a longer list, swipe up or down with two fingers to select several items at once. Then touch and hold any selected item to pick up the whole group, even if some of those tasks are offscreen. You can also drag individual to-dos and headings.

A single tap selects a to-do, and a second tap expands it. Double-tapping works too. Inside a to-do, checklist items are easier to reorder by touch. You can also cancel a to-do or checklist item by pressing and holding its checkbox.

Cultured Code has also made the sidebar easier to resize with a finger and given buttons throughout the Mac app larger tap targets.

The update follows Siri AI and Spotlight integration in Things 3.24 and more flexible scheduling for repeating to-dos in Things 3.23. You can find Things for Mac on the Mac App Store.

#3056. These Billionaire Investors Made Big Bets Against Tech Stocks. Should You Worry?

Paul Singer's Elliott and Paul Tudor Jones' firm added Nasdaq put options last quarter. Their filings show those bets are less one-sided than they look.

By Jonathan Ponciano – Nov 24, 2026 at 7:48PM EST

10 stocks we like better than Invesco QQQ Trust ›

Tech stocks slid again on Tuesday, and some of the market's most famous investors have been positioning for that kind of drop. Quarterly filings show that two billionaire-run firms added big bets against the Nasdaq-100 during the third quarter.

The bets use put options, which give the holder the right to sell at a set price and generally rise in value when the underlying investment falls. The filings, called 13Fs, were made with the SEC on Nov. 16 and show holdings as of Sept. 30.

Image source: OpenAI (AI-generated illustration).

Paul Singer's Elliott Investment Management held puts on 5.46 million shares of the Invesco QQQ Trust (QQQ -1.99%), which tracks the Nasdaq-100, according to its latest 13F. The filing values them at $4.04 billion, with only its Phillips 66 and Triple Flag Precious Metals stakes representing a bigger value.

Importantly, that figure is the value of the shares the puts cover, rather than what Elliott paid for them or what it could make. The filing doesn't show the strike prices or expiration dates, so the size of the actual bet is unknown.

Three months earlier, Elliott held puts on 3.48 million QQQ shares, valued at $2.56 billion, according to its prior filing. It also raised its puts on the VanEck Semiconductor ETF (SMH -7.26%) to 800,000 shares from 250,000, covering $487 million of shares.

But Elliott isn't only betting against tech. It also reported puts covering $1.27 billion of an industrials fund, $903 million of a consumer staples fund, and $865 million of a gold miners fund. It cut its puts on a technology-software fund nearly in half, to $873 million. As a whole, the spread looks more like protection across the whole market than a single bet against tech.

Paul Tudor Jones' Tudor Investment held QQQ puts covering 8.55 million shares valued at $6.32 billion, according to its 13F. That's up from 4.74 million shares, or $3.49 billion, in its prior filing.

However, Tudor also raised its QQQ calls, which gain when the fund rises, to 7.75 million shares, or $5.74 billion. So its puts outweigh its calls, but not by much. Its biggest bearish line wasn't tech at all: puts on the iShares Russell 2000 ETF, which tracks smaller companies, covering $8.75 billion of shares.

Separately, Stanley Druckenmiller isn't betting against tech, but he isn't betting on it either. He told the TomorrowX conference in Austin this month that he's "taking a break" from stocks and is close to neutral on equities while he waits for a clearer outlook.

Not much. These filings have real limits. Besides omitting strike prices and costs, a 13F doesn't show short sales or positions in securities outside U.S.-listed securities. A put can be an outright bet on a decline, or it can be insurance for a firm that owns a lot of stocks. Both Elliott and Tudor hold billions in other positions that those puts may be protecting.

The data is also somewhat stale. The filings show positions as of Sept. 30, and these firms trade often. Any of them could have changed by now.

What the filings do show is that experienced investors are paying for protection, especially against tech stocks and the broader Nasdaq. For long-term investors, the takeaway isn't to sell. Instead, check how much of the portfolio rides on a handful of names (particularly AI names), and make sure it's an amount they can live with if selling continues.

#3055. CarPlay Ultra coming to these cars, according to Apple

Last year, Apple officially announced CarPlay Ultra, the next-generation version of CarPlay that it first teased way back at WWDC 2022.

CarPlay Ultra first launched for Aston Martin owners in the United States and Canada. What about other automakers? Here’s what we know.

9to5Mac is sponsored by Sony: Score Sony’s INZONE noise-canceling earbuds for 38% off. These deliver immersive 360 Spatial Sound, active noise canceling, low-latency wireless connectivity, and much more.

Updated November 24, 2026: Latest on Hyundai, more.

In December 2023, Apple said that Porsche and Aston Martin would be the first automakers to support next-generation CarPlay starting in 2024. That deadline came and went, and Apple confirmed in January that next-gen CarPlay had been delayed but was still in development.

Apple doesn’t offer a timeline on when CarPlay Ultra will actually be available through any other brand beyond Aston Martin. The company also does not have a dedicated list of automakers that have signed on to support CarPlay Ultra listed on its website.

When Apple announced the next-generation version of CarPlay at WWDC 2022, however, it stated that several brands had committed to supporting the platform. In May of last year, Apple touted that three new partners had signed on: Hyundai, Kia, and Genesis.

However, several brands have also dropped their plans to support CarPlay Ultra. Mercedes-Benz was originally on Apple’s list, but abandoned its plans to support next-generation CarPlay in 2024. According to the Financial Times, Audi, Volvo, Polestar, and Renault have also decided against supporting CarPlay Ultra, despite originally being touted as partners by Apple.

With all of that said, here is the full list of automakers who plan to eventually support CarPlay Ultra, as of April 2026.

What do we know beyond this list? Not a whole lot. Interestingly, Top Gear reported that the Hyundai IONIQ 3 EV would support CarPlay Ultra. Hyundai announced the IONIQ 3 in April, but has not commented on whether the vehicle will support CarPlay Ultra as rumors suggested.

Mark Gurman at Bloomberg has also reported CarPlay Ultra will launch for “least one major new Hyundai/Kia model in the second half of this year.”

While Apple has touted Ford as a partner for CarPlay Ultra, the automaker recently signaled it’s not too impressed with the first version of a platform.

In a recent interview, Ford CEO Jim Farley was asked whether the company is “considering” CarPlay Ultra support. Here’s what he said:

“We are. We don’t like the execution in round 1 of Ultra, but we’re very committed to Apple. I’ve talked to Tim many times about this.”

It’s better than a flat “no,” but perhaps not the enthusiasm Ford drivers might have hoped to hear.

The question at this point is whether any other automakers have ditched CarPlay Ultra. Ideally, Apple will provide a full list sooner rather than later, but in the meantime, this is the only information we have.

#3054. Google will make AI agents use new gateways to reach Gmail and Drive

Agents must switch from Workspace's regular APIs by February, and need a person's approval before sending email.

Google has made its Workspace MCP servers and CLI generally available and says AI agents must use them instead of existing REST APIs from February 1, 2027. Every call is checked against company policies, sensitive actions need user confirmation, and a new addendum bars AI tools from training on Workspace data.

Google will require AI agents to reach Gmail, Drive and other Workspace apps through new, dedicated gateways, it said on Tuesday. Regular apps can keep using Workspace’s existing APIs, but agents must switch by February 1, 2027.

The gateways are Workspace MCP servers, which use a common standard for linking AI tools to apps, and a command-line tool. Both are now generally available. Google put an early CLI version on GitHub in March.

Google says its APIs were built for apps that work at human speed, where a valid login meant the user wanted the action. Agents act on their own at machine speed. So every request now gets checked against company permissions and data-loss rules.

Agents can draft emails and summarise documents on their own. But they need a person’s sign-off before sending email, changing Drive sharing or making bulk edits.

Each agent also needs its own sign-in ID with tight limits and usage quotas. Google already gives its Gemini coworker agents their own accounts. It will begin billing for that usage on April 1, 2027.

A new AI Tools Addendum adds rules on data. AI tools cannot use Workspace data to train models or build rival services, and cannot scrape it. They must also delete it when a user disconnects.

Google also tells developers to screen for prompt injection, hidden commands in emails or files that can hijack AI agents. Some controls are still to come, including letting users see and revoke agents’ access themselves.

Other firms are drawing lines too. In October, Charles Schwab said it blocks outside agents from moving client money.

#3052. Trump Says Inflation Could Help Pay Down the National Debt. Here's What That Means for Your Retirement Savings

Investors must work a little harder to protect their wealth.

By Will Ebiefung – Nov 24, 2026 at 8:00PM EST

10 stocks we like better than S&P 500 Index ›

According to Bureau of Labor Statistics data, the average price of a can of soda in the U.S. is around $0.60 when bought as part of a 12-pack -- up 80% from its price in 2019. While this is an extreme example, it highlights the devastating impact inflation can have on your purchasing power and the real value of your stock market returns.

Unfortunately for investors, inflation remains a problem. And a devastating warning from President Donald Trump suggests it could get worse before it gets better. Let's dig deeper into the market's challenges and discuss strategies investors can use to stay ahead of the curve.

For many investors, the Trump era has been a bit of a headscratcher. The administration has deliberately pursued disruptive policies, such as massive tariffs that can make it harder for many U.S. companies to do business. But instead of crashing, stocks have gone gangbusters, with the S&P 500 (^GSPC -0.50%) jumping 25% since his election victory in November.

To be fair, some of this is luck. Trump has been in the right place at the right time to oversee the rise of generative artificial intelligence (AI), which has single-handedly added trillions to the value of America's tech industry. That said, White House policies have also played a role.

Trump's One Big Beautiful Bill Act helped lock in corporate tax cuts while also slashing regulations in the energy industry and introducing goodies such as allowing companies to write off certain categories of research and development expenses for tax purposes. Big tech is also happy with the administration's generally pro-AI stance, which is crucial at a time when public pushback against data center construction is growing.

That said, while Trump has managed to keep Wall Street happy so far, the administration has struggled to rein in other macroeconomic challenges that could undermine investor returns over the long haul. The biggest challenge is inflation. Tariffs and the Iran war have helped push the U.S. inflation rate to around 4% as of October, which is well above the Federal Reserve's target of 2%.

Higher inflation hurts investors' real returns and encourages the central bank to continue raising interest rates. This generally hurts stock valuations by making it harder for businesses to access the capital they need to invest in future growth.

Image source: Official White House Photo.

When asked about the situation earlier last month, Trump's response was alarming. In an interview with Time magazine, he suggested "certain levels of inflation" could help pay down the national debt "very rapidly." The logic may be that by lowering the value of the dollar, inflation will also devalue America's $40 trillion in borrowings, making it easier to manage. These remarks suggest the White House is willing to tolerate high inflation for much longer than investors will be comfortable with.

Trump's warning suggests that the U.S. government doesn't have a strong plan to bring down inflation or manage the national debt. In fact, both of these problems could get worse over the coming months as the war in Iran (along with the war in Ukraine) continues to drive up military spending and create lasting bottlenecks in the global economy.

That said, this isn't the time to panic. And it can pay to look toward the wisdom of investing legend Warren Buffett, who advised investors to never bet against America in his annual shareholder letter during the height of the COVID-19 pandemic in 2021. Over the long haul, the country has consistently bounced back from crises only to emerge stronger than ever. And there is no reason to assume this time will be the exception.

The recent midterm results have also already eased fears in the oil markets, as many traders expect the new Democrat-controlled Congress to impose more checks and balances on Trump's foreign policy.

The economic situation remains uncertain, but the long-term outlook is bright. And investors can stay ahead by increasing portfolio diversification to avoid being overly exposed to underperformance in any specific asset class.

#3050. You can now DM Meta’s Muse on Instagram to turn saves into plans

Meta's personal AI agent now takes requests in Instagram's inbox, starting with the posts you have saved.

Meta has added its Muse AI agent to Instagram direct messages, inviting users to send it a DM to turn saved posts into plans, such as a trip. Muse already worked in its own app, in WhatsApp and on Instagram profiles, and Meta says it does not read private messages unless users allow it, though Reuters reported staff found it reading encrypted chats.

Meta’s Muse AI agent can now be messaged in Instagram DMs, where it can turn posts users have saved into plans. Meta announced the change through Muse’s own Instagram account on Tuesday, using a long-planned trip as the example.

Muse launched in the US in September as an agent that books, buys and negotiates for users. It works in its own app and in WhatsApp, and later that month users could add it to their Instagram profiles.

The DM option puts Muse where the saved posts already sit. Meta has not said which countries get it. Beyond the US, Muse is live in Canada and has launched in Australia, and it reached the UK this week.

Yet Reuters reported last week that Meta staff found Muse reading encrypted messages. Meta called those isolated incidents.

Users can also make Muse ask before it sends messages or buys anything. In September, though, a YouTuber said Muse shared his address with a Facebook Marketplace buyer before asking him. Meta said it was looking into it.

#3048. Apple Home accessories: Here are my five top picks for your smart home

Apple Home is kicking off a new era with Siri AI-driven products like HomeView, making it a great time to upgrade your smart home with Apple Home-compatible accessories. Here are my top five picks.

iOS 27 upgraded Apple’s HomeKit Secure Video service (included with iCloud+) in several key ways. You’ll now get searchable videos, highlighted clips, 4K support, and more.

I have two recommendations for HomeKit Secure Video-compatible cameras. The main difference is video quality, and whether they’re designed for outdoor use or only indoors.

Smart locks have always offered convenience, but with the advent of Ultra Wideband-supported locks, they’re better than ever.

Aqara’s U400 smart lock was among the first to introduce Ultra Wideband, which enables your door to lock and unlock automatically when it senses your presence. Unlike prior smart lock automations that relied on Bluetooth, Ultra Wideband offers excellent reliability and precision for a great overall experience.

Want to open your garage door with a quick Siri command, or via CarPlay or the Home app on iPhone? Smart garage door openers with Apple Home support can deliver that, and my recommendation is the meross MSG150HK.

meross says the MSG150HK is compatible with “the vast majority of Chamberlain, Lift-Master, and Craftsman brand openers.” And it supports security features like automatic notifications when your door is left open, or every time it opens and closes.

Smart plugs are often a gateway to building out a smart home. And my favorite option, both for cost and convenience, is Tapo’s multipack of smart plugs.

Tapo sells its smart plug in a 2-pack at a great price—currently only $8 per plug. These plugs are compact and offer seamless, quick setup through the Home app without needing a separate app.

Controlling your thermostat entirely from your iPhone or a HomeView can prove extremely convenient. That convenience can also save you money by making it easier to stay on top of your electricity usage.

Aqara’s W200 smart thermostat is a beautifully designed, easy-to-use accessory that comes with a bonus Apple feature that’s hard to find: Adaptive Temperature, which can remove lots of the need to manually update the thermostat.

What are your top Apple Home accessory recommendations? Let us know in the comments.

#3047. Skip the knockoffs: Real PITAKA aramid fiber cases start at $18.99 this Black Friday

Scroll through Amazon for five minutes and you’ll find dozens of $10–20 cases that look, through a thumbnail, almost identical to $50+ aramid fiber ones. Same dark weave, same slim profile, same pitch.

Once you actually snap one onto a phone, the differences are obvious. You handle your phone for hours every day, so rough seams around the charging port, awkward cutouts, low-quality materials will make you regret your purchase instantly. With PITAKA’s Black Friday sale taking up to 30% off selected cases, it’s worth breaking down what actually separates a real aramid case from a cheap lookalike, why you should spent the extra money on PITAKA’s high-quality cases.

Plenty of budget cases get the woven look by printing a pattern onto plain plastic. If you’re looking for that style, go for it, but it won’t behave like woven aramid fiber, which lets a case stay rigid and thin without adding much weight.

Even genuine aramid cases aren’t all made the same way. The weave, resin, thickness, and surface finish all change how a case feels in use. PITAKA uses woven aramid fiber in two main weights: 600D and 1500D. Those numbers measure yarn density; the finer 600D weave feels a bit smoother and produces a slightly thinner shell than 1500D. Whatever case you choose, look past the word “premium” and check whether the maker actually spells out what the case is made of.

Most aramid cases stick to plain black and gray. PITAKA’s Fusion Weaving method blends colored fibers and multiple weave styles directly into the shell instead of printing a graphic on the outside. PITAKA says the process requires tight control over fabric tension and how fibers cross between layers. In practice, it means you can pick something colorful like the Sunset colorway without giving up the feel of woven fiber, or stick with classic Black & Grey if you prefer a quieter look.

Online listings spend almost all their time showing off the back of a case, even though your fingers spend just as much time on the sides, buttons, and bottom edge. An awkward camera cutout makes quick shots annoying, a tight port opening fights bulkier charging cables, and sharp edges dig into your hand on a long call.

Rather than selling one shell in ten colors, PITAKA splits its lineup into three builds:

If you use a magnetic charger, wallet, or grip, how the magnets are built into the case matters just as much as the outer material. Sticking a separate magnet ring inside a shell usually adds extra layers and thickness.

PITAKA’s Amber Magnet Film process bonds coated magnets directly with the aramid fiber and resin under heat and pressure. That keeps the magnets enclosed without bulking up the case, which is the kind of detail you won’t spot in a photo but will notice in your pocket.

Spending more on a case doesn’t guarantee it’s better, and plenty of $20 cases are completely fine. Genuine aramid fiber by itself doesn’t guarantee better drop protection either. A thin shell like Edge is made for people who hate bulky cases. If drop protection is your main concern, look at a cushioned option like Cairn or Summa, and compare actual edge coverage and model-specific testing instead of judging by price or material alone.

What you’re really paying for with a higher-end aramid case is how it feels and fits every time you pick up your phone.

If you already want a thinner, better-finished case, Black Friday takes some of the sting out of the price. PITAKA’s Amazon offers run November 19–30, with discounts varying by device and colorway:

Buying directly from the PITAKA official website? Code PTKPR12 takes an extra 5% off from November 10 through December 31. It’s separate from the Amazon sale, so double-check eligible products and your final total at checkout.

#3046. Anthropic Has Plunged 30% From Its Peak. Here’s the Price at Which I’d Buy.

Anthropic's historic IPO is already losing momentum, but a deeper sell-off could present a compelling buying opportunity.

By Adam Spatacco – Nov 24, 2026 at 8:00PM EST

10 stocks we like better than Anthropic ›

Following months of anticipation, artificial intelligence (AI) developer Anthropic (ANT -6.54%) made its public market debut on Nov. 19. While the maker of Claude initially received an enthusiastic reception, the excitement has been short-lived. Less than a week after going public, Anthropic stock has already started selling off.

Indeed, Anthropic's revenue is growing at an extraordinary rate. But smart investors are not overlooking the capital-intensive nature underpinning the company's expansion. Furthermore, competition across the large language model (LLM) landscape raises important questions about Anthropic's path to profitability.

Let's explore what's driving the sell-off in Anthropic stock and assess the valuation at which the company could become a compelling investment.

Anthropic completed the largest initial public offering (IPO) in history, surpassing the $75 billion raised by Space Exploration Technologies back in June. Including the full exercise of the underwriters' option to purchase additional shares, Anthropic's IPO generated $93.5 billion in gross proceeds.

The company also completed a concurrent $26 billion private placement involving Nvidia, Microsoft, Alphabet, Broadcom, Advanced Micro Devices, and Micron Technology. Combined gross proceeds from the two transactions reached $119.5 billion.

When Anthropic began trading on the Nasdaq, shares opened at $111.50, or about 34% above the offering price of $83. Shares subsequently climbed to an intraday high of $115.10 before reversing course and closing their first day of trading at $97.17. As of this writing (Nov. 24), Anthropic stock is hovering around $80, representing a decline of 30% from its high.

Some of the selling pressure likely reflects momentum traders locking in profits, but attributing the entire decline to short-term trading overlooks several important fundamental concerns.

Anthropic's growth is difficult to dispute. According to its S-1 filing, the company generated approximately $17 billion in revenue during the third quarter, representing 1,127% growth year over year. Furthermore, Anthropic ended October with an annualized revenue run rate of $81 billion.

Revenue growth is only one part of Anthropic's financial profile. The company has $900.9 billion in infrastructure and computing commitments, including $451.6 billion expected to be incurred before Dec. 31, 2030.

While these obligations shouldn't be confused with conventional debt, they illustrate the capital requirements required to develop and operate frontier AI models. Anthropic's ability to generate sustainable profits depends heavily on whether customer demand and premium pricing can justify these investments.

Anthropic competes against OpenAI's ChatGPT, Alphabet's Gemini, Meta's Muse, and an expanding ecosystem of open-weight models. As generative models become more sophisticated and less expensive to operate, Anthropic may face pressure to lower its prices while continuing to invest aggressively in computing capacity.

Unlike Alphabet or Meta Platforms, Anthropic doesn't have a mature, highly profitable advertising or cloud computing business that generates cash to help subsidize its AI infrastructure investments. As a result, investors are being asked to place enormous amounts of faith in Anthropic's ability to translate its revenue growth into durable earnings and free cash flow at some point in the future.

Given Anthropic's lack of profitability, a traditional price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio isn't particularly useful in this analysis. Instead, I'd value the company relative to its annualized revenue run rate. At $80 per share, Anthropic's market capitalization is roughly $1.1 trillion. This equates to 13.5 times its annualized revenue run rate from October.

I am more interested in Anthropic stock at $50 per share. At that price, the company would boast an implied market cap of about $690 billion, equivalent to 8.5 times its annualized revenue run rate. Anthropic's growth could allow the company to grow into this valuation relatively quickly. For example, if its annualized revenue run rate doubles to roughly $160 billion, a $690 billion valuation would represent just 4.3 times that figure.

With that said, investors shouldn't assume Anthropic's current growth trajectory will last indefinitely. Moreover, the company will need to demonstrate that its revenue can fuel sustainable free cash flow despite its infrastructure commitments.

Although Anthropic is one of the most premier businesses leading the AI revolution, an exciting company doesn't always make an attractive stock at every price. At $50 per share, I'd be more comfortable initiating a modest position and gradually building exposure as Anthropic makes progress toward profitability. Until then, I think patience is warranted.

#3045. Anthropic lets MCP servers ship skills and run background jobs in Claude

Shopify, GitHub and Supabase are among the first to use the new features in Claude and Claude Code.

Anthropic has opened Skills over MCP in public beta, letting apps that connect to Claude ship playbooks alongside their tools. Tasks, for long background jobs, and Elicitation, which pauses for user input, are now generally available, with File Uploads coming soon.

Apps that plug into Claude through MCP can now also tell it how to use them, Anthropic said on Tuesday. The feature, Skills over MCP, is in public beta in Claude and Claude Code.

MCP is the open standard Anthropic launched two years ago to link AI agents to outside apps and data. Servers built on it already list the tools Claude can use. With skills, they can also ship step-by-step guides and best practices, which Claude loads only when needed.

Shopify uses skills to help Claude design and update online stores, and HubSpot to onboard customers. Skills update with the server, so users have nothing extra to install. More apps are opening up, too: Canva opened its MCP server to all developers on Tuesday.

The beta is on by default for Pro, Max and Ultra plans. Team admins can switch it on, and Enterprise support is coming soon.

Two other features are now generally available. Tasks lets a server run long jobs in the background while Claude keeps working, which ZoomInfo uses for deeper research. Elicitation lets a server pause and ask the user for input.

GitHub, for example, makes users type a repository’s name before an agent deletes it. Supabase confirms costs before creating a paid project. A fourth feature, File Uploads, will soon let Claude send PDFs, spreadsheets and images to servers.

The features are part of MCP, so servers that support them also work in other compatible apps. Anthropic says MCP now sees over 700M SDK downloads a month. In August, OpenAI and four rivals agreed on a standard for packaging skills and MCP servers.

Skills carry risks, too. That same month, researchers found malicious agent skills that stole passwords and keys after about 1.7 million installs.

#3042. Three xAI co-founders launch Epochal to teach AI to predict the future

Their first product lets AI agents browse a trillion-page archive of the web, frozen at any moment since the 1990s.

Guodong Zhang, Zihang Dai and Manuel Kroiss, three of xAI’s co-founders, have launched Epochal, a startup building AI that forecasts events. Zhang has put in $100M of his own money, Bloomberg reported. Its first product, Time Portal, lets agents browse the web as it was at past dates, so they can practise forecasting without seeing the outcome.

Three of xAI’s co-founders have launched Epochal, a startup that wants to teach AI to forecast events. Guodong Zhang, Zihang Dai and Manuel Kroiss announced the company and its first product on Tuesday.

Zhang has put in $100M of his own money, Bloomberg reported. No other investors have been named.

All of xAI’s co-founders have since left the company, as Elon Musk rebuilds it after its merger with SpaceX. Another co-founder, Igor Babuschkin, raised $1.1bn for his own startup, River AI, in August.

Today’s AI models learn from an internet where they can already see how things turned out, Epochal says. People, by contrast, have to make choices before they know the result.

Its first product, Time Portal, lets AI agents browse the web as it looked at any moment over the past 30 years. Epochal says it covers more than 1 trillion pages, down to the minute on busy sites. A matching Linux sandbox sets its clock, software and downloads to the same date, so agents cannot spot the trick.

To test it, Epochal ran forecasting agents on 347 live questions from prediction markets Kalshi and Polymarket. Weeks later, it replayed the same questions through Time Portal. In its own test, the replayed forecasts closely matched the originals, with a correlation of 0.98.

Developers can try a limited version for free. Epochal has not said how it gathered the archive or whether the pages are licensed.

#3041. AirTag 2 has two big improvements that make it worth the upgrade

AirTag 2 (now only $18, down from $29) launched earlier this year after a five-year wait, and in my experience there are two big improvements that make it worth the upgrade.

Precision Finding is Apple’s best AirTag feature, letting you get step-by-step, highly precise directions to your lost item. But with the original AirTag, you had to be in fairly close proximity before you could benefit from Precision Finding.

With AirTag 2, Apple added a second-generation Ultra Wideband chip that makes Precision Finding now available from up to 1.5x farther away than before. It’s a huge increase that I’ve definitely noticed.

This expansion of Precision Finding to greater distances means the feature is now available a lot more often than with the old AirTag. For this reason alone, I highly recommend AirTag 2.

When you’re trying to find a lost item, Precision Finding isn’t the only tool AirTag offers. There’s also a built-in speaker that can play a sound, triggered by your iPhone, to help you track it down.

With AirTag 2, Apple has made the built-in speaker 50% louder than before. The company says this enables hearing it from up to twice as far away.

I’ve been impressed by how loud the AirTag speaker is able to get now. Between the new speaker and upgraded Precision Finding, Apple has made AirTag 2 better in the ways that users are likely to care about most.

You can buy AirTag 2 for $18 on Amazon (regularly $29) for a limited time.

Have you upgraded to AirTag 2? What’s your experience been like? Let us know in the comments.

#3039. DICK'S: 3 Key Takeaways for Long-Term Investors

The retailer borrowed $1 billion to buy back stock during a dip, a move that concentrates future earnings for remaining holders but leaves the debt load open to question.

By The Motley Fool Team – Nov 24, 2026 at 8:00PM EST

10 stocks we like better than Dick's Sporting Goods ›

On its third-quarter 2026 earnings call, held on Nov. 24, 2026, DICK'S (DKS +14.59%) raised its full-year profit outlook as customer demand for athletic apparel and footwear remained steady. Long-term investors care because the retailer is expanding its high-margin digital offerings while generating reliable cash flow from new experiential store formats. Three things management said on the call stand out.

DICK'S is expanding its Field House locations, which are scaled-down versions of its House of Sport experiential stores, featuring sports facilities alongside retail space. These stores generate high first-year omnichannel sales, which measure total revenue across physical stores and digital platforms, while delivering strong earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation, and amortization (EBITDA) margins.

When stock prices dropped in the third quarter, management issued $1 billion in senior debt to buy back shares at what it viewed as an attractive valuation. This aggressive buyback reduces the total share count and concentrates future earnings growth for remaining shareholders.

GameChanger, the company's youth sports mobile application that offers livestreaming and team management software, is expanding from baseball and softball into basketball. The digital platform provides recurring subscription revenue that carries significantly higher profit margins than physical stores.

Footwear sales are outperforming overall store growth, and management isn't hiding its satisfaction about customer response to new product launches. The company retains structural advantages through its deep brand partnerships, expanding digital media network, and dominance in youth sports data. Management is watching inventory levels across the athletic footwear market while maintaining pricing discipline.

Integration work continues at Foot Locker, where management is closing underperforming stores to build a healthier store fleet over time. Long-term market share expansion remains the central focus as new store formats mature.

#3038. London startup Sequent raises $2.2M to mathematically prove code safe

Backers include Metaplanet, the firm of Skype co-founder Jaan Tallinn, who led Anthropic's 2021 Series A.

Sequent co-founders Ramana Kumar (left) and Charles Cooper at the Alan Turing memorial, after whom the company’s product Alan is named.

Sequent, a London startup that uses mathematical proof to show software obeys its safety rules, has raised $2.2M in pre-seed funding. Frachtis co-led the round with Metaplanet, the investment firm of Skype co-founder Jaan Tallinn, the man who led Anthropic’s 2021 Series A.

Its product, Alan, goes after what testing cannot do. A test checks the cases someone thought to try, while a formal proof shows the code follows its rules in every case. Writing proofs by hand takes specialists months or years, which has kept the method locked up in fields like aircraft controls.

AI has changed that maths, as the models suit the repetitive grind that proofs demand. With Alan, engineers state their safety rules in plain language, such as no user being able to withdraw more than their balance.

The AI then hunts for the proofs, and a separate checker called HOL4, which uses no AI, confirms every step or throws the proof out.

The company was born from a costly mistake: the CEO, Charles Cooper, who leads Vyper, one of the two main programming languages on Ethereum, in 2021 he accidentally introduced a flaw into its compiler. In July 2023, attackers used that bug to drain more than $60mn from older pools at the exchange Curve and other projects.

After the attack, Ramana Kumar, a former Google DeepMind safety researcher, offered to help prove the compiler correct. He had formed, having co-created CakeML, a compiler proved correct down to the instructions a computer runs, and the work grew into Sequent, where he is now CTO.

Curve has become the first paying customer. For one type of its pools, Alan has proved that no user can take more than a set limit from depositors, whatever they do and in whatever order.

Whenever the pool’s code changes, “we can prove depositors’ money stays protected by the same limit,” Curve CEO Michael Egorov said in a statement.

Cooper argues the lesson reaches well beyond crypto. Banks and governments have long leaned on keeping their old code private, he says. AI-powered attacks are eroding that shield, while cheap proofs hand the advantage back to defenders.

Crucially, AI never gets the final word. At DeepMind, Kumar studied how AI finds shortcuts that satisfy a rule’s letter while missing its point. So engineers sign off on every rule themselves, and each proof must pass HOL4, whose core is small enough for experts to inspect line by line.

Alan works on Vyper smart contracts today, with Solidity and Solana support in development and Rust, C, TypeScript, and Python on the roadmap. Early access starts at $99 a month, and the founders’ next target is the Vyper compiler itself, the place where the original flaw lived.

#3034. Dollar Tree: 3 Key Takeaways for Long-Term Investors

Customer store visits accelerated to 3.8% in the quarter, a turnaround that matters more for a long-term holder than any single margin lever.

By The Motley Fool Team – Nov 24, 2026 at 8:12PM EST

10 stocks we like better than Dollar Tree ›

On its third-quarter fiscal 2026 earnings call, held on Nov. 24, 2026, Dollar Tree (DLTR +11.18%) reported net sales of $5.1 billion. The discount retailer is attracting higher-income shoppers while expanding its multiprice assortment, which sells goods above traditional $1 to $2 price points to boost overall transaction values. Three key takeaways from management's comments highlight the company's long-term trajectory.

Dollar Tree expanded multiprice items, which are products priced above its traditional $1 to $2 baseline, to 18% of total sales. Shoppers who combine opening price items with higher-priced merchandise generate larger receipts and boost overall store productivity.

Customer store visits grew 3.8% in the third quarter, accelerating from 0.4% in the second quarter. Value-conscious consumers are visiting stores more frequently as inflation presses household budgets, while broader merchandise offerings encourage single-trip shopping.

Rising diesel fuel and transportation costs present ongoing headwinds, with every $1 change in diesel fuel prices impacting annual domestic shipping costs by about $40 million. Management relies on operational remedies before considering store price increases.

Customer traffic is accelerating across every income bracket, and management isn't hiding its satisfaction with store execution. The business relies on a dense network of 9,500 stores and tight inventory control to support free cash flow, which represents cash left over after operating expenses and capital spending. Leadership is watching elevated diesel fuel surcharges and ocean freight volatility heading into fiscal 2027.

The leadership team remains focused on executing its multiyear growth initiatives while maintaining pricing discipline across store categories.

#3031. 1 Reason I Haven’t Bought Oklo Stock -- and Probably Never Will

By Ryan Vanzo – Nov 24, 2026 at 9:00PM EST

Oklo (OKLO -7.56%) is in trouble. Or at least its shareholders are. This year, shares of the nuclear energy stock have fallen 73%.

Last year, Oklo peaked with a market cap of nearly $30 billion. Today, that valuation has fallen to less than $4 billion.

The company is still set to benefit from AI's rising need for more energy. And most experts believe adoption of small modular reactors (SMRs) -- which Oklo develops -- is set to rise over the coming decades.

But there's one major reason I'm not buying Oklo stock at its current discounted valuation. In fact, I might not invest in the company at any price.

Oklo has several notable SMR projects in its pipeline. But SMR adoption isn't expected to occur en masse until the 2030s. It may be until the 2040s that SMR capacity contributes meaningfully to the global energy landscape.

Oklo may outpace the industry in terms of near-term adoption. But the company isn't even cleared by regulators yet to build an SMR system in the U.S. Even if approval is achieved on an accelerated basis -- as management believes -- it will likely still be years before the company generates meaningful revenue.

Notably, Oklo has a different business model from SMR peers such as NuScale Power (SMR -6.52%). NuScale primarily sells its SMR systems to utility providers, which finance and own the asset. Oklo, however, finances and owns its facilities, resulting in higher capital expenditure intensity and potentially creating a drag on near-term cash flows.

Oklo isn't approaching financial distress. The firm has more than $1.5 billion in cash and cash equivalents on the balance sheet, plus more than $1.5 billion in marketable debt securities. But analysts increasingly believe the company will need more capital to execute on its long-term growth runway. Consensus estimates call for Oklo to burn around $6.3 billion in free cash flow from 2026 through 2030.

With its valuation now below $4 billion, share dilution will become more onerous for Oklo investors. While I may give up some upside potential, I'm sticking to the sidelines until Oklo's cash flow problem stabilizes. Otherwise, the cheaper the stock gets, the harder it becomes for the company to finance its future, offsetting the "cheaper" valuation investors can secure.
