Diluted earnings per share was a record $9.45, up 265%. We generated $4.5 billion of cash flow from operations and returned a record $4.9 billion to shareholders. Our proven operating model, competitive advantages, speed to market and ability to drive scale are all delivering compounding benefits. Our modernization efforts are driving significant operating leverage. Operating expenses were 7% of revenue, the lowest in our company's 42-year history.

ISG, our most profitable business, has grown significantly over the past several years and drives the vast majority of our growth and profit. In fiscal '24, the year we began selling AI servers, ISG generated 38% of our revenue. Over the last 4 quarters, that contribution has increased to 68%. The trend is even more pronounced within operating income, where ISG's contribution has gone from 54% to 83%, and I expect the trend to continue into our next fiscal year. Over the same period of time, ISG's operating income rate expanded 2 points.

We achieved that expansion despite the tremendous growth in AI servers, supported by strong growth in Dell IP storage, the insatiable demand for compute and the efficiencies generated by our modernization efforts. Technology is driving material business outcomes and the demand for AI infrastructure and data center modernization remains strong. As AI infrastructure becomes more complex, our competitive advantage strengthen and our momentum accelerates. Our engineering and design capabilities are differentiated. We develop purpose-built bespoke solutions optimized for each customer's specific requirements, often working through many design iterations that contemplate not just the infrastructure, but the data center as a whole, designed for power, cooling, efficiency and software.

Our technical teams are leveraging AI and the proprietary knowledge we've built over the last 13 quarters to streamline and accelerate the design work, allowing our engineers to deliver complex designs in hours and quickly work through a large number of iterations. Our procurement capabilities and world-class supply chain are differentiated, especially in today's constrained supply environment. In manufacturing, we fully test the complete solution at L11 and beyond, including full rack power up, thermal compliance and scale-out and scale-up network validation before anything ships. Our deployment services team can stand up a rack within 6 hours of delivery. Our on-site support services help customers achieve 99-plus percent utilization with fewer spares than our competitors.

Together, these capabilities get infrastructure live faster. On large deployments, we can deliver time to first token 4 to 6 weeks faster than competitors while providing industry-leading total cost of ownership. That allows customers to convert backlog into revenue sooner and more reliably. And of course, innovation remains central to our advantage. In Q3, we were the first OEM to ship a fully liquid cooled networking rack, extending our first-to-market leadership. We are now the only OEM shipping DLC 100% scalable units across compute, accelerators and networking with a standard L11 rack design, and we will be shipping storage liquid-cooled L11 racks in the near future.

The proof point is in our order momentum, $180 billion over the past 4 quarters, with a majority of our new orders based on NVIDIA's Vera Rubin NVL72. We also led the industry with the launch of our AMD-based PowerEdge R9815 and R9825 platforms, delivering 238 world records in industry benchmarks in the R9825 alone. At the same time, AI technology continues to advance rapidly. Models have progressed from one-shot responses to reasoning to recursive capabilities and now agentic systems that act, manage and orchestrate workloads. As customer zero, we are moving from using AI as a tool and an adviser to using AI as an operator.

The first wave of AI answered questions and delivering productivity improvements of 10% to 40%. In the use cases, we are seeing agents drive productivity improvements an order of magnitude better, 10x or more by accelerating work and putting intelligence directly in front of decision-makers. Realizing those outcomes starts with strong leadership. Companies must simplify, standardize, automate processes before digitizing them or augmenting them with intelligence. They must also modernize their data architectures, including semantic data layers that provide context around their data and intellectual property. Agents generate significant token demand, increasing the need for modern, disaggregated infrastructure across AI and traditional servers, Dell IP storage, data management solutions and networking.

While enterprise traction is accelerating, the vast majority of customers remain in proof-of-concept and tool adoption phase. The broader agentic adoption opportunity is still ahead of us. Overall, AI and the quest for intelligence is expanding our TAM across our portfolio. This is no longer simply about IT budgets. Data centers are becoming value centers, driving growth, productivity, speed and intelligence across the enterprise. Now let's start with the results. Starting with ISG. Revenue increased 198% to a record $42 billion. Operating income was $7.1 billion, with an operating income rate of 17%. In AI servers, demand continues to accelerate. In Q3, we booked $60.2 billion in AI orders and recognized a record $22 billion in AI server revenue.

We exited the quarter with a record $132.3 billion of AI server backlog. Behind every customer engagement and every order is a rigorous due diligence process, resulting in a fully vetted backlog. Every AI order is vetted for access to capital, end customer quality, trade and export compliance and access to land and power. As I mentioned, each design is bespoke, optimized through multiple iterations with the customer. Through this tight collaboration, we know our customers well and have a high conviction that our backlog will convert to revenue. Our pipeline grew sequentially and remains multiples of our backlog, again, after converting $180 billion over the past 4 quarters. Additionally, our customer base and opportunity pipeline continues to diversify.

We now have over 7,500 Dell AI Factory customers. Our customer base spans neoclouds, sovereigns and enterprises. Within the neocloud segment, we remain highly selective about the partners we work with and the end customers supporting their demand. The global opportunity is expanding as more data centers are built outside of the United States. Across nearly every top country around the world, there are 2 to 3 sovereign projects. Enterprises were the fastest-growing portion of our opportunity pipeline expansion sequentially, providing further evidence that enterprise AI adoption is gaining traction. Internally, we continue to invest in our capabilities, ensuring we maintain our competitive advantage, deliver value for our customers and position for the substantial opportunity ahead. Moving to traditional servers.

Revenue was up 235% as demand remained exceptionally strong, supported by multiple growth drivers that are expanding our TAM. Enterprises increasingly recognize that compute is critical to both the growth and the operations of their business. They are buying more compute to accommodate growing workloads, refreshing their installed base and modernizing their data centers to free up power and space to be positioned for the AI era. Sequentially, we are seeing increased demand for CPU-based compute to support AI and inference workloads. Higher content continues to be a long-term secular tailwind. Servers contain more compute value with higher core counts, greater memory and storage capacity, increasing the value of each system.

Underneath all of this, cyber resilience and security are also driving refresh activity. Much of the installed base requires new hardware to meet current security and performance requirements. These needs cannot always be addressed through a software patch. We are executing very well in a supply-constrained environment, and we expect to gain share this quarter. Turning to storage. Revenue was up 24% as strong demand for our Dell IP portfolio drove revenue growth and improved profitability. Storage has always been critical as enterprise workloads and data grow. In the AI era, it is becoming even more important as data grows at exponential rates. Our storage opportunities are also expanding as AI evolves.

AI workloads are creating new demand drivers like key value caching, context layers and agents that need to store data, memory and state. For an enterprise, its data is its intellectual property, but siloed and without context, it's just data. Agents need that context, and that's why we've expanded the Dell AI Data Platform with a unified semantic layer and an enterprise knowledge graph. Together, they give nearly every application and agent the same trusted current view of the business without rebuilding context from scratch every query. This lowers token consumption, cuts compute costs and speeds time to production, all while keeping the customers' most sensitive data governed inside their own data center. Our storage offerings continue to expand.

Our Dell IP portfolio is resonating with customers, and we expect to gain share this quarter. Demand for Dell IP storage grew for the seventh consecutive quarter, and our Dell IP mix is at an all-time high. Demand remained broad-based with exceptional strength in North America. We also continue to see strong demand for unstructured storage, supporting AI workloads with triple-digit demand growth for the third consecutive quarter. PowerStore delivered a record demand and has now grown double digit or better for 10 consecutive quarters. PowerFlex grew double digits for 3 consecutive quarters and data protection delivered double-digit growth.

Storage growth, greater scale, the mix shift to Dell IP and meaningful sequential improvements in profitability at the solution level continue to be significant drivers for ISG profitability. Our Dell IP performance and accelerating pace of product development give us confidence in the opportunity ahead. Turning to CSG. Revenue grew 3% in a softer PC unit market as the industry adjusts to higher price points. Customers are prioritizing their budgets near term to servers and storage, electing to defer some PC-related refresh. The installed base continues to age, building deferred demand that we expect to refresh in the future. In closing, we continue to deliver a record year with record revenue, EPS, cash generation and capital return to shareholders.

The demand environment we see today remains strong and has not changed. Sophisticated customers are planning years in advance, giving us better visibility into future demand. AI server demand continues to accelerate, supported by a broadening customer base and expanding global opportunity. Our record $132.3 billion of AI server backlog has been fully vetted through our rigorous due diligence process. Traditional server demand remains strong, benefiting from traditional workload growth and aging installed base, heightened security requirements and the growing AI inference demand. Dell IP storage continues to grow and drive incremental profitability. As AI infrastructure becomes more complex, our competitive advantages are more pronounced and our TAM expands, increasing the need for modern disaggregated architecture.

Infrastructure demand continues to outpace supply. As we look into next year, the gap between component supply and end-user demand continues to widen. Our world-class supply chain is well positioned to navigate these constraints and deliver for our customers. Our operating model, speed to market growth and ability to drive scale are producing compounding benefits across the business. Together, these drive significant cash flow, shareholder return and long-term value for our shareholders. I'm proud of the team's performance and expect the momentum to carry into next year. With that, let me turn it over to David to walk through the financials and our outlook.

David Kennedy: Thanks, Jeff. The team executed exceptionally well, driving record revenue, record EPS and record shareholder returns. These results demonstrate the strength of our operating model, which is driving growth, expanding profitability and generating significant cash flow. Total revenue was up 103% to $54.9 billion. Gross margin dollars grew 105% to $11.7 billion. Gross margin rate was 21.2%, up 10 basis points. Operating expenses were up 20% to $3.8 billion, primarily due to variable compensation tied to our outperformance. We continue to drive significant operating leverage with OpEx down 480 basis points to 7% of revenue. Operating income grew 213% to $7.8 billion.

Operating income rate increased 490 basis points to 14.2% of revenue, driven primarily by scale and pricing discipline despite the impact of record AI mix. Net income was up 245% to $6.1 billion, primarily driven by strong operating income. Diluted EPS increased 265% to a record $9.45. Moving to ISG. ISG delivered record revenue of $42 billion, up 198%, marking the 11th consecutive quarter of double-digit or better revenue growth. AI server momentum continued to accelerate with $60.2 billion in orders, our second quarter with orders above $60 billion, a record $22 billion in revenue and $132.3 billion in ending backlog, all of which has been subject to our rigorous review process.

To expand on Jeff's comments, every customer goes through a credit oversight and due diligence process supported by DFS' risk management team. We evaluate the company, its financial capacity and its underlying end-user contracts. We run the due diligence process at 2 key points: when we agreed the purchase order and again before production begins, helping us actively manage risk. When we use DFS financing, it is selective and short term, bridging the customer from purchase order to cluster go-live. Traditional server and networking revenue was a record $15 billion, up 235%. Storage revenue was $4.9 billion, up 24%, with strong demand across our Dell IP portfolio, driving revenue growth and significant margin contribution.

Our margin-rich Dell IP storage demand has grown for 7 consecutive quarters, and our Dell IP mix is at a record high. ISG's Q3 operating income surpassed what we delivered in FY '26 and was a record $7.1 billion, up 308%, marking the 10th consecutive quarter of double-digit or better growth. Operating margin was 17%, up 460 basis points, primarily driven by scale. Building on last quarter, the benefits of scale continue to improve profitability across the entire portfolio. You're seeing that scale in the decoupling of revenue growth and operating expenses driven by 2 factors: strong demand is supporting record revenue. Additionally, our modernization efforts continue to drive operating expense efficiencies.

We also maintained strong operational and pricing discipline in a dynamic environment, reflecting the team's strong execution and continued focus on supporting our customers. Most of these benefits are structural and are reflected in our higher fourth quarter margin rate expectations. However, rates will sequentially moderate as the benefit from a stronger North America sales mix normalizes. Turning to CSG. CSG revenue was up 3% to $12.9 billion. CSG operating income was $0.7 billion or 5.5% of revenue, roughly in line with expectations. CSG provides important scale to our supply chain and drives significant cash generation given it's our most capital-efficient business. Moving to cash and the balance sheet.

We delivered another strong cash quarter with cash flow from operations of $4.5 billion, driven primarily by sequential revenue growth and higher profitability. We ended the quarter with $16.3 billion in cash and investments, up $2 billion sequentially, and our core leverage ratio is at 0.7x. We returned an all-time record $4.9 billion to shareholders this quarter, reflecting the second consecutive quarter of heightened shareholder return, averaging $4.6 billion against a $1.9 billion run rate last year. We repurchased 9 million shares at an average price of $488 per share and paid a dividend of approximately $0.63 per share.

Additionally, the Board of Directors approved a $25 billion increase in our share repurchase authorization, reflecting our confidence in continued strong free cash flow generation, commitment to shareholder return and long-term value creation. We remain committed to our long-term capital allocation framework, including our commitment to return at least 80% of adjusted free cash flow to shareholders. Turning to guidance. Given the momentum we are seeing in ISG, we're raising our fourth quarter revenue growth and non-GAAP diluted EPS expectations. We expect $56.25 billion revenue at the midpoint, up 69% year-on-year, driven by ISG growth of roughly 120%, with AI server revenue up sequentially to roughly $23.5 billion.

Traditional servers continue to grow triple digits with storage growing in the low teens. Operating expense is expected to remain roughly flat sequentially and just under 7% of revenue. We expect operating income rate to be roughly up 175 basis points with, both ISG and CSG similar year-over-year. We anticipate a diluted share count of roughly 634 million shares and I&O of roughly $450 million. Diluted non-GAAP EPS is expected to be $8.40 at the midpoint, up roughly 115% (sic) [ 116% ]. Our Q4 guidance implies a record FY '27 with record revenue of $202 billion, up nearly 80%.

Full year operating income rate is expected to be up roughly 350 basis points and is well above our expectations entering the year. Importantly, we expect this expansion despite the mix pressure of $78 billion in AI server revenue, more than 3x larger than last year. Non-GAAP diluted EPS is expected to be $29.68, up nearly 190% at the midpoint. And briefly on FY '28, as Jeff mentioned, demand in ISG remains robust and growth will be driven by multiple demand vectors. AI server demand continues to accelerate, and we will be well positioned to capture that growth. Data center modernization will drive growth in both traditional servers and storage.

Traditional workloads and data keep growing, aged installed bases need refreshing and customers are hardening cybersecurity. At the same time, inference and agentic workloads are extending infrastructure demand into traditional servers and storage. Within a supply-constrained environment, we continue to prioritize ISG. While we expect the PC unit environment to remain soft next year, the impact is manageable given the strength of our infrastructure business. While the base is much higher, the EPS levers we outlined at our Investor Day roughly a year ago remain the same. We continue to focus on revenue growth, margin accretion and operating leverage, which together drive significant cash generation and shareholder returns. In closing, we delivered another exceptional quarter with record year-to-date results.

Over the past 3 quarters, revenue was $145.8 billion, up 82%. Diluted EPS grew 231% to $21.32. We generated record cash flow from operations of $10.8 billion and returned an all-time record $11.2 billion to shareholders. The team executed exceptionally well with growth across the business. ISG demand remains robust. And in a supply-constrained environment, we continue to prioritize storage and servers. The modernization work we've been driving for the past several years helped drive operating expenses to 7% of revenue, an all-time low in our 42-year company history, while strengthening our competitive advantages across innovation, go-to-market, services and supply chain. We remain focused on capital efficiency and cash generation.

We're excited about Q4 and remain confident in our ability to create long-term value for our shareholders as we go into next year. Thank you to the team for their execution, and thank you all for your time today. Now I'll turn it back to Paul to begin Q&A.

Paul Frantz: Thanks, David. Let's go to Q&A. [Operator Instructions]

Operator: We'll take our first question from Mark Newman with Bernstein.

Mark Newman: Congrats on great numbers. Besides the strong revenue growth here, you've also got pretty strong operating margin improvement across all the ISG components. As we go forward, how do we think about how the operating margin will change going forward? Because I think you've got -- you've had this ability to benefit from rising costs of memory because you've had some supply constraints with your competitors, perhaps more supply constraints, you've passed on perhaps more than the cost increase. So not only is operating margin increased, but gross margin has also increased on a product-by-product basis. Just going forward, how should we think about that?

And what's embedded in this guidance regarding profitability for the main components of ISG, AI servers, traditional servers and storage?

David Kennedy: Sure, Mark. It's David here. I'll start. You're right. Look, the starting point here is the strong demand and ultimately the revenue growth in the ISG business. It's broad-based. So pick your geography, customer segment, customer vertical. It's as broad as it's ever been. It's obviously anchored with the $22 billion of AI shipments, which is a record and 35% higher than the previous record as we go even higher again in Q4. The traditional server growth, 235%, obviously drives the P&L. And look, ultimately, pleasing to see storage growth back up what we saw in Q2 and deliver 24% growth in Q3.

All that growth means from a rate perspective, the operating leverage that's driving into our P&L is exceptional. Our OpEx as a percentage of revenue within ISG improved 8 points year-on-year and 2 points quarter-on-quarter. So true scale and this idea of decoupling revenue growth from OpEx performance is truly on show and it validates our own modernization journey that we're doing within the company. And ultimately, that's sticky, that's structural and will endure as we kind of go forward from a P&L perspective. That OpEx obviously allows us then to absorb as we -- you see AI server grow almost 3x year-on-year. We're able to absorb that into the rate.

You saw ISG op inc up almost 5 points year-on-year to 17% of revenue. And ultimately, as we look into Q4, you're seeing more of the same. We've added revenue dollars. We've added margin dollars. We've added rate. So we've taken up the guide across the board in relation to that. And ultimately, that's what we'll look to do, continue to drive and see revenue growth totally decoupled from that, the OpEx performance. We'll continue to find scale, and we're committed to continued significant scale into the P&L, and it really sets us up well to drive growth going forward.

Operator: And we'll move to our next question from Amit Jawaharlaz Daryanani with Evercore.

Amit Jawaharlaz Daryanani: Jeff, you spoke about in your prepared comments about the gap between supply and demand continues to widen in reflection of what's going to happen next year, I think. And that's in a big stark contrast, I think, to what investors are worried about that AI spending might be approaching a peak fairly soon. Can you just unpack what do you think is driving the gap from your perspective in that supply-demand dynamic?

And then when I think about you folks getting to a Q4 revenue run rate of about $56 billion, without asking you for a formal fiscal '28 guide, can you just talk about which businesses or segments that you see have visibility to grow from this exit rate as you go into fiscal '28?

Jeffrey (Jeff) W. Clarke: Sure, Amit. I mean, look, as we have moved through the year, I think we've been consistently saying this demand is durable. The appetite or the demand for intelligence broadly continues. We've seen no slowdown of that. I think our AI orders of another $60 billion quarter. We now have $180 billion of orders in the last 4 quarters. We've shipped nearly $66 billion. All the while, the 5-quarter pipeline continues to build. We've added 4,500 Dell AI factory customers in the last 3 quarters. It was 3,000 in the first 8 quarters. It continues to grow. There are more customers in our 5-quarter pipeline than we have served to date.

All signs are pointing to the continued demand appetite for intelligence, particularly as we've moved from a training, which has driven the market initially to now inference making our way and progressing to agentic and ultimately to recursive learning. We see the pattern continuing. And in fact, we would say for the first 3 years of -- November '22 through October of '25, it was essentially a market driven by single shot sort of AI, you ask it a question, you get an answer. Now we're seeing that change where AI is becoming the doer or the operator. And we're seeing that same benefit inside of our own company.

David spoke to our record low operating expenditures and our modernization activities, all driven by the fact that we are seeing tremendous efficiency in our organization driven by now agentic. And we fundamentally look at this, you get asked why that's the case. It's real simple. Work is really 3 components. There's a component of work that you define what it is, you actually do it and you verify it. The action, the operating of the work is being increasingly moved towards agentic. And that is driving, we believe, an incredible growth rate in tokens and token consumption, the infrastructure that goes along with it, and we don't see that slowing down.

So when I look at the growth categories in our business and whether that's in our storage business, whether that's in our traditional server business and certainly on the AI side, it's inference, it's agentic. We're seeing KV cache need. We're seeing recursive learning need. We're seeing the agentic inference need, the resulting harnesses to operate this. And our forecast remain, I think, unchanged from the last time we talked about this topic. We still see tremendous token growth through the end of the decade. 87x, I think, was the last number I talked about, 3,600 quadrillion tokens. Training demand continues to grow 5x.

We're still tracking over 200 gigawatts of build-out of shells and power to provide the homes for all of this compute capability that is being needed. So again, no slowdown. I look at our own use inside our company. Our token growth is greater today than it was when the fiscal year began. Our use of agents, any given day, there are 100,000 agents spun up across our organization by our developers and knowledge workers consuming tokens. We have enterprise-wide agents driving a significant token use inside our company, driving again the efficiencies we talked about. And then we're going to double that number in the next 90 days.

So I think we as a kind of customer zero see this. The customers that we work with across neoclouds, across our sovereign and enterprise space continue to reinforce it. And we think the demand is very durable as reflected in our order rate and our backlog.

David Kennedy: And I think, Amit, I mean to build on that, and Jeff has set the table in terms of the robustness of the demand that we see, I think the linkage point tied to next year that you referenced. But if you think through our long-term value creation framework, and the tools of our toolbox in relation to EPS generation continue to be there, continue to be strong. So number one, growth that drives everything, with profitable growth back to the leverage of the OpEx and then ultimately generating free cash flow that we can return to our shareholders.

All of those give us a very agile list of tools in our toolbox that we can work with as we continue to observe the appetite for the intelligence in the ecosystem.

Jeffrey (Jeff) W. Clarke: Yes. And maybe to wrap the bow and since you asked this portion of it, Amit, is -- and that demand is ahead of supply. In fact, we think the demand is further ahead of supply in calendar '27 than it's been in '26.

Jeffrey (Jeff) W. Clarke: Yes. And then obviously, I think I mentioned in the prepared remarks, the notion of security and resiliency requirements driving demand. And we're seeing this broadly across the neoclouds and enterprises, I think financial services, the EDAs and semi companies, HFTs, pharma, to name a few that are very advanced in their AI deployments. This is a 4-quarter trend. It is by far the fastest-growing part of our traditional server business. It initially started as inference. It's now agentic AI. It continues to be a TAM expansion of the traditional server marketplace.

And in your modeling, I suspect we'll get to this, but to help everybody, the ASPs of agentic servers and inference servers are roughly twice the ASP of a traditional server. So we see significant growth. That demand continues to be out there. Getting supply, obviously, is key to fulfill it. And we're excited about the prospects of our traditional server business continuing to grow.

David Kennedy: Yes. I guess to build on it in relation to the credit and capital element of that discussion. Again, like Jeff said, it's not a new process. We've had this rigorous process in place, and we've been very consistent, I think, in the last 3, 4 cycles here in relation to that, whether it's the credit assessment, the financing options where required, think of the investment-grade contract of the end user. Given the inflationary environment that we're operating in now, we don't think that's the correct way to measure the true value of what is happening in the server marketplace. There has been significant unit TAM destruction with the inflation that has been in the marketplace. If you take what has traditionally been 20% of the units, which have been 1P towers and 1P racks, that would have been 20-ish percent of the units, 2% of the revenue. That market under $3,000 servers is gone. So industry-wise, there are fewer units.

But what's interesting and I think very telling is the content of every server that we sold and shipped in the quarter was significantly different. Let me explain a little bit. So as we think about value and you think about these ratios that I mentioned earlier where an 18G server can consolidate 12 to 14 of our old 14G servers, that's built on a premise they're more capable. That capability is built on more cores, more DRAM and more NAND. We shipped and sold more cores in Q3 than we did the previous quarter and year-over-year.

We shipped more cores and more -- or excuse me, more bits of DRAM per server than we did last quarter and last year. And we shipped more bytes of storage in the servers we shipped this quarter than we did last quarter and last year. So the content per server is going up significantly, not inflation adjusted, absolute content, more cores, more bits, more DRAM per server, more productive, more powerful servers capable of being deployed, albeit in fewer units, taking on significantly greater workloads. That's what we're seeing in the marketplace. That has been, I think, consistent trend now for several quarters, and I think that will continue going forward.

On the storage side, a very -- it's a different trend, but a similar outcome. What we're seeing is greater attach of our higher-value storage products, our Dell IP portfolio. The Dell IP portfolio, we ran across a bunch of numbers, but 7 consecutive quarters of growth now. I think PowerStore has grown 10 consecutive quarters of double-digit growth. The unstructured products continue to grow quite nicely. The demand of them was in triple-digit range.

We are seeing more attach of storage in our AI business, particularly around the unstructured products, our PowerScale and ObjectScale product that continues to bode well as we go in the future because the demand drivers for storage in the future around the very same things that I described in servers, the agentic workload, agentic AI, KV cache, multimodal workflows and recursive learning all drive incremental storage. And in fact, incredible amounts of storage as you have to start looking at the traces and logs of every agent. If you start looking at the artifacts the agents create. If you look at some of the retrievable corpora that the agents create.

That is all driving significant storage growth and storage opportunities in the future. Again, it can go on with KV cache, the multimodal workflows when you start going into imaging, you start going to video, audio, sensor drives more bytes of storage that has to be ultimately stored. And ultimately, you're going to see that storage grows and grows and grows not by GPUs that are deployed, but by the bytes that have to be retained and that compound storage over time. Those are the growth drivers. That's where we're seeing the opportunities and where the focus of our business is.

Operator: And we'll move to our next question from Erik William Richard Woodring with Morgan Stanley.

Erik William Richard Woodring: So just on the ISG operating margin, really strong 17% this quarter, obviously, up sequentially and year-over-year despite AI servers being very strong. Can you just help us understand the bridge as we look to the fiscal 4Q ISG operating margin, just understanding how triple-digit traditional server growth and strength in AI servers in 4Q kind of contribute to that step down in ISG operating margins? Just trying to understand what might be changing there and what that might mean preliminarily for fiscal year '28, please?

David Kennedy: Yes, sure, Erik. Yes, like I said earlier, if you look at our Q4 guide, we're adding more revenue, more margin dollars, more operating margin rate into the guide versus 90 days ago and again versus 180 days ago. So you're seeing this consistent improvement in our performance in relation to the scale benefit we touched on earlier as we move forward. One element, obviously, you mentioned AI server. We continue to raise the bar there. So you see $23.5 billion into the Q4 guide. That's running its way through.

And then look, as we touched on earlier, as we look through the Q3 performance in that 235% growth from traditional server, a nice kind of tailwind mix of North America business in there in terms of the operational execution. We've modeled here that will normalize its way back in. But ultimately, obviously, our ISG operating margins here for Q4 are above the high end of our range. So very strong performance and a good indication of the strength in the P&L.

Jeffrey (Jeff) W. Clarke: Yes, Erik, I would step back maybe and look at it from an annual basis. If you look at the guidance that we rolled out at the beginning of the year and with the guidance that we just summarized for the year and for Q4, we will have added nearly $58 billion of ISG revenue, $28 billion of that in AI servers and $30 billion of that in core servers or traditional servers, networking and storage. And in doing so, our operating income has expanded a little over 400 basis points. So the macro theme as we've grown significantly in AI, the core business continues to grow, and you're seeing that expansion.

And I think with the prospects of the demand durability, the demand outlook that we see going forward and the leverage of our operating decisions that we're making with modernization, we can continue to see performance in that range.

Operator: And we'll move to our next question from Joseph Cardoso with JPMorgan.

Joseph Cardoso: Maybe just switching gears here. In your prepared remarks, you mentioned new orders are now coming in and largely on Vera Rubin. Just curious if you can just talk to how we should be thinking about Rubin rack pricing, services attached and margin opportunity compared with Blackwell for Dell? And then I also believe in your prepared remarks, you talked about liquid cooled networking and storage. As that gets added at the rack level, how material can that be for Dell? And also how does that influence margins for the company?

Jeffrey (Jeff) W. Clarke: Well, at a macro level, we're still operating the business in the mid-single digits. We continue to see the growth that we described, the $60 billion of order in the quarter, the $180 billion over the past 4 quarters and a growing backlog and 5-quarter pipeline. We have priced Vera Rubin with the expected delivery date with all of our customers when their availability of buildings and power, et cetera, are lined up. The opportunity to attach networking and storage, I think we've been consistent on is an opportunity for margin improvement across our businesses. We continue to focus on that. We continue to see nice attach rates. We still have work to do.

I look at our -- if Arthur Lewis was in here from our ISG business, we would talk about how do we grow our storage business inside all of these accounts. That's what we continue to focus on. I just made reference about all of the new storage opportunities that exist around AI and agentic AI. That's where our focus is with our storage solutions at an individual software-defined storage layer at an appliance layer and at a rack level for all of these large deployments.

Again, a lot of agentic AI is going to be done in the enterprise, where we have a large footprint today, where we have significant coverage today and where our teams are focused on delivering the right products for enterprise scale as well as driving the rack scale products for the largest clusters and neoclouds in the world.

Operator: And we'll move to our next question from David Vogt with UBS.

David Vogt: Maybe, Jeff, big picture thematically, can you kind of share your perspective on the server market, particularly if we start to see some deflation or maybe steady pricing for DRAM and NAND? And what that means from a customer demand perspective, pricing? Presumably, there are customers on the sideline given the rapid increase in pricing that we've seen across the CPU server market. But would love to kind of get your perspective in terms of where you think pricing goes, demand? I know it's a difficult question, but also sort of configurations and maybe specifications in an environment that's maybe not as inflationary from a component perspective.

Jeffrey (Jeff) W. Clarke: Well, I'll start with not as inflationary is still a cost increase to our customers in the form of price. And given the significant inflation that's occurred over the past year, even a moderating inflationary number still leads to higher-priced products for our customers. From a macro view, when we look at the supply picture and our supply outlook, there's nothing that suggests that we're going to see price declines in enterprise NAND and DRAM for servers. The demand for those categories of memory continues to be way ahead of the supply. As more DRAM wafer capacity is set forth for GPUs and specifically building HBM, it comes at the expense of all other types of memory.

We think that crunch continues clearly into '27. And while the rate of inflation won't be the same as we saw in '26, we still believe the market is inflationary. Customers are spending their budgets today. We don't -- I don't know of a customer that's on the sideline that doesn't buy as much as they used to, but I'd also tell you that server they're buying today, if it's a 17G or an 18G server from us, is significantly more capable than the thing that it's replacing. So if you were to take a 14G that we sold 5 years ago, 4 years ago, and it's being retired, that product was $7,500, give or take.

While today's 18G product will be more expensive than that, it replaces 12 to 14 of them. The consolidation rate is significant and customers are benefiting from that. And while they're tying all of the questions together, while that may mean fewer units, it's a more capable machine, and that is what's being deployed in small businesses to the largest corporations in the world to meet their needs. But customers aren't on the sideline in servers. It would be different if we were talking about PCs. I think companies are deferring their PC purchases to ensure they have the infrastructure to work in what is going to be a very disruptive era with agentic technology really reinventing companies.

And that's what we see happening in the marketplace. So do I think the rate of increase slows? Yes. Do I still think that a significant price implication to our customers? Yes, because a smaller percentage on a large number is still a lot of dollars. Customers are spending their budgets. We see them active in the marketplace, and we believe that will continue into '27.

David Kennedy: And I think, Jeff, to build on that, I think the customers are trying to be resourceful and agile there, too, in terms of our DFS offering. So for investment-grade customers, the originations growth we've seen in PCs, storage and servers, up 55% in Q3. So you can see there's an appetite and the need to get infrastructure built out. So even in a budget crunch in the near term, the ability to turn CapEx into OpEx and understand what that looks like is a differentiated capability that we have in the marketplace. And I think our customers have appreciated the flexibility and being able to take advantage of that as part of their IT build-out.

Operator: We'll now take our final question from Tim Long with Barclays.

Timothy (Tim) Long: I wanted to go back to the traditional server, some of the comments you made about a little bit more CPU type of servers to neoclouds and probably to sovereigns as well. Curious if you could just somehow quantify the pace or how that's looking, how margins look for those type of products? And then when you're selling these customers CPU servers compared to GPU servers, is the attach rate different? So maybe if you could just scale kind of how big and strong that business is and what it means for some of the other dynamics that we look at across the business?

Jeffrey (Jeff) W. Clarke: Sure. Let me try. A traditional server sold into a non-GPU application, and we separate the business, there's a GPU, that's the AI server business. There's the traditional server basis non-GPU based, which I tried to talk about earlier. The fastest-growing component of that is inference-driven and agentic AI-driven. It's not the largest portion of our traditional server business, which is our traditional enterprises and traditional applications, the things that we've talked about before. When I think about these servers going into these new workloads, it is across neoclouds who are deploying them that's in the financial services market.

It's in the EDA market, it's in the semis market, high-frequency traders, pharma, et cetera, they're very advanced in their AI deployments. They are driving agentic AI across their enterprises. And we believe that market continues to grow as the next iteration or evolution of agentic takes place, which is recursive learning. All of that drives more compute. More agents, more compute. The harness is essential to this. And the harness and the work that the harness does is really a CPU task. It's these things about how you manage containers, how do you manage sandboxes, manage I/O, how do you orchestrate that workload, which is CPU-driven is what we're talking about here.

And I referenced earlier, those types of servers are roughly twice the ASP as an enterprise-class server running an enterprise workload. The margins in those classes of devices as all of our -- across our server portfolio is well within our product-by-product internal marks that we make for our server products, and we feel very comfortable about that business and the prospects of growth are significant.

Paul Frantz: All right. And Jeff, please close it out.

Jeffrey (Jeff) W. Clarke: Sure. Thanks, Paul, and thanks, everyone, for joining us today. Demand continues to exceed supply, and our world-class supply chain positions us well to capitalize on the opportunity. We are looking forward to Q4 and capping off a record year. Our full year revenue guidance of $202 billion and non-GAAP diluted EPS of $29.68, nearly up 190%. We head into FY '28 with strong momentum and confidence in our ability to continue creating long-term value for shareholders. Thanks again for your time today. Happy Thanksgiving to everyone.

Operator: This concludes today's conference call. We appreciate your participation. You may disconnect at this time.

#3002. I Put Xiaomi’s 18 Pro Max Camera to the Test and I Love the Results

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

Xiaomi's bonkers dual-screen phone is here and I've tested its camera.

Editor at Large; Lead Photographer, Europe

Editor at Large; Lead Photographer, Europe

Xiaomi has taken the wraps off its latest 18 Pro Max Android phone in Paris. I’ve had the phone for the past few weeks and have been putting the camera to the test in my beautiful home of Edinburgh, Scotland, as well as on the beautiful (and rainy) streets of Paris. You can check out my review of the phone if you’re keen to hear more about that wild rear screen on the back, but here I wanted to share some of my favorite photos I’ve taken with the phone so far.

The images seen here are taken with the phone’s various built-in camera modes, largely the black and white mode, as I love the dramatic, filmic look it produces. They’re presented either as-shot or with minimal adjustments using the phone’s built-in editing tools.

Taken using one of the phone’s built-in color styles, I love the vibrancy in this shot. The reds really pop, while the wider angle of the main camera emphasizes the tunnel effect of the alleyway, drawing the eye to the person and their dog.

I may be spoiling the rest of the images here by saying that this is my absolute favorite shot I’ve taken, but there we go. I took this using one of the dedicated black-and-white modes, and I think the tones here are perfect. Excellent dynamic range and contrast, and just the right amount of film grain. I positioned the figure between the buildings and had the phone almost on the floor to turn the rain-soaked tiles into a reflective surface to add some drama to this scene. I then applied a wide cinematic crop in post to give it that extra edge. Lovely stuff.

Most of my favorite photos with the phone were taken using the black-and-white mode. It’s no surprise; I shoot in black and white very often on my Leica Q3 43, and I used the monochrome mode for my favorite shots with Xiaomi’s Leitzphone earlier in the year.

The phone captures excellent black-and-white photos at night, too.

And by exposing for the bright highlights in this scene, I was able to create this stark, moody image of my handsome orange cat, Toulouse. Is he the best cat you’ve ever seen? Of course he is.

Back in color, this UFO that had presumably crash-landed in this Parisian market looks great in this filmic color mode. The oranges and reds pop against the other tones in this scene.

While this quick street portrait is similarly punchy.

I used manual mode here, taking full control over the white balance and exposure settings to achieve the tones I wanted. It’s a great-looking shot with excellent dynamic range. Xiaomi’s phone doesn’t appear to go too hard with its software processing either, meaning that even fine details look quite natural. Other Android phone-makers could take note.

As with the photo of Toulouse the cat, I exposed for the highlights here, forcing the rest of the scene under this bridge into shadow. As a result, it looks moody and dramatic but crucially it also looks exactly as I hoped it would. Many phones would try to artificially lift the shadows here, which would ruin the vibe I was going for.

I took this with the phone’s telephoto zoom lens, aiming to focus more on the digger as the subject and use the water for reflection. I love how this shot looks, especially in black and white, as the cloud detail behind it is especially noticeable.

While here I used the full wide angle of the main camera in order to create a lot of negative space around the figures, emphasizing the size of the building around them.

That building was Le Grande Arche in Paris and despite it being a miserably cold, wet and cloudy day I think the phone has captured a satisfyingly stark scene here.

I don’t like flying, so I distracted myself on the flight out to Paris by taking photos of things with the Xiaomi 18 Pro Max, including this man having a look out of the window.

And this shot of my plane’s wing somewhere above the UK. Again, in black and white. When it looks this good, why would I choose anything else?

And while we’re still in black and white, a particularly friendly pigeon. Hi, friend!

And to round us off, this dude in shades looking at a menu.

I’m genuinely really thrilled with so many of the shots I’ve taken with this phone. The black-and-white mode in particular is spectacular, and I’m looking forward to taking more shots with it over the coming weeks and months.

Editors’ note: Andrew Lanxon’s travel costs to attend Xiaomi’s launch event in Paris were covered by Xiaomi. The judgments and opinions of CNET are our own.

#3001. 74% of shoppers trust AI agents for buying advice – but checkout is another story

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Shoppers who use AI agents spend 8% more than the average buyer and purchase 23% more items per order.

Twenty percent of holiday shoppers are using AI agents as their first stop for research and advice, but they are not ready to have agents make purchases, according to the latest Salesforce research.

Also: What to know about early Black Friday sales

Salesforce surveyed more than 2,500 shoppers in the US, UK, Canada, and Australia and found that 74% of shoppers trust recommendations from AI agents. Salesforce research forecasts AI-driven shopping recommendations to drive $75.8 billion in Cyber Week spending, up 13% from 2025.

Also: Want to try ChatGPT Wallet? Read OpenAI’s liability disclaimer

Brands are also being noticed by AI agents, with 30% of shoppers saying they were first introduced to a new brand via AI. And most importantly, 1 in 10 (11%) shoppers would avoid a brand if an AI agent told them to.

Here are some of the key findings from the 2026 holiday shopping research.

Retailers that use AI shopping agents are seeing bigger orders and more loyal customers. The survey found that shoppers who use AI agent referrals are twice as likely to make a purchase. In addition, 39% of shoppers have used AI agents on an e-commerce site, and 80% had a positive experience, while 75% felt more loyal to the brand as a result of the AI agent experience.

Shoppers who use AI agents spend 8% more than the average buyer and purchase 23% more items per order. Brands that use AI agents are seeing seven times faster sales growth than brands without them.

1 in 3 consumers has used an AI agent, including the widely adopted Meta Muse, now used by 12% of all consumers. Grok Bot is also in high demand.

The survey found that 28% of consumers give their agents multiple tasks per day. The most common use of AI agents is price comparisons, product reviews, and brainstorming for gift items. Brand discovery is a major benefit of AI agent use cases.

Agents as advisors are growing, but agents are not buying products yet, with only 19% of personal agent users using logic to check out. Only 9% of consumers allow their personal AI agents to have unrestricted access to their financial details, and 36% have set up a separate credit card for their AI agents.

Also: ZDNET’s favorite tech devices for 2026

The majority of consumers (73%) are not comfortable giving personal AI agents their payment information, and 49% are not interested in agents making purchases on their behalf. Consumers do not want to share their purchase history or personal data that could potentially lead to unwanted charges. Shoppers will abandon an AI agent after 2-3 mistakes. If an AI agent makes a bad recommendation, 1 in 3 consumers will blame the AI.

Retailers must adopt AI shopping agents in order to compete. Retailers must be able to service and respond to shopper agents. The ability to detect intent, buying signals, sources of dissatisfaction, and other consumer-related buying patterns at machine scale (significantly faster and higher volume than human scale) will require retailers to invest in AI agentic engagement capabilities.

Also: 50 AI agents tried to build a thriving Minecraft civilization – it didn’t end well

Today, AI agents advise consumers on their holiday shopping journeys, but in the very near future, they will autonomously make purchasing decisions with little to no involvement from their human counterparts. The future of shopping will be more autonomous, highly personalized, and nearly frictionless. Brands that invest in agentic AI will garner the most loyalty and future business.

#3000. Roku Drains Iconic Fish Tank Screensaver to Reel Viewers Into Roku City

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

Tech > Home Entertainment > Media Streamers

Fans of the Roku Aquatic Life screensaver will need to find a new way to just keep swimming.

Roku users may be getting that sinking feeling, as the platform is retiring its classic animated Aquatic Life screensaver.

The popular animation featuring realistic aquarium life will be replaced by the Roku City screensaver on Dec. 1. Roku City is the platform’s signature purple skyline, featuring rotating digital billboards packed with brand sponsorships and clever pop-culture Easter eggs. (Seattle’s short-spined raccoon, Jimothy, has made an appearance.)

That doesn’t mean all fish-filled options have been flushed. Several third-party Roku wallpaper apps offer a variety of aquarium options to choose from. But if you’re sticking to what Roku itself provides on its streaming boxes, the move away from the aquarium screensaver also means switching to an alternative that’s filled with advertising.

“It seems like this is a way for Roku to convert a popular screensaver into a way to make money, or at least generate more engagement, via the Roku City version,” said CNET Senior Editor Ty Pendlebury, who covers home entertainment options including the Roku streaming boxes.

A Roku representative didn’t respond to a request for comment.

Viewers who miss these specific fish can still watch a YouTube version of Roku’s Aquatic Life screensaver for as long as the company chooses to keep this nearly 3-minute video on the internet.

The Aquatic Life screensaver loss is a drop in the ocean compared to other changes at the streamer this year. Roku was purchased by Fox for $22 billion in June, which puts the streaming platform under the same ownership as Fox’s Tubi and Fox One channels. That deal is expected to close in 2027.

#2998. You can use Google’s Spark AI agent, renamed Tasks, for free now – with limits

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

At least if Tasks disappoints, it won't cost you - unlike OpenAI and Anthropic's subscription-based agents.

Just months after its release, Google is making its Spark agent free and officially renaming its capabilities “Tasks.” You can now toggle to it from the standard Gemini Chat setting. Reports show the rebrand started gradually in mid-October.

Also: Ready for a Siri AI agent? Apple under pressure to upgrade its assistant faster

(Disclosure: Ziff Davis, ZDNET’s parent company, filed an April 2025 lawsuit against OpenAI, alleging it infringed Ziff Davis copyrights in training and operating its AI systems.)

If Tasks sounds familiar, it should: The company already has a product called Google Tasks, which lets you turn emails into a checkable to-do list on the side of your inbox, among other places like Chat and Docs. This is the agentic version, obviously.

Gewirtz, ZDNET’s AI tester-in-residence, wasn’t blown away by then-Spark when he tried it last month, but had reason to believe in its eventual improvement. It’s unclear whether Tasks is meaningfully different from Spark, aside from being out of beta.

Abilities aside, what sets Tasks apart here is cost. Dots and Duet haven’t exactly impressed thus far, so free alternatives don’t have a high bar to reach yet.

Also: I tested OpenAI Dot and Anthropic Duet for weeks

During Gewirtz’s test, when the agent was part of his $20 per month Google AI Pro plan, he used only 20% of the total five hours of usage on “four fairly substantial tests.” Without an AI plan, Gemini’s context window is 32k tokens.

At launch in September, Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg said Muse is “free to use for up to 100M tokens per week,” though Meta’s help center is not so explicit. As with most agentic products, more frequent users may want to buy more access, but more casual users now have two options to compare.

Also: Don’t use Muse? How Meta’s AI agent can still access your private messages

As with other agents, Tasks, which runs on its newest Gemini 4 Hydrogen model, can handle a variety of jobs for you, from grocery shopping to booking appointments and analyzing your heating bill. Agents like these are designed for a chronically overwhelmed society trained by a reliance on tech to seek convenience and productivity in nearly every aspect of life.

The feature is free in the US, Canada, Korea, Japan, Australia, and India. US users can also start tasks by emailing or texting Gemini, and can have the agent call businesses for them (except in Indiana, Louisiana, Minnesota, Montana, and Nebraska).

The change from Spark to Tasks comes just a day after Google retired Gems (which let you tailor Gemini to specific tasks), and converted existing Gems into Skills. The new landing page for Tasks emphasizes personal finance and cost-cutting as a use case, positioning itself alongside personal finance features from Anthropic and OpenAI.

“Put Gemini on the hunt for ways to save. Identify recurring expenses you no longer need, get alerts for your most-desired deals, and more,” the page reads.

Also: Want to try ChatGPT Wallet? Read OpenAI’s liability disclaimer

“You can adjust task settings, disconnect Google and third-party apps, or delete chat history anytime,’ Google’s blog on the release said. Google’s new Memory summary feature for Gemini lets users view and edit the personal info the chatbot has on them.

Workday (WDAY +1.79%) reported third-quarter results highlighted by an acceleration in AI-driven bookings and an upward revision to its full-year profitability and revenue guidance. So, you know, us releasing a new capability does not necessarily mean that customers uniformly turn it on in their systems, you know, the next day. But, you know, what I can tell you, and I mentioned it in my prepared remarks already, that we have an incredibly large customer base ramping quickly. We have now more than 2 million users who are provisioned with Sana self-service agent, which is the marquee experience when it comes to working through Sana AI with Workday. A large number of customers who are in our lighthouse programs who are actually not just adopting the UI change, but changing their HR processes around it.

And so, you know, there is a bit of, you know, progress over time, so that change cycle is landing at all of the organizations out there, including yours. But I can assure you that as time progresses, you know, rate of adoption will increase, and eventually, you will have it too.

John DiFucci: Okay. Well, I look forward to that. Thank you for thank you for the answers.

Aneel Bhusri: I guess just on that question, it is not either/or using you know, using cloud or an OpenAI front end, with Sana. Every customer is gonna default to using Sana if they wanna use something with it. that is fine too. But it is now the default user experience, and it is just a matter of time before every customer takes it on.

John DiFucci: Okay. We look forward to it. Thanks, Aneel.

Operator: Your next question comes from the line of Brad Alan Zelnick with Deutsche Bank. Brad, please go ahead.

Brad Alan Zelnick: Brent. Thanks so much for taking the question. I wanted to ask about the Sana and Claude plug-in I think you introduced it at Rising. And I appreciate it is still in beta. But what feedback have you gotten from early adopters? what is the overall interest level? And how does it inform both the product strategy for this integrated offering and the way that you bring it to market and monetize it? Thank you.

Gerrit (Garrett) Kazmaier: Yeah. As you know, it has been received incredibly well predominantly because you know, every organization has their own ecosystem. We have customers who are using Anthropic and Claude for part of the employee experience. We have customers who are using Microsoft Copilot, Teams, or Slack. And our strategy has been from day 1 that Sana should meet you where you are. So we are strategically making all of our AI capabilities through Sana available in all of the premier AI experiences.

And the beautiful thing in that is, right, if you are an organization who is using Cloud, you can practically get all the benefits of Sana and roll it out immediately before touching or changing anyone's work experience around it. So it is not in beta. It is in early adopt. So, basically, you know, that is a more progressed state already. You know, we have customers using it in their in their landscapes already at scale. And we continue on the same strategy. We have just announced our co pilot integration with Sana. And since you asked about what is different, I think there is something really important to point out.

Our integrations are always AI to AI, which means when Claude uses Sana, they are not just using APIs, and it is based off of the customer's prompt if it works or not. Actually, Claude calls into Sana or Copilot calls into Sana, and all of the reasoning, the lawfulness, the guardrails, the correctness, is all being processed on the Sana side, and then being returned, you know, from our orchestrator into Claude, for instance, or Copilot as the consuming experience. I mean, as said, right, for customers, it is the fast track towards AI adoption. And we are really excited about it.

Operator: Your next question comes from the line of Brent John Thill with Jefferies. Brent, please go ahead.

Brent John Thill: Thanks. Zane, on the US business, it decelerates to 1 of the lowest growth rates we have seen in our model. And maybe that is just a byproduct of international growing, but you would grown The US market 12 to 15. The last 3 quarters. This 1 came in 9.8. So I am just curious. Maybe there is something we are missing. Maybe it is the international business is kicking in or perhaps maybe there was some execution issues in the quarter. Can you just maybe clarify what happened?

Zane C. Rowe: Yeah. Sure, Brent. I alluded to it in my prepared remarks. It was look. First off, I will say we have been very pleased with the international business. Been really outperforming our expectations through the course of the year. The U. S. Business was impacted significantly by our push towards more of the ecosystem. And us getting involved in AI activity as it relates to professional services. If you look at that, that is a total revenue look. The sub revenue growth was higher than the total revenue growth, and that was most impactful in The US business. But, you know, again, a good call out on the international side. We are pleased to see 15% growth there.

And we did not see that as significant on the international front as we did on The US.

Brent John Thill: Okay. Across those topics and you did not see anything that was unusual then.

Zane C. Rowe: No. No. We were. Like I said, we were pleased. It was just we are pushing heavily on The US side to rely more on the ecosystem and to drive more of those deployments with our partners. So it is predominantly on The US.

Robert Enslin: And The US customer base is really adopting AI really fast. They are ahead in terms of UMSA signings. So the customer base is very strong on the AI side as well.

Brent John Thill: Okay, great. Thanks. Thanks, Brent.

Operator: Your next question comes from the line of Samik Chatterjee with JPMorgan. Samik, go ahead.

Samik Chatterjee: Yeah. Hi. Thanks for taking my question. Maybe if I can ask you about the FTE deployment you are talking about, and this sounds like you are looking at a higher base of FTE engagement as you go into next year. Can you talk about sort of which customer cohorts you are focusing on and also the AI products that you are seeing sort of being the focus of the engagement that your customers need the most sort of help with. And also maybe how to think about it in terms of impact on the cost for next year? Thank you.

Gerrit (Garrett) Kazmaier: Yeah. Maybe, you know, I add the first part to it, and then Robert can, because I think 1 important part to understand here is that, you know, the FTEs that you are referring to, they are part of the core engineering and technology organization. It is not all encompassing of our AI activation you know, forward deployed engineers, which are supporting the presales and post sales side. Those 50, they are really, you know, part of our AI engineering teams.

They are working with our large and most sophisticated customers, and they are basically focused on, of course, helping those customers to get into production with complex scenarios, but more importantly, improving our AI systems and our AI deployment technologies so we can scale this back to all of our customer base. You see this specifically with our advanced offering, like Sana, Sana self-service, Sana Concierge. And those offerings where, you know, we strategically deployed them and saw incredible success in basically both creating better deployment technology that Max spoke about, lowering our implementation cost. And improving the AI system on our side that we bring back to the rest of our customers.

So we are scaling up that function because we saw so much merit, you know, across all of these fronts for our services team, and for our core AI engineering organization.

Robert Enslin: Yeah. And then I will just add on the. On Circle Consumption of 4 deployed engineers, we continue to see expansion in talent acquisition. Driving significant expansion. We have a lot of activity going on with, decision intelligence, Workday Data Cloud, Sana Learn, These solutions require a lot of work. In all of our agents. Actually, you got any questions?

Operator: Your next question comes from the line of Adam Wood. With Morgan Stanley. Adam, please go ahead.

Adam Wood: Maybe if I could just ask 1 on the margin side of things. You raised the full year margin guidance this year. To 31.5%. Could I just kind of confirm the at least 33% for next year is off that new base? Zane C. Rowe: Sure, Adam. Yes. So you know, I think Anil has alluded to, you know, following Steve Jobs and thinking about, you know, being a startup and acting like a startup and we are taking that to heart across the company. So if you look at the employee base we have and just our focus on doing things in smarter ways and really driving efficiencies throughout the organization that is what is got us to the 31 and a half.

I called out in excess of 33 which we have been fairly consistent on since financial analyst day. So we will let you know if we have upside to that, you know, as we enter FY 2028. I would say it is not predicated on future restructurings. We have focused on how we are hiring, being very thoughtful about where we are investing and how we are growing the business and doing so in a smart but efficient way. And then as it relates to gross margins, as you have seen, we have been fairly consistent all along.

If anything, we see a little bit more pressure in gross margins as we pivot more and more to the public cloud with our customer base. And, obviously, as we lean into AI, but I will say even as we look at our portfolio of AI offerings, currently, their gross margins are still more or less the same as our gross margins for the other part of the business, but we are encouraged by the progress we are making on that front too. So net, we feel very good about the profile. We are investing in the company, margin growth heading into next year, and we will give you more color on potential upside as we get into FY 2028.

Adam Wood: Just to build on. Thanks for that.

Aneel Bhusri: I do not think we need necessarily more heads. Operator: Your next question comes from the line of Tal Liani with Bank of America. Tal, please go ahead.

Tal Liani: Hi, guys. I have a very high level question. When I see your results and I look at Salesforce and ServiceNow, I see companies that really try hard on AI. But the core business is either flat or down. And the question I have is. At the high level is, I understand that you have great technology. I see. I can see the product. Aneel Bhusri: Maybe I will start it with that. No. it is it is a it is a great question. You know, I would say there are some markets in the US in particular, like the Fortune 500 market. Salespeople like to sell the new stuff, and this new stuff is selling well. As it relates to the budget, I think, to be honest, it is a bit of both. there is an AI budget that is separate from HR and finance. And then there is a budget for HR and finance. And trying to figure out ways. Do they buy a new module from Workday, or do they buy flex credits and new AI products? And so I think that is really the conversation that is happening.

And as I talked about the go to market changes going into next year, we have gotta be very focused on both core business as well as the new AI products and incent the salespeople accordingly.

Gerrit (Garrett) Kazmaier: And I think, you know, there is, you know, I think, you know, the framing for our customers is, you know, really value driven. For instance, they look into the spend in shared service centers. They look in how much they are spending on HR case delivery. Which are substantial amounts of money for them. For them, the ability to convert, you know, a very high spend into a smaller software spend with us it is really compelling. So it is not like a software-to-software transition. They are looking at their company spend all up in any specific function. And, frankly, they are seeing AI leverage with that. Right?

And that is where they can free up money or can divert, you know, funds for growing or stay flat with headcount like we do, and reinvest that into AI automation. that is where we are seeing lift across all of our products. You know, from Xtend to Sana Learn to Data Cloud to our agents. They are basically tapping into that opportunity, and our customers are not seeing it as a constraint or contradiction if they are running software spend.

Operator: We will now take 2 more questions. Next question comes from the line of Rishi Jaluria with RBC Capital Markets. Rishi, please go ahead.

Rishi Jaluria: Oh, wonderful. Thanks so much for taking my questions. Maybe just a simple 1 on, you know, thinking through the impact of AI on margins, not even right now, but over the next, you know, 1 or 2 years, you are you are seeing nice early adoption of AI throughout your customer base. You are talking about further ARR inflection going from here. Maybe 2 pieces to that, though. As we think about just greater usage and credit adoption, what sort of tools do you have, whether it is multimodality, efficiency or something else to kind of protect your own gross margins from AI, putting aside the public cloud that you just talked about. And same with the FDEs. Right?

I recognize you are working with Accenture, but as we think about just getting. Doing more handholding, having, you know, more human resource intensiveness, what. How should we think about the impact of that on your overall margins? And, again, any tools you have to kind of protect yourself from margin degradation as you see that inflection in AI adoption in the customer base. Thanks.

Aneel Bhusri: Yeah. You know, I personally see it as margin expansion. I love the consumption model. it is a model that I have always admired the hyperscalers have that more scale and more usage drive more margin. You know, the FTEs, the beauty of that model is that you get these agents live in weeks, not years. And as soon as the agents are live, they are they are producing revenue and consumption for work day. And to the question you asked about the multimodal, we are absolutely multimodal. We are always choosing the lowest cost path from a foundational model perspective. I will let Garrett talk more about that.

But when we look at the future of consumption and what we can do with agents and be very efficient with it, I think it is actually a margin expanding opportunity.

Gerrit (Garrett) Kazmaier: Yeah. Like Anil has said, right, you know, this is a largely unoptimized space, you know, in AI overall. We are, you know, deliberately being multimodal and having active model routing because of many of the tasks that we are doing You know, the previous generation's models are already saturating our evaluation and accuracy criteria. We have an enormous range of models that we can deploy and really, you know, strike the right price performance characteristics that we need. So we do not feel that we have any cost or margin pressure from different tier models. You know, quite the opposite, actually.

We just announced our partnership with Safe AI and Jasper, which are adding a new component on model routing to it, making it efficient. We have just increased the coverage of our models that we are using internally or across our AI agents. And as Anil has said, you know, actually, frankly, we feel there is an opportunity for us to expand rather than see compression on the margin side because the space overall is unoptimized. And the way how we have approached it by being model agnostic, being task specific, and partnering with all of the model providers on picking the right models for any specific task has so far really paid dividends for us.

Rishi Jaluria: Alright. Very helpful. Thank you.

Operator: Your last question comes from the line of Scott Berg with Needham. Scott, please go ahead.

Scott Berg: Hi. Thanks for taking questions here. I wanted to follow-up on the FDE commentary. I know there is been a couple of questions asked, but you have gotten into this with Accenture, and I assume the other partnerships will be of similar going forward, How do you think about the long term opportunities with those customers? Will this fundamentally change maybe the amount of software agents that you are able to sell these customers? Or is it really more just about speeding up the delivery and the use case of them? A question I get asked often. Does it actually change the size of the pie? Or just does it allow the Thanksgiving pie to be eaten more quickly? Thanks.

Aneel Bhusri: I think it is definitely both. there is no question it speeds up. Speeds up usage. You know, when we think about a typical cloud software deployment, a year used to be a great standard. Maybe now you can get it in 6 months for a large enterprise. We are talking about weeks for agents. And, you know, a lot of the agents are built on the same dataset. And so once the partner or Workday is in there, solving 1 problem with the data and with the agent, they can move on to other problems. And it is all it is all gonna be about discovery on the customer side, figuring out what problems they are looking to solve.

And so now have 17 agents in the market. That list will continue to grow. And I would hope that you would see these customers adopting many agents. Think the self-service and Workday concierge are good places to start, but the work intelligence 1 it is kind of a no brainer. You can see how 4 or 5 agents could be up and running pretty quickly, and so it is not 1 and done and that. And that is a pattern we are seeing even in the early days of adoption.

Scott Berg: Very helpful. Thanks for taking my questions.
