#2996. Top Wall Street analysts find these 3 stocks attractive as long-term investments

Investors have been grappling with stock market volatility, weighing elevated oil prices, persistent geopolitical tensions, the Federal Reserve's rate hike and a debate about AI safety. For all that, it helps to look beyond short-term noise and focus on stocks with strong long-term growth potential.

Top Wall Street analysts' recommendations can help investors gain clarity, as these experts conduct in-depth research to pick stocks with attractive growth prospects.

Here are three stocks favored by some of Wall Street's top pros, according to TipRanks, a platform that ranks analysts based on their past performance.

Enterprise software and cloud infrastructure company Oracle (ORCL) recently announced better-than-expected results for the first quarter of fiscal 2027. The quarter benefited from solid growth in cloud infrastructure revenue.

After hosting a series of investor meetings with Ken Bond, Oracle head of investor relations following Q1 earnings, Guggenheim analyst John DiFucci reiterated a buy rating on the stock with a price target of $400. Oracle remains a Guggenheim Best Idea, he said.

"We continue to believe ORCL is a decade stock, driven by the massive (and profitable) opportunity ahead for AI training and inferencing," said DiFucci. He also cited the traditional Public Cloud business and additional AI-enabled cloud database and cloud applications for his bullish stance. DiFucci expects all the factors to drive revenue and profit acceleration over the next few years.

While Oracle delivered 850 MW of data center capacity in Q1 FY27, Bond cautioned that Infrastructure as a Service revenue in any quarter depends more on the timing of when that capacity comes online, than on the headline MW number. DiFucci expects IaaS growth to stay strong, with full-year growth expected above Q1 FY27's 120% constant currency rate. Management expects total revenue growth to accelerate sequentially throughout fiscal 2027, as the faster-growing infrastructure business makes up a larger share of the mix.

DiFucci addressed concerns regarding customer concentration, saying OpenAI's share of total remaining performance obligations has dropped from 80% last June to about 50% now, and is expected to keep falling as new contracts are signed with new and existing customers.

DiFucci ranks No. 263 among more than 12,490 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been profitable 62% of the time, delivering an average return of about 17.5%. See Oracle Insider Trading Activity on TipRanks.

Space systems and launch services provider Rocket Lab (RKLB) was recently initiated as a buy with an $80 price target by Raymond James analyst Brian Gesuale.

"RKLB has assembled launch, spacecraft, components, payloads and optical communications, with Neutron and Iridium completing medium-lift and applications/spectrum in 2027," said Gesuale.

The 5-star analyst highlighted that with the completion of the Iridium acquisition, Rocket Lab will become the only vertically integrated space company with positive free cash flow (FCF). The deal will add a deployed constellation valued at more than $3 billion, globally coordinated L-band spectrum and about $500 million in earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation, and amortization (EBITDA) and $300 million in free cash flow (FCF).

Gesuale highlighted RKLB's strong revenue and backlog growth and progress toward positive EBITDA and FCF in 2027/2028. Rocket Lab is moving from a heavy investment phase into monetization, with estimated revenue growth of 59% in 2026, the analyst said, noting that RKLB's backlog has more than doubled to almost $2.4 billion from $1.1 billion in Q3 2025.

Given strong growth projections, the analyst expects RKLB's gross margins to expand from about a 35% trough in 2027 to about 47% by 2030, while R&D spending is estimated to decline from ~35% of sales in 2026 to about 10% in 2028, creating substantial operating leverage as the platform matures.

Gesuale ranks No. 369 among more than 12,490 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been profitable 63% of the time, delivering an average return of about 17%. See Rocket Lab Statistics on TipRanks.

J.P. Morgan analyst Doug Anmuth recently upgraded Meta Platforms (META) to buy from hold and raised his price target to $820 from $640. Despite the year-to-date underperformance of META, the 5-star analyst still sees significant upside, as Meta is in the early stages of launching frontier models and AI-powered offerings beyond advertising, particularly the Muse AI agent and Meta Model API access.

"Frontier models are at the core of Meta's product and monetization pipeline over a multi-year period, and its path toward superintelligence," said Anmuth.

In the summer of 2025, Meta set a goal to rebuild its Meta Superintelligence Labs team and deliver frontier AI models within a year, the analyst said. The team appears to have met its goal, rapidly advancing from the rollout of Muse Spark 1.1 in July to Muse Spark 1.3, which is competitive with Claude and GPT models, Anmuth said.

Meanwhile, Meta's Watermelon product will expand opportunities in consumer products, business intelligence, and Family of Apps engagement, the analyst said. The product will enhance internal operations and overall efficiency, said Anmuth, who's confident of Meta's ability to bring consumer-driven AI products to its extensive user base of 4 billion and views its distribution network as a competitive advantage.

While Meta has focused on frontier models and AI product development, Anmuth also sees solid opportunity in its AI infrastructure capacity, which he believes will support future compute needs.

Anmuth ranks No. 832 among more than 12,490 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been successful 57% of the time, delivering an average return of about 9.40%. See Meta Platforms Financials on TipRanks.

#2995. How to Turn Off Apple Intelligence Feature by Feature in iOS 27

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

Whether you want to drop a few AI features or as many as possible, here's where each control can be found in iOS 27.

iOS 26 lets you turn off Apple Intelligence with one toggle. iOS 27 doesn’t. Apple folded its AI settings into a new Siri menu centered on Siri AI and dropped the master switch along the way, so opting out now means working through several parts of Settings. Siri AI’s controls are in the Siri menu, Screen Time can block Writing Tools and image creation, notification summaries have their own switch and each app’s Siri & Search settings control what Siri learns from it. This guide walks through every step in order.

Individual features can still be disabled, but they’re scattered across several menus in Settings and Screen Time rather than being consolidated in one place. Here’s the current map of what can be turned off and where to find each control.

If your device is not running the newest software, turning off Apple Intelligence all at once only takes a few taps in Settings and doesn’t affect any core iPhone functionality. Here’s how to do it on iPhone, iPad and Mac.

You can still disable some of Apple’s AI features if your iPhone is running iOS 27. It just won’t be as easy as tapping the main toggle.

To disable Siri AI, go to Settings > Siri and toggle off the control. Beware, though, that this will disable your voice assistant entirely, as well as disable conversations in the new dedicated Siri app and block you from using Apple’s Visual Intelligence. Additionally, your HomePod speakers will not be able to recognize your voice or help with personal content if they’re on the same iCloud account as your iPhone.

Keep reading for how to disable some of the individual Apple AI features.

Since the first Apple Intelligence features rolled out in iOS 18.1, some people have opted out of the new technology. Tools such as Image Playground, Genmoji and message summaries can use up to 7GB of your device’s internal storage — a sizable chunk, especially if you tend to run against the upper limit of its free space.

Even if storage is not an issue, you just may not be interested in Apple’s set of AI features. A recent CNET survey finds that just 19% of US smartphone owners are choosing to upgrade their devices to take advantage of new AI features. And a recent ZDNET/Aberdeen survey reveals that the majority of US adults say they will not use most AI features, and just 8% would consider paying extra for them. Some AI features are more welcome than others, with 58% of respondents saying using AI for photo editing would be valuable.

Or, honestly, you may not want to deal with features that are creating inaccurate summaries or that can be replicated without Apple Intelligence.

(Earlier iOS 18 updates re-enabled Apple Intelligence automatically even if you had turned it off, but as of iOS 18.4, the setting is honored.)

Read more: Did a well-meaning friend send you a message about Apple Intelligence possibly reading your private information? Here’s what’s actually going on.

I’m not an AI crank — I appreciate features such as notification summaries and the Clean Up tool in the Photos app. And yet, Apple Intelligence is also a work in progress, an evolving set of features that Apple is heavily hyping while gradually developing. I wouldn’t hold it against you if you wanted to not be distracted or feel like you’re doing Apple’s testing for them (that’s what the developer and public betas should be for).

Remember that Apple Intelligence works only on the new iPhone 18 lineup, the iPhone Duo, iPhone 17, iPhone 17 Pro, iPhone Air, iPhone 17E, iPhone 16, iPhone 16E, iPhone 16 Pro, iPhone 15 Pro or M-series Macs and iPads, plus the newest iPad mini.

If you’re concerned about the storage requirements of Apple Intelligence, you can find out how much the system is using by going to Settings > General > iPhone (or iPad) Storage > iOS (or iPadOS).

See how much space Apple Intelligence is using in Settings. This is what it looks like running iOS 26, but the settings flow is the same.

Note that even after turning off Apple Intelligence, the storage still shows up in the iOS Storage list. However, I was able to confirm that if the phone’s storage fills up and the system needs that now-inactive space, iOS reclaims what it needs.

Maybe you’re finding some Apple Intelligence features helpful while others are annoying (or just highly amusing). You can turn off specific features in the settings for apps to which they apply.

For example, to disable text summaries in Messages notifications, go to Settings > Apps > Messages and switch off the Summarize Messages option.

Some features are not as app-specific. Writing Tools, which use Apple Intelligence to proof or rewrite text, appear as an option when you select text, regardless of the app. To turn that off, you need to disable Apple Intelligence system-wide.

Also note that nearly every app includes an “Apple Intelligence & Siri” option in Settings, with a Learn from this App option (turned on by default). That applies just to whether Apple Intelligence and Siri can monitor how you use it to make suggestions; it doesn’t affect any particular Apple Intelligence features.

Another option for restricting what Apple Intelligence can do is buried in the Screen Time settings. Screen Time is designed to control which apps and features can run on another device, such as the iPhone used by a child in your household. But it’s also helpful for tracking how much time you’re spending on the device and, in this case, turning off some components of Apple Intelligence.

Turn off selected Apple Intelligence features in the Screen Time settings. This is what the settings look like with iOS 26. It may look different if you are using iOS 27. The settings flow is the same.

If you haven’t upgraded to iOS 27 yet, make a good backup first.

If you aren’t on iOS 27, you can turn off Apple Intelligence with one tap. (You can see what software your iPhone is running by going to Settings > General > About and seeing what iOS version you’re running.)

If you’re on iOS 26 or earlier, here’s how to disable Apple Intelligence. Open Settings (iPhone or iPad) or System Settings (Mac) and choose Apple Intelligence & Siri. Then turn off the Apple Intelligence option. Confirm your choice in the dialog that appears by tapping Turn Off Apple Intelligence.

Turn off Apple Intelligence entirely with one switch if you are running iOS 26 or an earlier software version.

Curiously, the Clean Up tool in Photos sticks around even when Apple Intelligence is turned off, perhaps because the first time you use it the app downloads resources for it and holds onto them.

#2994. 5 new Apple Health features you should try in iOS 27.3 – if your phone qualifies

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Apple's redesigned Health app arrives in December with some major upgrades, but not every iPhone will get the full experience.

Apple is kicking off a new and improved Health app next month with the release of iOS 27.3. Instead of just recording and displaying your health-related stats, the app will tap into Apple Intelligence to analyze the data and dispense advice on how to improve your health and fitness. But that reliance on AI means you’ll need the right type of iPhone to enjoy all the benefits.

Also: Apple could build its AI health chatbot from this study – how to enroll

Here are five helpful new features built into the app, along with what you’ll need to access them.

First up, the app will offer suggestions based on data from different sources. For example, it might advise you to go for a walk at a nearby park if it detects that you’re not getting enough exercise. It may show you articles and videos about sleep if it finds that you’re not well-rested. It could also highlight possible conditions based on your lab and test results. You can easily view these recommendations from the Insights screen.

Also: Health is Tim Cook’s defining legacy – and your Apple Watch proves it

A new feature called Health Age compares your physical health to your actual age to show how you’re doing. The analysis draws on certain stats and lab data, such as your resting heart rate, sleep, heart rate variability (HRV), cholesterol, and A1C (average blood glucose levels), to deliver a health age, which may differ from your chronological age. The results can show you areas that may be of concern or that you need to focus on.

Also: Apple Watch Series 12 review: Finally, the health tracker I’ve been waiting for

With a new feature called Movement Evaluations and an iPhone and Apple Watch, the Health app can assess your flexibility, strength, balance, VO2 max (maximum oxygen absorption), and overall movement. You perform a physical routine while your iPhone “watches” you via the camera. Using built-in AI, the app will provide audio and visual feedback in real-time to tell you how you’re faring.

Apple promises that the analysis is performed on your device without recording, storing, or sharing the video.

The new app will be able to correlate your test results with data collected by your iPhone and Apple Watch to give you a more comprehensive picture of your health. Plus, Apple and Quest Diagnostics have teamed up to offer people in the US an optional $119 bloodwork panel that covers more than 50 biomarkers to scan for different health and medical conditions.

Also: I tested the Apple Watch Series 12 heart-rate claims against my gold-standard Polar strap

Normally, you need an Apple Fitness+ subscription to fire up workout videos to help you exercise. But the new Health app will come with its own comprehensive set of training videos. Available from the Insights section, a series of strength exercise videos are designed to help you build your body strength. The videos cover all the key areas of your body to give you a full workout.

Some of the new features, such as the strength videos, will be available to all iPhone users. But the ones that rely on AI will run only on phones that support Apple Intelligence. That means you’ll need an iPhone 15 Pro or Pro Max, any iPhone 16 or 17, an iPhone 18 Pro or Pro Max, an iPhone Air, or an iPhone Duo.

Holiday shoppers have reached their breaking point

There's nothing quite like hearing "Your call is important to us" for the 15th time while trying to track down a missing holiday package. And apparently, I'm not alone in my frustration.

A new survey from voice AI company PolyAI found that 69.4% of respondents would be willing to speak with an AI voice assistant instead of waiting for a human customer service representative if they were guaranteed zero wait time.

The survey of 1,087 U.S. consumers, conducted in November 2026, suggests that despite reservations about AI replacing human workers, many Americans are open to the technology when it solves an everyday problem.

With Black Friday deals already underway and Cyber Monday just days away, AI could offer some relief from one of the biggest headaches of holiday shopping.

According to the survey shared with Tom's Guide, nearly 68% of respondents say automated phone menus frequently or almost always fail to resolve their problems no matter how much customers try to get around them. Just one in four consumers reports having their issue resolved on the first call.

Poor customer service is also affecting where people shop. Some 64.4% of respondents have abandoned a holiday purchase or canceled an order because of a bad customer service experience.

Perhaps the most entertaining findings from the survey are what people would rather do than navigate an automated phone menu:

Sign up to the Tom's AI Guide weekly newsletter summing up all the biggest AI news you need to know. Plus, analysis from our AI editors and tips on how to use the latest AI tools!

While Gen Z is often associated with AI adoption, millennials were the most receptive to AI-powered customer service in this survey. More than 75% said they would use a voice AI assistant if it meant eliminating wait times.

Perhaps more surprising is that 62% of baby boomers and older respondents said they would do the same.

However, consumers aren't necessarily ready to give up human customer service entirely. Nearly 68% of respondents said they would feel comfortable using voice AI if they could be transferred to a human representative when necessary.

Shoppers surveyed also wanted AI to do more than answer basic questions. They were interested in assistants that could tell them whether something was in stock, solve a problem without asking for the same information twice or text them a receipt or boarding pass before they hung up.

Of course, there's a big difference between an AI assistant that sounds human and one that can actually get things done. Much of that comes down to how well a company has integrated AI into its existing customer service systems.

We've all been stuck on a customer service call, pressing buttons and repeating ourselves just to get through to someone who can help. Conversational AI promises to make that experience a little less painful.

Instead of sitting through a lengthy phone menu, you could simply explain that your package was delivered to the wrong house or that you need to change your flight, much like you would with a human agent. What do you think about AI customer service? Share your thoughts in the comments.

#2992. Everything Is Falling Apart, and AI’s Fingerprints Are Everywhere

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

AI is rewriting the web in its own imperfect image, making software flaws easier to find and easier to exploit, while introducing plenty of its own imperfections.

I have struggled to find the time to write this story about why everything keeps breaking because everything keeps breaking.

Microsoft Outlook? Broken, for a bit. Air traffic control? Had some issues. Bank with Chase? Monday was not great. But even before that, you had issues if you ran a website with PHP, or had a grocery store freezer connected to the internet, or owned crypto. I am almost certainly forgetting some.

Something must be behind all of this, you might think — a massive cyberattack campaign, maybe or AI agents running amok across the internet? But the answer is more complicated than that. All of these issues, and the ones that will happen after I write this, are probably unconnected, at least in the concrete sense. But they exist in a world where the infrastructure of the internet and the whole human world it undergirds looks increasingly precarious.

Adam Meyers, senior vice president of counteradversary operations at cybersecurity company CrowdStrike, called last month “Black October.” This month? “Blacker November.” December probably isn’t looking great.

“This is not getting better, unfortunately,” Meyers told me.

One big reason for all of this, although not the only one, is artificial intelligence, but maybe not in the ways you expect.

If it’s connected to the internet, it’s at risk. Websites, sure. But also utilities like power plants and water treatment facilities or, for some reason, grocery store freezers.

In the olden days, like six months ago, a hacker taking control would have required a fairly complicated set of skills, honed over a long career, perhaps in the employ of a government or criminal organization.

Artificial intelligence, especially models developed and released this year, has changed things. AI has “democratized” hacking, cybersecurity experts told me. Things that used to require the capabilities and focus of a team of people with a clear goal can be done by a 20-something with an AI model and a specially designed program around it. And you don’t have to be a big or valuable target anymore to be worthy of a hacker’s attention.

At the same time, AI has made it easier to find vulnerabilities. These models and agents — essentially AI models that can do things on their own — can comb through websites or code and find problems that might have escaped the notice of humans. And they can do so more cheaply, meaning they can be turned on code that might not otherwise have gotten a close look. So many vulnerabilities are being exposed that it’s been given an appropriately bleak name: the vulnpocalypse.

Even that defensive advantage is a double-edged sword. Before, it might have taken weeks before a newly discovered vulnerability could be exploited. Now it might take days, even hours. If you’re responsible for a website or any of those things connected to the internet that may or may not still be maintained by their creators, you may not be paying attention and know you should update. You may find yourself liable if a breach leads to a leak of customer data. You may not have the know-how to fix it.

Another risk introduced by AI is that the technology, trained on all the lines of code its creators could find, is really good at writing code. Software engineers know this, and companies are now maintaining smaller teams of human engineers using AI to write more and more software. That code might be OK, but it might not be, and there’s a chance no human ever looked at it to be sure.

When I connected with John Strand over video chat, he was in Germany for a conference, and he was smiling. That wasn’t good. “You need to understand that whenever an offensive security person smiles and gets excited,” he said, “it’s bad.”

As owner and CEO of Black Hills Information Security, Strand’s job is to test systems for weaknesses, to think like an attacker and poke holes in a client’s defenses. He says he’d been getting a bit bored with the work after decades of the same techniques until the cyber capabilities of AI models started to explode at the end of 2025. New AI models were great at finding weaknesses in code, and AI agents could do the boring, time-consuming part.

“You’re seeing something that can automate the kind of grinding grunt work of offensive security and bring that to a human operator much faster,” Strand said.

Things have only accelerated since the summer. AI agents are capable of more autonomy. And attackers have better tools to refine the often blunt instruments of AI models — harnesses. While an AI model can do a lot of things, a harness provides the tools and direction that allow it to do a specific thing more effectively. Think Anthropic’s Claude Code or OpenAI’s Codex, but for hacking. Perhaps the biggest, most notable harness used by hackers is Artex, a significant-enough threat that the FBI issued a warning.

In September and October, a hack of major South Korean banks led to the theft of personal information. Meyers says CrowdStrike determined the attacker was likely a 26-year-old in China using Artex. After asking AI how to do the attack, the hacker succeeded, then asked the AI how to sell the stolen data on Telegram.

“Anybody out there can now be a nation-state-level hacker just by using the tool,” Meyers said.

Despite efforts by major AI developers to limit who can access their biggest and most capable models, the hacking and exploit skills attackers need are within the means of models already in the hands of attackers. That includes open-weight models that hackers can run on their own hardware, away from the guardrails and peering eyes of AI companies and government agencies.

“The genie’s out of the bottle, and there’s no putting it back in,” said Gary Barlet, public sector chief technology officer at Illumio, a firm that specializes in ransomware and breach containment.

AI-powered hackers, whether they’re individual vibe-hackers or government-backed cyberwarfare units intent on damaging critical infrastructure, always have an advantage. They just have to be right once, as the saying goes. Defenders have to be right every time.

The good thing is that the defenders are using the same tools as the attackers. And sometimes they have a head start. Programs like Anthropic’s Project Glasswing, OpenAI’s Daybreak and Google’s Fairwind let cybersecurity experts and high-profile targets like banks and healthcare providers have early access to the most capable models from those developers, often with fewer limits on what the models can find. The goal is to get a jump on patching and fixing the easiest and riskiest problems.

It still might not be enough, and Big Tech leaders know it. In an October appearance at the Stanford Graduate School of Business, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said he no longer thought we’d be able to “just patch all the bugs” and that the problem is one that “is still something that we have not, as organizational leaders or countries or individuals, taken seriously.”

And defenders may not have much of a lead in patching bugs anyway, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella said at the New York Times Dealbook Summit. Previously, when patching a critical system, you might have a week to test it before pushing it to production. “Right now the patch needs to go instantly from being available to being patched in production because it’s being exploited in the wild,” Nadella said. “That’s going to create instability.”

The PHP vulnerability widely reported in October — with an urgent notice from the PHP Foundation for website owners to patch — stemmed from work through Patch the Planet, part of OpenAI’s Daybreak.

That’s just one high-profile recent disclosure. But there has been an avalanche of them. The National Vulnerability Database has received more than 10,000 instances of common vulnerabilities and exposures so far in November, after more than 17,000 CVEs in October. For comparison, in October 2025, that figure was less than 5,000.

“There’s effectively this big backlog of security issues in the open-source world that hadn’t been discovered until AI was able to just spend tons of time analyzing it and finding these vulnerabilities,” said Matt Wyckhouse, CEO of Finite State, a cybersecurity company focused on connected devices.

It goes well beyond open-source software. The connected devices Wyckhouse focuses on include things like refrigerators and smart home gadgets — the kinds of things that probably didn’t have to be connected to the internet, but are. The source code of the firmware and software powering those products has been seen by far fewer eyes than something like PHP, an incredibly common coding language used by much of the internet. The code running these devices may not be on GitHub or floating around the internet, but an AI model might be able to reverse-engineer it and find an exploit. And suddenly an attacker can turn freezers into ovens. If you think ground beef is expensive now, imagine what would happen if a major retailer’s stock of hamburger all spoiled overnight.

“Refrigeration has to work for our society to function, as it turns out,” Wyckhouse said.

Wherever the vulnerability is found, it has to be patched. That’s where the backlog of issues is really wreaking havoc. Companies that create or just operate software are swamped with important, critical issues that have to be fixed now because it could only be hours before an attacker can exploit it. It’s why your computer and the software on it have to update so frequently these days.

“It’s daunting the amount of work and the amount of time it’s going to take to clean this whole thing up,” said Ted Miracco, CEO of the mobile security firm Approov.

And patching isn’t perfect. Sometimes it’s not a cyberattack that causes a system to go down but the fix to prevent it. Software updates are believed to be responsible for several of the recent high-profile outages, including Apple’s issues on Tuesday.

Things get even hairier if the code isn’t great to begin with or presents new problems of its own. And with AI writing even more of it, that’s a growing issue.

In the backdrop of all of this chaos is the fact that software engineering is one of the industries most disrupted by AI. Models trained on miles of code are great at writing something that works — no matter how many holes are in it. And to CEOs eager to cut costs and boost their companies’ stock prices, the temptation is to lay off engineers and have fewer people use AI to do all that coding.

Big Tech has been laying off staff by the thousands this year. Microsoft’s October announcement that it was offering buyouts to 60,000 staff became a key talking point just weeks later when the system powering its Outlook email service went dark for a day. Might things break less often if more people were on hand to maintain them?

“I wouldn’t be surprised if companies start to backtrack on that more,” said Ryan McCurdy, vice president of marketing at the database security firm Liquibase.

Companies might also have more junior developers writing and releasing code that would have previously gone through senior developers, with AI replacing the productivity, but not the experience, McCurdy says.

That means the problem isn’t just the vulnerabilities in existing software, but the vulnerabilities being written into new software or patches to existing software by AI. The same technology is causing the problem, providing the solution and complicating that solution.

The main thing we can do now is just… wait. Wyckhouse told me he thinks the next two years are going to be a period of growing pains as vulnerabilities are found and patched. The end result should be that everything is more stable.

“I think software is going to be an order of magnitude more secure by the end of the next year or two than it is today for this reason,” he said. “It will hurt a bit.”

Whether you’re an ordinary phone user or a major corporation, updating your software has become more important than ever.

“You’ve got to patch. You go for a flu shot, and you go and have your preventative healthcare,” Meyers said. “You need to do the same thing when it comes to cybersecurity.”

We don’t have to put up with it, Barlet says. “I think we need to start having higher expectations from the companies we’re consuming from,” he said.

#2991. Google Wallet comes to your iPhone – but without this feature

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Tech > Services & Software > Operating Systems > Mobile OS > iOS

The new Google Wallet app brings Gemini agentic shopping to US-based iOS users - sorry, no tap-to-pay.

The Google Wallet app is available for iPhone users in the US for the first time. iOS users who download the new Google Wallet app can manage online payments for faster checkout at places that support Google Pay. However, Apple restricts Google’s ability to offer tap-to-pay service on the iOS app, so users won’t be able to use Google Wallet for contactless checkout on iPhone.

Also: You can use Google’s Spark AI agent, renamed Tasks, for free now – with limits

The new Google Wallet app lets you digitize physical cards, including payment, loyalty, and membership cards, as well as boarding passes. Google Wallet app users on iOS will also be able to view receipts and track orders pulled from Gmail in one app.

There used to be a Google Pay app for iOS, but it was discontinued in 2024. The old Google Pay app also didn’t support tap-to-pay on iPhone, but it offered limited functionality, including support for loyalty and gift cards, as well as purchase tracking.

The biggest difference between the old Google Pay app for iOS and the new Google Wallet is the AI component, which supports agentic shopping, likely as Google’s longer-term play.

One of Google’s goals for the Wallet app on iOS is to make it a central place to manage purchases made by its AI agents. The Agents section in Google Wallet for iPhone lets you manage and monitor purchases made through Gemini.

Agentic commerce is on the rise, as evidenced by the growing use of Meta’s Muse. Gemini can make purchases and payments through the Tasks feature, which lets you give Gemini permission to buy the items you want and set your maximum budget.

Also: Google Wallet just turned your Android phone into a digital house key

The Google Wallet app for iOS becomes the central hub for purchase management in agentic commerce through Gemini. In it, you can view active tasks to see which purchases Gemini is working on, as well as completed purchases and receipts.

Google has been working on two technologies to support its agentic commerce strategy: Universal Commerce Protocol (UCP) and Agent Payments Protocol (AP2).

UCP is a technical language that enables AI agents to communicate with retailers and make purchases, while AP2 is the payment framework that establishes rules and authorization for agents to make payments.

Google Wallet serves as both the AI-powered wallet and the consumer-facing record of transactions made by Gemini.

Also: Google Wallet has a lot of new tricks – these 5 are my favorites

Along with Google, major retailers supported the development of UCP, including Shopify, Walmart, Target, and Etsy. When Google announced AP2, more than 60 organizations became involved, including PayPal, Salesforce, Mastercard, and American Express.

#2989. 90% of employers reject resumes that look like AI – yet half use AI to interview

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

In today's job market, do applicants really have a choice of whether to comply with AI hiring tools?

Hiring managers are more suspicious than ever of AI use in applications, and it’s impacting who they consider. At the same time, they’re turning to AI to help screen more candidates — meaning those videos you’ve seen on the internet of people pranking AI interviewers aren’t going away anytime soon.

New data from hiring systems firm Greenhouse found that “nine in ten US employers (90%) believe they’ve turned away real candidates because those applications seemed fake or AI-generated.” Greenhouse clarified that it doesn’t know whether employers are putting applications through AI detection tools or not.

Also: How many jobs is your state losing to AI? This dashboard tracks the cuts – and the cost

“The survey data is self-reported, so it reflects what employers believe has happened, not a measured outcome,” Greenhouse’s Head of Voice AI Ophir Samson told ZDNET via email.

Employers are also reacting to AI by adjusting their hiring processes: 86% of those surveyed reported changes to account for AI’s impact. 57% of them did so by adding another human interview.

“As jobseekers rely more on AI to polish and send out their job applications, employers are finding it harder to tell who’s actually right for the role,” the report stated, echoing an ongoing push-and-pull between applicants and hiring teams. AI resume screeners automatically toss a majority of applications they deem unfit, so applicants try not to get tossed by formatting their material for the screener, which then backfires anyway.

The report shows how a tough economy and an influx of AI hiring tools are colliding, arguably to benefit employers over applicants. Greenhouse noted that, ironically, AI tools are helping hiring managers while also making resumes untrustworthy, and applicants would rather be interviewed by AI than not at all.

Also: How to beat the AI algorithm and get the job of your dreams

“A growing number of employers are using AI not just to filter candidates out, but to have conversations with more candidates, earlier, through AI-powered voice technology,” Greenhouse said, adding that “half now use AI interviews to hear from more candidates, and 40% of those have found strong candidates they would have missed.”

Greenhouse itself offers a voice AI screening interview tool. Samson told ZDNET that an HR professional ran 200 candidates she’d rejected through Greenhouse’s tool, and it suggested 19.

“All five of the finalists came from that group, and she ultimately hired one from the group,” Samson said.

What we don’t, and maybe can’t, know is the inverse: whether AI screeners influence hiring managers to turn away candidates they actually should have considered. At least in Greenhouse’s case, Samson said Voice AI doesn’t make hiring decisions or “automatically advance, reject, or rank candidates.”

“Recruiters review every output, and one recruiter owns the outcome and can explain how they reached it,” he said.

Greenhouse’s report surveyed 1,347 hiring managers and recruiters across the US, UK, Germany, Australia, and Ireland from late September to mid-October, and found that half of employers using voice AI “say the early-stage candidate experience has improved.”

Also: ‘So perfect, they are literally identical’ – Your AI-polished resumes are recruiters’ new top stressor

It’s unclear what “improved” means there, though, and whether applicants themselves would agree with that. Still, when given the choice, only 7% of applicants in the US would turn down an AI interview, per an earlier Greenhouse report. Additionally, “70% of those who’ve had a live AI interview say it helped them show their skills,” that report said.

But how swayed is that by the state of the US job market? October’s job report was better than expected, but it’s still been a tough year overall for job-seekers. Greenhouse’s findings could be as much a reflection of how desperate applicants are as an endorsement of or comfort with AI screenings.

“The job market could be a factor. Our Future of Hiring Candidate Report shows 81% of job seekers were rejected from a job in the past year without speaking to anyone at the company, human or AI,” Samson said. “But I’d be careful about reading the data as desperation. Candidates are setting clear conditions: nearly half (49%) want to know if a human will review their responses and 40% want to know how they’ll be evaluated.”

Also: Why replacing staff with AI backfires – and 5 ways smart leaders generate real value instead

Samson said that a software engineer named Ryan Quinlan, who was hired at Blissway, initially thought “talking to an AI” sounded stranger, but that it ultimately “felt like a conversation” that let him mention skills he’d forgotten to include on his resume. Samson said that Ryan has been “a ‘maybe’ on paper,” but that the AI interview helped him get over the line to be considered.

“For most applicants, a human conversation was never on the table,” Samson said. “The real choice is a resume lost in a pile, or 15 minutes to tell their story.”

Greenhouse found that while employers are using AI to screen more candidates, most are maintaining human oversight over the most important decisions in the hiring process.

“Of all the tasks employers would hand to an AI agent, deciding which candidates to advance came last, at just 7%,” Greenhouse said.

A recent California law aims to protect employees from being fired by AI systems that make determinations about their performance without a human co-signing the assessment. As with many AI productivity tools in the workplace, proper adoption ideally equates to more time for human workers to handle more important tasks.

Also: 92% of HR say staff can train for AI jobs – but half of companies still hire outside

“Of employers who’ve saved time with AI, 85% put it back into candidates, most often by spending more time with shortlisted candidates (45%) and interviewing more candidates earlier (40%),” Greenhouse said.

The main question around AI interviewers remains whether they’re correctly capturing your interview the way you’d hope a human interviewer would (though that’s still deeply subjective and out of applicants’ control anyway).

“When AI interviews are implemented thoughtfully and transparently, they pay off for both candidates and recruiters,” Samson said. “Every candidate who uses our Voice AI can opt out, and about 90% rate the experience as excellent.”

Cats make a wonderful household pet, but cleaning their litter box is not so much fun, which is why I’ve tried several automatic litter boxes over the years to see if any could make it less of a chore.

The latest model I’ve been using, the Homerunpet Self Cleaning Cat Litter Box Kit, is the most expensive, and largest one I’ve yet brought into my house. I — or more specifically my cats — have been using it for about two months, and they seem to have taken to it well. However, before you spend upwards of $600 on this thing, there’s a few things you should know first.

This self-cleaning litter box is designed for cats up to 25 pounds, works with a variety of litter, a 12L waste bin with odor control, and has an app that lets you monitor your cats' weight.

This litterbox is huge. The box it came in was larger than ones I got with microwaves. Measuring 23.62 x 28.07 x 27.44 inches, you’re definitely going to need a lot of space for it, so I would not recommend it if you’re planning to put it in a smallish bathroom.

The HomeRun Pet litterbox looks kind of like a cement mixer. The main part of the box is a large drum with a hole in its side; this is where your cat enters and does its business. When they’re done, and after a minute or two, the litterbox rotates this section to empty the waste into a small storage bin on the side, and then refreshes the clean litter from a reservoir.

To the right of this main drum is a reservoir into which you pour fresh litter. The machine will draw from this reservoir to replenish the main tray.

No more scooping! When the machine empties itself, waste is funneled into a small bin on the right side, which you line with an included plastic bag. When the bag is full — you'll get an alert on your phone — you simply pull the bin out and remove the bag. Replacement bags cost $35 for a pack of 60. With two cats, we’ve had to replace the bag once every two weeks or so.

There’s actually two trays; a second one, which sits directly below the drum, can be used if you want to completely empty the litter box. And, every piece of the litter box that could possibly get dirty can be removed and washed.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

This being a “smart” cat litter box, you get all sorts of updates via the HomeRun app — when it needs to be emptied, when you need to add new litter, how long your cats take, and how many times they go per day.

One interesting feature of the HomeRun Pet is that it has a built-in scale, so you can keep tabs on your cats’ weight. I initially had to wait until each of mine used the box to figure out which was which, but after that, it would tell me which cat had gone, and when. Of course, if your cats are very close in weight, it might have trouble telling the difference. If that’s the case, you can adjust the weight error value, so it can better distinguish between multiple pets.

The app also lets you customize all sorts of things, like the type of litter you’re using, cleaning schedule, and even “kitten protection,” to prevent the device from activating automatically.

In order to use the HomeRun, your cat has to step up about a foot to get inside the opening; knowing how a cat of mine had trouble walking in his later years, I highly doubt he’d have been able to make it up. Something like the PetSafe Smart Self-Cleaning Litterbox would make more sense (and it’s a lot cheaper and takes up a lot less space).

The Homerunpet Self Cleaning Cat Litter Box Kit is not a small investment; even with Black Friday sales, you’re still going to spend $659 at Amazon on this thing. And, it takes up a lot of space. However, it does make cleaning up after your cat incredibly convenient - just slide open a tray, remove a bag, and you’re all set. Is that worth the price of a nice TV? That’s for you to decide.

Follow Tom's Guide on Google News and add us as a preferred source to get our up-to-date news, analysis, and reviews in your feeds.

Michael A. Prospero is the U.S. Editor-in-Chief for Tom’s Guide. In his spare time, he also tests out the latest drones, electric scooters, and smart home gadgets, such as video doorbells. Before his tenure at Tom's Guide, he was the Reviews Editor for Laptop Magazine, a reporter at Fast Company, the Times of Trenton, and, many eons back, an intern at George magazine. He received his undergraduate degree from Boston College, where he worked on the campus newspaper The Heights, and then attended the Columbia University school of Journalism. When he’s not testing out the latest running watch, electric scooter, or skiing or training for a marathon, he’s probably using the latest sous vide machine, smoker, or pizza oven, to the delight — or chagrin — of his family.

#2987. Nutanix (NTNX) Q1 2027 Earnings Call Transcript

CEO transition overshadows a record margin quarter as the company eyes AI growth.

By Motley Fool Transcribing – Nov 24, 2026 at 10:53PM EST

Need a quote from a Motley Fool analyst? Email [email protected]

Nutanix (NTNX -5.16%) reported first-quarter results that exceeded prior guidance while simultaneously announcing a leadership transition. Chief Executive Officer Rajiv Ramaswami plans to step down once a successor is appointed, marking the end of what he described as the company's second strategic chapter. Management indicated that the company is entering its third chapter, focused on establishing the Nutanix Cloud Platform as a foundation for enterprise artificial intelligence and cloud-native workloads. The company maintained its full-year revenue outlook but raised its operating margin and free cash flow targets for fiscal 2027, citing ongoing operational efficiencies and a healthy demand environment.

Operator: Good day, and thank you for standing by. Welcome to the Nutanix First Quarter 2027 Earnings Conference Call. [Operator Instructions] Please be advised that today's conference is being recorded. I would now like to turn the conference over to your speaker for today, Rich Valera, VP of Investor Relations. Please go ahead.

Richard (Rich) Valera: Good afternoon, and welcome to today's conference call to discuss first quarter fiscal year 2027 financial results. Joining me today are Rajiv Ramaswami, Nutanix's CEO, and Rukmini Sivaraman, Nutanix's CFO. After the market closed today, Nutanix issued a press release announcing first quarter fiscal year 2027 financial results. If you'd like to read the release, please visit the Press Releases section of our IR website. During today's call, management will make forward-looking statements, including financial guidance. These forward-looking statements involve risks and uncertainties, some of which are beyond our control, which could cause actual results to differ materially and adversely from those anticipated by these statements.

For a more detailed description of these and other risks and uncertainties, please refer to our SEC filings, including our most recent annual report on Form 10-K as well as our earnings press release issued today. These forward-looking statements apply as of today, and we undertake no obligation to revise these statements after this call. As a result, you should not rely on them as predictions of future events. Please note, unless otherwise specifically referenced, all financial measures we use on today's call, except for revenue, are expressed on a non-GAAP basis and have been adjusted to exclude certain charges.

We have provided, to the extent available, reconciliations of these non-GAAP financial measures to GAAP financial measures on our IR website and in our earnings press release. Nutanix will be participating in the UBS Global Technology and AI Conference in Scottsdale on November 30, the Raymond James TMT and Consumer Conference in New York on December 7 and the Barclays Global Technology Conference in San Francisco on December 10. We hope to see some of you at these events. Finally, our second quarter fiscal 2027 quiet period will begin on January 16. And with that, I'll turn the call over to Rajiv. Rajiv?

Rajiv Ramaswami: Thank you, Rich, and good afternoon, everyone. Earlier today, we announced that I am working with the Board to identify and recruit my successor and will be stepping down from my role as CEO after a successor has been appointed and assumes the role. This was a thoughtful decision that I came to with the Board, grounded in a shared belief that now is the right moment to plan for Nutanix's next chapter of leadership. What drew me to Nutanix 6 years ago was the rare combination of a category-defining platform, a deeply loyal customer base and a team that consistently executes at the highest level.

Our competitive position is the strongest it's ever been and the market opportunity in front of us is the largest it's ever been. I will work closely with the Board to ensure a seamless transition. Until the process is complete and my successor assumes the role, I remain fully committed as CEO of Nutanix, and I will continue to drive our FY '27 strategic priorities forward. I will also continue to serve as a senior adviser to the company for a period of time after my successor is in place.

It has been an honor to lead this company, and I look forward to supporting the Board in identifying Nutanix's next leader who can build on our transformation and the opportunities ahead. With that, let me turn to the quarter. We delivered quarterly revenue of $772 million, above our guidance range, and grew our ARR 15% year-over-year to $2.63 billion. We also saw another quarter of solid free cash flow generation. In Q1, we continue to see success in the marketplace with our cloud platform. Our largest and most notable wins this quarter demonstrate the appeal of our solution to businesses that are looking to adopt hybrid multi-cloud operating models and deploy modern apps and AI workloads alongside traditional apps.

Increasingly, customers are looking to do this while retaining their existing hardware, including servers and external storage. Our largest win in the quarter with a North American-based Fortune 100 provider of financial services reflects ongoing traction with our solutions supporting external storage. This customer chose the Nutanix Cloud Platform to run their business-critical applications, including SQL databases and virtual desktops, and plans to utilize their existing Dell PowerFlex storage arrays going forward. During Q1, we also saw significant wins on our solutions supporting Dell's PowerStore, Everpure and NetApp, which became generally available at the end of the quarter.

On the new logo front, our largest win in Q1 was with a North American-based medical technology company looking to replace their incumbent vendor. They selected the Nutanix Cloud Platform for their business-critical VM workloads, along with our Nutanix Kubernetes Platform for their cloud-native and AI applications. Going forward, they also plan to use NC2 on Azure to extend workloads into the public cloud. We believe wins like this reinforce that when enterprises modernize their IT, they view Nutanix as a complete future-ready partner. Another win with the government agency in the APJ region also reflects traction we are seeing with customers using our platform for AI. This customer chose the Nutanix Cloud Platform to establish an internal GPU-as-a-Service offering.

They plan to run multiple AI applications, including video analytics and vision language models on this service. On the investment side, we completed our acquisition of Ryax Technologies in Q1. We plan to incorporate Ryax's GPU utilization and smart scheduling technology into our platform to enable greater efficiency and resource utilization for AI and cloud-native workloads. We also saw strength in our service provider business in Q1, signing several 7-figure deals with managed service provider partners across the Americas and EMEA regions. We view this performance as validation of the investments we've made to enhance our platform's multi-tenant and operational capabilities for service providers. Finally, our platform continued to receive industry recognition in the first quarter.

Nutanix was named a leader in the 2026 Gartner Magic Quadrant for Distributed Hybrid Infrastructure, our third consecutive year, and a challenger in the Gartner Magic Quadrant for Container Management. Notably, Gartner also recognized Nutanix as a leader in their new Server Virtualization Magic Quadrant, positioning us highest in ability to execute. We believe these recognitions reflect what we're seeing in the market. The Nutanix Cloud Platform has become a preferred destination for enterprise customers seeking a proven, seamless alternative to legacy virtualization providers. In closing, our business performed solidly in the first quarter, including ARR growth of 15% year-over-year and solid free cash flow performance. I believe the fundamentals of our business remain healthy.

We remain focused on delighting our customers while driving sustainable, profitable growth. And with that, I'll hand it over to Rukmini Sivaraman. Rukmini?

Rukmini Sivaraman: Thank you, Rajiv. I am grateful for your many years of leadership. And thank you, everyone, for joining us today. I will first start with our Q1 '27 results, then provide guidance for Q2 '27 and an updated view of our full year fiscal year '27 outlook. In Q1, we reported results that were above the high end of the range for all guided metrics. In Q1, we reported record quarterly revenue of $772 million, higher than the guided range of $755 million to $765 million and the year-over-year growth rate of 15%. ARR at the end of Q1 was $2.633 billion, representing year-over-year growth of 15%.

NRR, our net dollar-based retention rate at the end of Q1, was 105%, down slightly quarter-over-quarter. In Q1, average billings contract duration was 3.4 years. Non-GAAP gross margin in Q1 was 88.5%. Non-GAAP operating margin in Q1 was a quarterly record of 32.1%, higher than our guided range of 26% to 28%. Our margin performance this quarter benefited from a favorable confluence of small operational efficiencies across multiple areas rather than a single outsized driver. Non-GAAP net income in Q1 was $216 million and fully diluted EPS was $0.73 per share based on fully diluted weighted average shares outstanding of approximately 295 million shares.

GAAP net income and fully diluted GAAP EPS in Q1 were $144 million and $0.49 per share, respectively. Free cash flow performance in Q1 was good at $209 million, representing a free cash flow margin of 27%. Moving to the balance sheet. We ended Q1 with cash, cash equivalents and short-term investments of $2.468 billion, up from $2.361 billion at the end of Q4. Moving to capital allocation. In Q1, we repurchased $50 million worth of common stock under our authorization. We also used about $74 million of cash to retire shares related to our employees' tax liability for their quarterly RSU vesting. Together, these actions helped manage share dilution. Moving to guidance.

Our guidance for Q2 '27 is as follows: revenue of $820 million to $830 million; non-GAAP operating margin of 27% to 28%; fully diluted weighted average shares outstanding of approximately 295 million shares. Moving to the full year. Our updated guidance for fiscal year '27 is as follows: revenue of $3.18 billion to $3.23 billion, unchanged from our prior guidance; non-GAAP operating margin of 24.5% to 25.5%, an increase of 50 basis points from our prior guidance; free cash flow of $875 million to $975 million, an increase of $25 million from our prior guidance and representing a free cash flow margin of 29% at the midpoint.

I will now provide a few points to note regarding our full year guidance. First, the assumptions I highlighted in our last earnings call about our robust market opportunity and growth drivers, server supply constraints, future start dates and growth in our renewal ACV cohort remain largely unchanged. Second, a note on revenue seasonality. We expect Q3 revenue to be seasonally down quarter-over-quarter by mid- to high single-digit percent relative to our Q2 guidance, a higher percentage than in the last couple of years, but in line with the years before that. Our quarter-to-quarter revenue seasonality can be affected by a number of factors, including revenue contributions from deals booked in prior quarters and business available to renew seasonality.

Finally, a reminder that the assumptions that I mentioned in the last earnings call regarding billings and free cash flow also remain largely unchanged. In closing, we are pleased to have exceeded all of our guided metrics for Q1 in a dynamic environment. I'd like to thank our customers, shareholders and partners for your continued support and our employees for their hard work in achieving these results. With that, operator, please open the line for questions.

Operator: [Operator Instructions] The first question today will be coming from the line of Sanjit Singh of Morgan Stanley.

Sanjit Singh: Rajiv, congrats on an awesome run at Nutanix. To pick up on that point, I was wondering if you could just give me a sense of why you think it now is the right time to have a change in leadership. And to the extent you'll be involved in finding your successor, what are some of the criteria that you think would be most important as we go into this next year of the company?

Rajiv Ramaswami: Sure, Sanjit. And it's a very good question and of course, top of mind. So look, it's been 6 years here for me at Nutanix. And in some ways, we've built the second chapter of the company after the founding era and establishing the HCI space. If you look at the Chapter 2 of what we built together with the team, it's completing the journey to becoming a subscription company, transforming it to be profitable and growing, expanding the product portfolio quite significantly from HCI to a platform company that works across clouds, that supports external storage that has cloud-native capabilities and now moving into the future AI capabilities. And so we've done a fair bit of work.

Chapter 2 is well established at this point, and there's a lot of opportunity in terms of driving growth with Chapter 2. And I feel like we are in a very good place there. Now the next chapter, Chapter 3 is the next 5 years of the company. And that is the next transformation to be done, and that's about establishing Nutanix as the platform for AI. And so we are at the beginning of the journey. We've gotten a good start. There's a lot to do over the next 5 years. And that's why I feel like we are at an inflection point, where we've got this Chapter 2 that's fairly well established at this point.

Now we have to continue to execute for the next many years and quarters on it. But we really have to build Chapter 3 and do so in a significant way. And so this -- as I've been talking to the Board for a bit here about this as well in terms of our strategic direction and the timing for succession. And so we came to the conclusion together that this is perhaps the right time, right, so that we can bring somebody in and also that we want to announce it ahead of time as we look for the appropriate next leader. And what do we expect of that person?

We want the person to really scale this journey, right, that we've been on already and really establish Nutanix, not only continue what we're doing, but also build on top of it to really build Nutanix as the AI platform company.

Sanjit Singh: I appreciate the thoughts, Rajiv. And then as a follow-up, Rukmini, when I look at the guide for the prior 2 years, I think last year, you guys had actually lowered the guide given the dynamic environment around the server supply chain issues. I think in fiscal year '25, you had reiterated the guide in Q1. So seeing you reiterated the guide, I guess, is not too much of a surprise. When you look at some of the metrics this quarter, I look at the customer adds were a little bit lower than last quarter and last year's Q1. The NRR ticked down.

I just want to get a sense of whether that's any sort of seasonal Q1 impact or anything that's poised to linger for the balance of the year.

Rukmini Sivaraman: Thank you, Sanjit. So yes, on the first question about the revenue guide. So you're right that it is early in the fiscal year. And we -- typically, as you alluded to, we did this in fiscal year '25 and prior years, we typically do not raise the full year revenue guidance after Q1, and there's still a lot to go and many variables to consider. So we're happy to have raised our operating margin and free cash flow guidance for the year and kept our revenue guidance unchanged. And then to -- I think your part of your other question was around new logos and NRR.

So on new logos, we believe that, that performance is affected by some reallocation we did in Q1. So we had a higher-than-normal reallocation of our customer and prospect accounts in Q1. And that had a bit of an impact on the new logo addition. We believe the impact of this is temporary and largely behind us, and we expect new logos to be up quarter-over-quarter going into Q2. And then the last bit, there's a lot of questions in there that you phrased, Sanjit. So the last bit on NRR, you're right, NRR did tick down slightly quarter-over-quarter, as I said in my prepared remarks.

And that, as we've talked about, was impacted by some factors we've discussed before, like our ASPs of new logos have been increasing over time, which means that it creates a bit of a headwind on expansion growth rate, which is reflected in NRR. This NRR is also impacted directionally by overall bookings performance in Q1. And of course, we continue to remain focused on driving adoption and expansion of our solutions within our customer base, and that continues to be a focus. But NRR can move around from quarter-to-quarter because of the factors I mentioned.

Operator: Our next question will be coming from the line of Jim Fish of Piper Sandler.

James Fish: Rajiv, it was great working with you and best of luck in your future endeavors. Maybe just as we think about the fiscal '29 Analyst Day targets that you guys referenced about 6 months ago now, a lot of the growth was dependent on AI and containers and a lot of the prepared remarks here, we're kind of talking about the traditional blocking and tackling around hyper-converged, including within VDI and database penetration. So, I guess my first question is really, how should we think about application penetration beyond VDI and database at this point? And secondly, how is the attach been trending on that AI and container base side of the story?

Rajiv Ramaswami: Yes. I think both -- to me, Jim, the future definitely is preparing for a world of cloud native and AI. And our cloud-native business is certainly coming along very nicely and growing very nicely year-over-year. Lots of good traction. In fact, we have been calling out NKP in prior quarters. On AI, I'd say that our -- we believe we have good product market fit at this point. In fact, one of the larger deals this quarter was very much driven by AI workloads, right? This government agency in Asia Pacific that we talked about, for example, using us as the platform for them to deliver AI internally, right, to all their customers.

So this is -- so we are starting to see good traction as customers and enterprises start using AI, it's still early days on that front, and that's the next transformation that we talked about. We are seeing more and more interest in open-weight models in terms of people using open-weight models as a counter to frontier models and starting to run them whether it be in their own environment or whether it be neoclouds or even on bare metal hyperscalers. So we do, I think, have a really good set of opportunities here to address, and we're seeing good traction. The AI numbers are still relatively small, but growing nicely.

And so to me, in addition to all the mission critical workloads, by the way, we highlight some VDI and so forth, but -- databases. But today, we are already at a point where we're running pretty much all enterprise mission-critical workloads, right? We can do complete transformation of anything that was running, let's say, on a legacy environment onto endemic environment, and increasingly, these very same customers are looking to use us for cloud native, new workloads and AI workloads.

James Fish: Got it. And then VMware introduced that essentials or express package that kind of lower end of the market, have you seen any change then as a result to your pipeline as a result? Or can you kind of talk about how that could be impacting you here on the net new customers?

Rajiv Ramaswami: Yes. So I think it's too early to tell on that. By the way, they just introduced it, vSphere Essentials Kit, I believe it's called. And this is kind of largely a market that they are not focused on, right, before. So we have to see how it does. But so far, it has not had any impact really and it's too early, but they just put it out there. We are fairly strong, and we are working to become even stronger in that segment of the market. Where, you know, this is more targeted at the lower end of our customer base, what I would call Tier 3 customers in our pyramid of sales.

And so Nutanix actually has a strong offering now with both HCI and external storage and being able to support a broader set of external storage platforms out there, even at the low end, a lot of that is IP attached, not necessarily fiber channel attached. So it starts playing to our strength. So it's too early going back to your question on VMware on that offering to make any judgment about how it's doing.

Operator: Our next question will be coming from the line of Matt Martino of Goldman Sachs.

Matthew Martino: Rajiv, thanks for the partnership and congrats on a nice run here. Maybe just one on continuity for the CEO search, given the number of initiatives underway across the portfolio and the go-to-market organization, how are you thinking about maintaining execution through the transition? And should we expect the strategic priorities you laid out at the Investor Day to remain consistent?

Rajiv Ramaswami: Yes. We have no plans to change any of the strategic priorities at this point, Matt. And I'm going to be here fully engaged continue to drive business as usual. I'm here on the call. I'll be here running the company still and help identify and onboard the new successor and help afterwards in an advisory capacity as well. So the idea here is to make this in terms of as continuous and as seamless as possible and not really miss a beat when it comes to execution here, both across products and across GTM.

Matthew Martino: Great. And then for either you or Rukmini just on server availability, can you just give us an update on server availability and lead times or conditions broadly in line with your planning assumptions? And are customers changing deployment timing, vendor selection or architectural decisions in response?

Rajiv Ramaswami: Yes. Maybe I'll take a crack and Rukmini, you can add on. So I think the lead times, I would say, for servers have stabilized. And depending on the configuration, some still have extended lead time, some will have shorter lead times. It tends to vary, very dramatically week by week, month by month. Pricing remains elevated. That has not changed at all, right? I mean there's still a huge shortage in memory. There's still a significant shortage of CPUs. And so we're still seeing significant pricing uplifts in the market, right? They are -- I mean, pricing uplift at this point are incremental compared to the big rise we saw over the last year.

But nevertheless, we look at that as a headwind. Now for us, while that's a headwind on the one front, some of it we are able to offset, of course, with all the alternatives that we have in place, the ability for us to sell our software to customers where they can use us without requiring them to change hardware, whether it be on, say, somebody else's HCI infrastructure or whether it be with external storage and the subset of external storage that we support, which is, of course, not yet complete, recall that we support IP storage and within that, we support Dell, Everpure and now NetApp as well, which went GA this last quarter.

So we still look at that and offer some of that more customers also using us in the public cloud now where they can get capacity faster than what they can get on-prem servers for.

Operator: Our next question will be coming from the line of Radi Sultan of UBS.

Radi Sultan: Rajiv, it's been a real pleasure. Maybe first, I've been hearing more 7-figure ACV new logo lands for external storage just in some of my own work. And so I'm just curious, are you seeing the more recent external storage new logos landing at higher ACVs than last year when you first rolled out external storage.

Rajiv Ramaswami: In fact, one of our largest wins this quarter was exactly that. It was with PowerFlex, right, customers using us with PowerFlex. And it was a significant large win for us. So yes, I mean, if you look at like certainly, right? I mean, external storage represents about 80% of the deployed infrastructure out there. Especially at the larger customers and the larger customers tend to have bigger estates and therefore, larger deal opportunities for us. And so we have a good pipeline of external storage opportunities. And now we've got Dell, PowerFlex, PowerStore. NetApp now coming on board, of course, and Pure, we're doing quite well with Pure together as well. So yes, no doubt about it.

It opens the door at these larger accounts where spending the time that they don't want to go change out their hardware. So it's certainly reflective of the fact that we do have quite a few large deals in that area.

Radi Sultan: Awesome. And then for Rukmini, could you just unpack the Q3 seasonality a bit more? How much is just the available to renew cohort? And then is this Q3 seasonality, what we should expect going forward? Or is this a dynamic very specific to the cohort this year?

Rukmini Sivaraman: Sure. Radi. So yes, the reason I called out the Q3 seasonality is because it is a little different from what we've seen in the last couple of years, but it is in line with the years before that, Radi. So it can move around somewhat from year to year. And I think the other thing I would say is that when I look at Q3 or any quarter-to-quarter variation, it can depend on orders that were booked in prior periods, but revenue showing up in the current quarter that can move those quarters around. So that's one factor. And then just how we see the -- the available to renew pool that's coming in.

And I believe your question was on the point I made about Q3 seasonality relative to Q2, correct, did I answer that? Is that your question, Radi?

Rukmini Sivaraman: Okay. Okay. Good. Yes. So that's what I'd call out. I think the reason we mentioned it was because it's a little bit different from the last couple of years. And to me, it's nothing more than just timing of when deals come in, when they show up in revenue and then a little bit of how the available to renew pool flowing into revenue.

Operator: Our next question will be coming from the line of Howard Ma of Guggenheim.

Howard Ma: I have two. My first one is, your calculated RPO bookings was down about 2% year-on-year. Is that due to server supply constraints and deal timing? Or was it other factors? It's because given the confluence of near-term growth catalysts like the external storage partnerships and more mature AI and Kubernetes portfolio. I'm just trying to understand the disconnect between the qualitative and the in-quarter bookings performance or if it was just timing.

Rukmini Sivaraman: Yes, Howard. So first, we believe that the overall environment is healthy. And as you alluded to, lots of drivers, even in our own business in addition to the overall demand environment that we believe is healthy overall. Now to your question, bookings in Q1, like you alluded to, which you all can calculate from an RPO bookings perspective, bookings in Q1 declined slightly year-over-year. And we believe that, that booking performance was affected by the higher-than-normal reallocation of accounts that I talked about in Q1, reallocation of customer and prospect accounts. And we believe the impact of that is temporary and largely behind us.

And then the other point that I'll make is that we also had fewer than expected large deals closing in Q1. And as we've said before, the timing of those large deals can vary from quarter-to-quarter. One other point that is worth noting here is that our software bookings expectations for the full year are largely unchanged compared to 3 months ago, and that is underpinned by a strong pipeline of large deals, the grow momentum with external storage and growth in cloud native and AI solutions that we've been talking about here.

Howard Ma: Okay. Great. And a follow-up either for you or Rajiv is how would you describe your pipeline visibility and the granularity of targeting Broadcom, VMware migrations I guess today versus a year ago? And if there are any additional go-to-market investments that you need to make to accelerate the migrations this year?

Rajiv Ramaswami: Maybe I'll start, and Rukmini can continue. So we -- that's a big chunk of our pipeline, right? It's hard to -- we've always said, it's hard to distinguish between what's -- just a pure Broadcom takeout initiative versus just a normal looking for modernization, et cetera. But there's still a lot out there of customers looking to migrate away, and these tend to be full-fledged migrations. And so if you look at what we've been doing, both from a product and go-to-market perspective, we continue to make that easier and easier for our customers.

I would say the biggest single thing that we've done over the last year has been supporting the external storage arrays, right, because that allows the customers to do in place migration with their existing hardware. And we are -- our solutions have been in the market for some period now, but still very much early and ramping, right? We've had Pure for a few quarters now, PowerFlex are a bit longer than that. PowerStore a little less than that, and NetApp now just became generally available. So that, I think, is a big unlock in terms of being able to go out there and get to a good subset.

It's still not the full set, but it's still a good subset of the installed base out there that we can now go and help customers migrate. The actual migration for a long time has been fairly easy to do once we have everything set up, it's a lot of it is automated. So we've done that work already. We've got the professional services, both with us and our channel partners going for quite a while. So to me, it's more getting -- working with the pace of customers, get customers to plan ahead of time so that they get time to go plan and deploy and get their migrations done before their next renewal cycle.

Rukmini Sivaraman: Yes. Ruplu, you're right, that is embedded in the guide to your point, a significant ramp in operating expenses throughout the course of the year, Ruplu. Operator: Our next question will come from the line of Param Singh of Oppenheimer & Co.

Paramveer (Param) Singh: First of all, Rajiv, it was great working with you over the last few years. You're definitely going to be missed. I did have a couple of questions here. And then I had a follow-up.

Rukmini Sivaraman: Param, I think I heard you say that more growth -- the growth discrepancy between product and support, is that the question?

Paramveer (Param) Singh: Yes. I mean if I just look at product revenue growth last quarter versus this quarter and your outperformance also seemed to be coming more from support and services in 1Q versus products. So I wanted to understand the dynamic behind that, Rukmini.

Rukmini Sivaraman: Sure. Yes. I think first, I'll start by saying that we don't run the business this way, right? The way we look at the business is ultimately on subscription revenue and professional services, which we also give you break out for. And the reason for that is product is mainly upfront. So when we -- depending on what we're recognizing in any given quarter, the product can move around, as you know, because it's -- the TCV of that is taken upfront, and that can vary with duration. So it does move around from quarter-to-quarter and year-over-year. Support, on the other hand, is ratable over time.
